speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It exposed the shortcomings and weaknesses of the systems.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On the other hand, it made practices that used to be impossible, possible now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was a jolt to the core of all our systems.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the pandemic dust settles, many health authorities are now in a reflective, in a soul-searching mode, rethinking how to improve their healthcare systems.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, for Indonesia, I am constantly in touch with the Health Minister and they are making a big effort to strengthen the accessibility to healthcare services throughout the archipelago.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: New Zealand is strengthening central national healthcare planning, to reduce the pressure on specialist and hospital care on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The UK is making a renewed push in integrated care between social and healthcare organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And just yesterday, we just heard Hong Kong is also doing a deep healthcare reform effort.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As for Singapore, we are embarking on a long-term and profound reform effort.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And there are two important considerations in driving this reform.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To reduce the disease burden and preserve the quality of life of our people in the coming years, we have to become healthier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, our COVID-19 response showed that as a people, each of us are prepared to do our part, have each other's backs and work together to fend off the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The things we do during the pandemic – vaccinations, tests, self-isolation – and these are all preventive care in action.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We found ways to integrate preventive care with acute care in hospitals, in our treatment facilities and with home recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We did surveys, focus group discussions and in-depth one-on-one interviews as well.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this engagement, we did not present our stakeholders with a blank canvas and ask them what we should do to improve health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, we presented a broad plan, a concept of what we planned to do.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And then, we asked them – looking at this, what is missing?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I want to say a few thank yous.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, thanks to all our stakeholders for their contribution.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I think they realised that this is a very important exercise, a very important reform, possibly the most significant in decades.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I want to especially mention about 50 family doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are from the College of Family Physicians Singapore, Singapore Medical Association, our Primary Care Networks, polyclinics and the National General Practitioners Advisory Panel.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They devoted a lot of time and energy in working with us in designing Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They meet almost every week, over weekends, on top of running their clinics.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I would also like to extend my appreciation to the many healthcare practitioners and partners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They range from nurses, allied health professionals, pharmacists, people who work for community organisations, unions, grassroots leaders, employers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They shared their views and contributed their ideas.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last but not least, I also want to thank the officers of MOH, who did a lot of the coordination, the staffing, the drafting and the preparatory work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I know they are very proud of being part of this co-creation effort with all our partners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One, I will go through, very briefly, the salient features of Healthier SG as a recap.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two, explain what this means to the two most important sets of stakeholders – residents and General Practitioners (GPs).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Three, I will speak more about its budget and financial implications, as this is only briefly covered in the White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One, to recap, there are five key components to Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We want to mobilise them to build strong relationships with their patients and play a bigger role in preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These will be developed between doctors and patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The health plan comprises an overview of the health status of the resident, the health goals to achieve and an action plan, which can include going for essential health screenings and vaccinations, and changes to your lifestyles.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This whole area is what we call "social prescriptions".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And doctors are saying that "social prescriptions" are often more important than drug prescriptions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This brings us to the third component, which is community partners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It may not be easy to follow diet or exercise advice and improve lifestyles by ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of us have tried, but to no avail.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we will draw on the effort of agencies such as Health Promotion Board (HPB), People's Association (PA) and SportSG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are organising many health-related activities on the ground, to create that supportive environment to help us change.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, each resident chooses the family doctor or clinic you wish to build a long-term preventive care relationship with.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And from there, we begin our journey towards better health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need the right IT systems, manpower and financing structure to make Healthier SG work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are in the background, but a lot of work has gone into these and they are extremely important.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The greatest impact is that residents will receive much stronger support to stay healthy and prevent any existing illnesses from worsening further.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we are making a big effort to support you, because it is almost human instinct to not do the right thing because of instant gratification. "Have a puff to destress now, worry about health later"; "eat the cheesecake now, worry about sugar later"; "eat the fried chicken now, it is very nice"; "laze around instead of exercising"; "binge watch Korean drama instead of having a good night's sleep".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Nothing bad will happen immediately or next day, but they accumulate to cause serious diseases, or can aggravate existing illnesses later.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Every grain of sand you keep dropping will become a bucket.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And, by then, it will be a big burden.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It can cost us, our organs, our limbs, our minds, our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To be on dialysis means you need to visit the NKF centre three times a week, each time five to six hours.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And the staff told me, that most patients there at NKF regret not correcting their diets and lifestyles while they could.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But now, it is too late to reverse.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have to live with dialysis the rest of their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, let us try to live without regrets.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can still enjoy many things in life, especially the good food – the char kway teow, the prata, the mee rebus, the occasional bubble tea with less sugar – just everything in moderation and without overindulging.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we will find joy in exercising, especially with friends.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will be able to snub out smoking or Juuling and not miss them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The support to residents – we must support residents to do all these.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first and most significant form of support is your long-term relationship with the family doctor.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And research has shown people with a dedicated family doctor are much less likely to develop serious illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Your enrolment with a dedicated family doctor is, therefore, a critical first step.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, since the release of the White Paper, there have been a few concerns on enrolment, and I might as well clarify them in this opening speech.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some residents are worried that once you choose a doctor, it is a final decision that cannot be reversed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not to worry, we recognise that there are times when a resident needs to change their doctor, either because they have moved houses, or have found a more suitable doctor.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And so, we have provided the flexibility for residents to change your enrolled doctor.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Nevertheless, when the time comes, please make your choice carefully and consciously.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Other residents are worried that once they enrol with a doctor, they cannot see other doctors – banned – including specialists that they are now seeing because of their chronic illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, please be assured that this would not happen.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You are free to continue to visit all other doctors, including your specialists.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But please choose one to be your dedicated family doctor whom you trust, who knows your conditions well and can work with you to practise preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the same vein, some residents are worried that their regular GP may become so popular that they get squeezed out by the demand.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will try our best to manage this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the enrolment process, there will be a dropdown list.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The doctor you regularly visit will be at the top for you.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, that will give you an edge over your "competitors".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we are working with GP networks and polyclinics to let us know who their regular patients are in order to facilitate this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are also doing this in stages, so that enrolment demand will not be so overwhelming, overnight.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You may also want to enrol early when the time comes to "chope" your regular GP.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are recommended for the general population and will be free.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Those with specific risk factors may be referred for further tests.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And there are more complex screenings, like colonoscopy, which is an invasive procedure and not appropriate to be made a standard screening for everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Although it is not free, it will continue to be heavily subsidised at our hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These changes are somewhat of a departure from most Government subsidy schemes, where some co-payment from residents is often required to reflect the sharing of responsibility and uphold the concept of individual effort.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Here, we have decided that since preventive care is very fundamental to healthcare, further subsidy is justified.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It does not contradict the principle of personal responsibility, because in the context of preventive care, personal responsibility and action are needed to make changes and lead a healthier life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fourth, we will enhance the subsidy for common chronic disease drugs at private GP clinics.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many residents gave feedback that there is a significant drug price differential between the GP clinic and the polyclinic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, even if they wanted to stick to one family doctor at a GP clinic, when it comes to taking medications, they will go back to the polyclinic where medication is cheaper.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This benefit will be available to all enrolled Singaporean CHAS card holders, including Pioneer Generation (PG) and Merdeka Generation (MG) card holders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I should add a small caveat, which is that the basis of calculating subsidies at polyclinics and for CHAS are different.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fifth, we have roped in important community partners, such as PA, SportSG, HPB and others, to organise more health-related activities for residents, from ball games and brisk walking; to Zumba classes and community gardening.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, while you may see your enrolled doctor only once or twice a year, outside of the clinic, you are not alone.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are enhancing public infrastructure like sports facilities, parks and park connectors, and community partners will support your active lifestyle.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many residents who already participate in the National Steps Challenge and the Eat Drink Shop Healthy Challenge are familiar with the Healthy 365 app.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is your virtual champion to nudge you to be healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The app awards Healthpoints for living an active lifestyle and making healthier food purchases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It does not just clock steps but also tracks physical activity through your heart rate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You may be dancing, lifting weights, doing community gardening, doing Zumba, Healthy 365 do not exactly know what you are doing, but it knows your heart rate is higher and from there, it derives that you are physically active and will award Healthpoints accordingly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthpoints can be exchanged for a range of rewards, such as public transport and many participating merchants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The reward is not large, but it has a way to give us psychological satisfaction that, "I have accomplished this exercise".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And it is a very effective nudge, especially when gamified.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, it will be able to track your calorie intake.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, you take a picture of your char kway teow and then, it will match against our database of different food and your calorie intake, and will monitor your calorie intake.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But you have to take honest pictures – do not just keep taking photos of vegetables!

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have also made Healthy 365 compatible with more popular digital health apps like Apple Health Kit, Fitbit and Samsung Health – all these are already compatible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will try to link it up with other commercial digital health apps.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That way, your lifestyle data captured by these commercial apps can be ingested into Healthy 365 and you can claim Healthpoints.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I should mention in this House that I do notice some of our Members have become a lot fitter visibly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I noticed Mr Desmond Choo over the months, big change.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And my Second Minister for Health Masagos Zulkifli.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think they should be Healthier SG ambassadors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To summarise: a dedicated doctor, a health plan with social prescriptions, full subsidy for nationally recommended vaccinations and health screening, full use of MediSave for chronic disease management, enhanced subsidy for common chronic drugs at GP clinics, more community lifestyle activities, more Healthpoints for leading a healthy life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They all come together, complement each other, to support residents to take personal responsibility and action to embark on their healthy life journeys.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second important group of stakeholders are our family doctors, from both polyclinics as well as private GP clinics.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will find themselves at the centre of this strategic long-term healthcare transformation plan.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: GPs need to earn a living by running their clinics.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must make sure that Healthier SG works for them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, from the time we conceived Healthier SG, we were very mindful that it should not take business away from GPs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, GPs will continue to attend to their existing patients and prescribe medication to them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What Healthier SG does is to enlarge their client pool, through enrolment for preventive and chronic care consultations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In line with this, GPs should be fairly compensated by MOH for their effort and advice in delivering preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This service fee is what we will describe loosely as a "capitated payment".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That means we do not pay the GP for every consultation, every test, every prescription and every service they provide.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, we pay them a standard fee, which is a base, per enrolled patient for maintaining a long-term relationship with the patient.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will cover the regular check-ins, ensuring the residents adhere with their health plans, the associated administrative work and also, reviewing the health plan annually.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is over and above subsidies for health screening and medication, which are separately funded.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For the Government, this method of payment and subsidy is not new.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is largely how we fund education, where polytechnics and universities receive a standard amount of budget per student.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even though some students take more classes or some students participate in more subsidised activities than others, we pay an average standard budget.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For GPs, it is also not a new concept.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: GPs who assist our healthcare clusters to manage complex chronic patients get a "Care Plus" service fee payment today of $100 per patient.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthier SG will broaden such schemes to cover preventive care for large segments of the population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And the fee will be similar or higher than the current Care Plus fee, depending on the health conditions of the enrolled residents.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We estimate that in the coming few years, Healthier SG service fees and revenue from subsidised services can grow as more residents enrol and become a significant component of the GPs' annual revenue – maybe a quarter or a third.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hand on heart, MOH has always been a very fair and prompt as a service buyer and I assure GPs that we will continue to be so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What MOH may not be very good at, is to minimise your administrative workload.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is unfortunately inevitable, as we need medical data of patients to be captured in our national health record system and paperwork is needed for payment claims.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will try our best to ease this administrative workload.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some GPs also do not have IT systems to support Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some are still largely using pen and paper.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH will also provide a grant to each GP clinic to help them be IT-ready for Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthier SG requires a lot of effort and resources to set up.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We spend about 6% of our healthcare budget on preventive care annually, such as to fund HPB.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With Healthier SG, in the coming few years, we will, and we want to grow this, perhaps to double the share of total healthcare spending.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In making these investments, our primary motivation is to reduce disease burden and the suffering of people and their loved ones.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Will there also be a financial payback, in terms of reducing healthcare spending in future?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will be good if this comes about, but it is too early to give a realistic estimate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because any impact in health of people would not happen immediately.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The impact will, perhaps, be discernible eight or 10 years down the road.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even so, we cannot reverse the rise in healthcare spending.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is not possible with an ageing population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What we can hope for is to slow down the rate of increase of healthcare spending.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, our national healthcare expenditure is expected to be about $22 billion a year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If this national medical bill, instead of tripling, doubles in the next 10 years, we would have saved much more than what we are planning to spend on preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the heart of Healthier SG is a philosophy of how we choose to live our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we put in a small effort every day, a bit of discipline every week, a bit of restraint every week, we can avoid big, life-changing suffering later.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can illustrate this logic from a personal perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Earlier on, I talked about the kidney dialysis patients at NKF and how they regretted not taking preventive action earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If they had practised preventive care, it would have cost them very little, in terms of effort and money.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They may have to see their GPs periodically for advice, moderate their food and sugar intake, which actually saves money, and take some medication as needed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when the disease is allowed to go out of control and dialysis is required, it costs about $25,000 a year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Taxpayers and donors have to help them foot the bill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the bigger cost, and what we are most concerned about, is the personal suffering.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some residents say, "I prefer not to do preventive care now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I prefer not to do health screening now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because if I know, I need to do something about it and the bill can be expensive".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I really hope we do not have such a mentality because even if you choose not to know now, the disease will make sure you know later.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And when the disease makes sure you know later, it will be even more expensive – not just in monetary terms, but in suffering, for you and your loved ones.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, since March this year, MOH has engaged more than 6,000 individuals through various channels to garner their views on Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These have contributed to the final White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When we consulted the public, we did not start from scratch.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We presented our thinking and implementation concepts on the Healthier SG strategy, and sought the public's views on their concerns, questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Through this process, we also realised our blind spots.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And from the public feedback, we were able to ensure that the plan will be more comprehensive, more effective and more practical.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The White Paper articulates how we will help Singaporeans to become healthier through various ways.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As to which doctor or clinic, they will have a choice.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will also have the flexibility to change doctors after enrolment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I would also like to clarify that family doctors under Healthier SG are not limited to those from private clinics but will also include doctors from polyclinics.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Seniors who currently visit polyclinics regularly can continue to do so and there is no need for them to transfer to a private clinic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These include subsidies for MOH-recommended screenings and vaccinations, and consultation fees for regular preventive care services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government will provide full subsidies for these healthcare services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means that you do not have to pay; the Government will pay in full for you.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, many Singaporeans already have chronic illnesses, and they use their MediSave to pay for the relevant treatments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Under the current regulations, they have to co-pay part of the fees.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many Singaporeans are already actively participating in the National Steps Challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Besides walking, if individuals engage in other activities, such as ball games, dancing, gardening or other workouts, they will also be rewarded.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With digital technology, there will also be rewards for eating healthily.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Hokkien, we say this is "wu jia go wu gia", which means "to have something to eat and also something to take away".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some people might think that going for check-ups, receiving vaccinations and seeing a doctor regularly are not necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We often hear stories about individuals, for example, a friend who smokes a packet of cigarettes a day and consumes fatty meat every week, but still lives to a ripe old age of 90.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The "winners" who lead unhealthy lifestyles without suffering from health issues are definitely in the extreme minority, who "struck the lottery".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we all know that out of those who bet on the lottery every week, the vast majority would lose money and only the rare few wins something.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In general, those who live unhealthily tend to end up as "losers", and the risk of falling ill is high.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we should not gamble with our health and our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In an earlier Lianhe Zaobao report, I came across a quote from Sun Simiao, a famous Tang dynasty physician, which I thought is very meaningful, and worthy of sharing here.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To him, a lower-skilled doctor can only treat a person's illness, a mediocre doctor can take care of a person's health and a superior doctor would be able to improve the health of the entire nation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Sun Simiao also said that an extremely capable doctor treats illnesses before they surface, a mediocre one treats an illness that is just starting, while a lower-skilled one treats an individual's known illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What Healthier SG aims to achieve is the vision of improving the health of the entire nation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthcare should not only depend on medicine but also on our lifestyle habits; it should not rely on hospitals but also the community; it should not just rely on doctors, but also on individuals and families.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Western medicine also has similar views on healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are two systems: one that emphasises the treatment of the disease and the individual, and the other, which is the population health system, seeks to improve the health of the nation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, both Western and Asian cultures have such concepts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthier SG is a long-term strategy that spans over many years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is an important turning point in Singapore's national healthcare policy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For MOH, this initiative is a heavy responsibility with far-reaching implications.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Its success requires the cooperation and effort of Singaporeans and the entire country.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthier SG involves a mindset change in the way we look at healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clinicians will need to constantly think of ways to prevent residents from falling sick, against instincts trained to treat as many suffering patients as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When conducting...health screening, we will have to deploy less precise but more scalable solutions, to identify residents...who have higher risks of falling ill." "Policy planners need to develop and evaluate programmes and initiatives across a multi-year Budget cycle, consciously investing in preventive care now to avoid years of pain and suffering later." "Every player needs to work closely, increasing the extent and depth of integration of their services." Unquote.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only by doing things differently and collectively can we achieve results beyond what traditional healthcare can deliver.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Western medicine, there is a distinction between different levels of health systems.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a higher level of health outcomes, going beyond what medical personnel alone can do but what a whole-of-society can achieve.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The saying, essentially, without translating it in detail, differentiates the outcomes of curative care, preventive care and population health.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Our heart rate goes up considerably at times.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It has been 57 years since Independence, six decades since MOH was set up during British colonial days – nearly a lifetime.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we should take stock, and ask ourselves, not just what comes next, but what if.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What if we reimagined our healthcare system today, anew?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Healthier SG is an important first step in this reimagining.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is an opportunity for a healthcare transformation, and I dare say, a healthcare revolution.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Earlier this year, during the debate on MOH's Budget, I called for change – a change agenda.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, speaking on Healthier SG, I will speak on helping residents and helping family doctors to help residents.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It was a central dogma for public healthcare financing in Singapore for many years, but we must judge policy – not based on dogma but whether it gets the job done, whether it achieves the desired goals.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The original idea for co-payment was to shape behaviour so that people look at the bill, consider what is value for money.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But what happens if co-payment discourages some residents from going for medically recommended screenings, medically recommended vaccinations, medically recommended treatments for chronic disease, even if the illness might become a bigger problem some years down the line and cause suffering that you cannot even put a price tag on?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In short, the behavioural nudge needs to be towards prevention and health, rather than a sludge that makes it harder to do what is necessary to prevent greater problems down the road.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We should make it as easy as possible for people to do the right thing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In our early days, with a young population, subsidy was very much centred on the acute hospitals.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Over the years, subsidy has become more and more decentralised so that care can be delivered with subsidy in the community, for chronic illness, closer to home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But with our ageing population, with seniors becoming less mobile, some finding it harder to go out, we also need to look at how care and, where needed, subsidy is delivered to patients and residents in the community – seeing through the eyes of our people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Ah Ma had been ill for some years – ill with a major stroke, bedbound, could not get out of the home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She was a PG Singaporean with a PG card but because she was not mobile, bedbound, she physically could not get to the polyclinic near her home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That meant she could not access the polyclinic care without a means test.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It meant she could not apply her PG card subsidies towards the remainder of the bill without having to go through a means test.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In contrast to an able-bodied Singaporean able to go to a polyclinic, walk in the door, access polyclinic care without means testing, and apply the PG card without means testing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The family engaged a home doctor from an established voluntary welfare organisation (VWO) for house calls, writing medicines, prescriptions on a piece of paper, a paper prescription.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The family would then bring the paper prescription to the nearby polyclinic and pay unsubsidised rates for the medication.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Had Ah Ma been physically mobile and able to get to the polyclinic in person, there would have been no such administrative hurdle.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we need to look at cases like this, see if there are ways to deliver care closer to patients' homes, and even have some medically necessary consultations in patient's homes, if needed.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And likewise, to see if the funding journey can be more straightforward for such home medical visits, where they are assessed to be medically necessary.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are also some Clementi seniors who have regular medical appointments at hospitals, needing blood tests.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They are wondering if some of these medically necessary tests can be done closer to home, or on occasion, at their homes, while still receiving some level of subsidy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It saves time waiting for some blood tests that may take several hours and it saves a trip back and forth, for blood tests that need to be done a few days before the medical appointment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because when a caregiver has to accompany a patient back and forth, the burden, the stress, the worry, does not just fall on the patient.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It falls on the caregiver who may have to take time-off from work and often it is the less well-off caregivers who have less bargaining power with the employer, less able to take time-off without worrying for the safety of their jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, for medically necessary treatments, Mr Speaker, we should look at how to bring the subsidy to the patient, if it helps prevent hospitalisations, reduce the burden of suffering, if it reduces the number of visits and the load on caregivers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is a broader point, Mr Speaker, how do we better support residents, and particularly, long-term patients, who continue living in the community and want to minimise visits to and from hospitals – patients with advanced neurological conditions like motor-neuron disease?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I asked a Parliamentary Question in Parliament yesterday but unfortunately; time ran out and I could not ask my supplementary question.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Look more closely at patient journeys, deeper at the challenges faced by caregivers, healthcare providers, seeing through the eyes of our people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: MOH has designated the Healthy 365 app as the "digital window" to programmes by PA, HPB, SportSG and other programmes as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But what happens for seniors who do not have a smartphone, who are not digital savvy, who are not quite comfortable using a smartphone app?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must make sure the digital window does not become a digital bottleneck.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There must be careful attention to ease of use, understanding what our seniors and elderly need and find easy to use.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Technology must serve, adapt and bend to the person, rather than getting people to bend to the technology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Seniors who feel left behind by digital change should not be treated as having fallen by the wayside, or not able to adapt.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just because a senior is not on a digital dashboard does not mean the senior is not there.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This must be in practice, not just in theory.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have met Clementi residents asking about what will happen at our national specialist centres that treat heart disease or cancer, for example.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A cancer patient might have lived in Tiong Bahru for many years but chooses to stay with a loved one in Jurong who can be caregiver while they undergo treatment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, she might want to see a specialist in the west, rather than in central Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some Clementi residents have asked: will it become harder to seek specialist care in a hospital outside your own geographical cluster?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to talk about care and how it takes time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Preventive care, chronic care, holistic care, it takes time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of these discussions are as much conversation as consultation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Talking with a patient that you have gotten to know over the years, understanding why they took up smoking, why it is hard to kick the habit, persuading them to make that change, for better health and to save their life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Talking with a senior who has just been discharged from hospital after an illness, helping that senior find hope and confidence again to go back to exercising and leading a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or making that time to be with a patient and a family through a difficult illness that may be getting worse, working through with the patient and family on what might be best in the difficult months and weeks or even days ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, it is so important for MOH to continue looking at what happens in the real world, understand how much time is needed to deliver holistic care and to support our healthcare workers and family doctors on that journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Paying family doctors to this important work, recognising the time needed is an important step.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It sends a message that the work must be done, is being done and needs to be recognised.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Will MOH also apply these important lessons to our public healthcare system too so that polyclinic doctors and healthcare workers can also be given more time, space and support to deliver that holistic preventive well-rounded care that we continue to work on and aspire to?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Healthier SG White Paper mentioned system enablers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We enable by making systems better, but this must also mean easier access, easier to navigate, fewer obstacles.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to talk about medical IT, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Earlier this year, I spoke on how across the public healthcare system alone, we have 14 million consultations each year.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And with more family doctors coming on board, connecting with the public sector IT system, it is all the more important that the IT continues to improve – enabling, empowering, not getting in the way.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even as the healthcare IT is enhanced, there must be attention to ease of use.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, people prefer paper records, manual processes, not because they are afraid of technology, but because they find that existing technology platforms are more cumbersome, that it takes more time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And in our design and implementation, we must continue looking at this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I previously called upon MOH to give this the same attention and focus, as the big firms do, like Apple and Google, because today, every patient, every healthcare practitioner knows how a well-designed IT platform from a major tech firm can do things.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And people will benchmark ease of use, elegance, against what the big firms do as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The White Paper mentions submission of patient data.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For capitation, Mr Speaker, MOH has said there will be a shift to capitation funding where clusters get a pre-determined fee for every resident assigned within a geographical area.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our people are what enables us to deliver care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Healthier SG means that the role of family doctors in the community will be ever more critical – doctors drawn from the community, serving, caring, looking after the community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, going upstream to ensure that no matter where you start in life, no matter your background, no matter whether your journey took longer or a detour, that your starting point never deters you from stepping forward on that journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I call upon MOH and this Government to provide the resources, energy and imagination to do what is necessary to keep our healthcare system fit for purpose today, for tomorrow and for a generation to come.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In February this year, the Member for Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC), Mr Leon Perera, made a very comprehensive Adjournment Motion speech on rethinking preventive health to generate better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Among his policy recommendations were for the Government to set short- and long-term targets for reducing the incidence of chronic diseases, encouraging more people to go for health screening by providing additional subsidies for MediShield Life premiums and nudging people to buy healthier food products providing a digital currency earmarked for their purchases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To its credit, MOH is now bringing preventive healthcare to the forefront of healthcare policy, through the Healthier SG programme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My speech today will focus on managing the cost of healthcare under Healthier SG, and measuring and improving the desired health outcomes of the programme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask the Minister if there will still be an annual MediSave withdrawal limit for chronic disease management?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: According to an answer to my Parliamentary Question, in 2019, some 15% of patients reached the $500 withdrawal limit – this is now being increased to $700 – most of whom had complex conditions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fifteen percent of patients in 2019 translates to about 20,000 patients in absolute numbers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These patients were restricted in the use of their own medical savings for chronic disease treatment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It could discourage them from seeking treatment for their conditions and lead to a further deterioration of their health.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could necessitate more expensive interventions down the road, like hospitalisations or amputations, which will drastically reduce their quality of life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will encourage residents with chronic diseases to see their doctor early and stay on with their disease management plan.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In answer to another Parliamentary Question that I filed, in 2018, about 563,500 local patients were seen at polyclinics for non-CDMP conditions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These patients were not eligible for the full subsidies and MediSave withdrawal allowances under CDMP.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Moving forward, under Healthier SG, can CDMP be expanded to all chronic diseases, so that more patients can benefit from it?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Polyclinic attendance has increased from under 410,000 10 years ago, to more than 550,000 in July 2022.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper acknowledged that many residents, especially retirees who no longer have company health plans, have been switching away from private family doctor clinics to polyclinics for their medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Cost is a factor in these decisions, with drug prices a key reason why medical treatment is often more expensive at GP clinics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I also note that a new subsidy tier for CHAS for common chronic drugs will be introduced.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore Citizens who are CHAS, PG or MG cardholders can opt to obtain these drugs at the private family doctor clinic which they have enrolled with.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the words "more comparable" suggest that CHAS, PG and MG cardholders will not necessarily enjoy the same low prices for drugs and medical consultations at private family doctor clinics as they do at polyclinics, let alone the other patients who are not eligible for these additional subsidies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister mentioned just now in his speech that the basis for computing subsidies for polyclinics and GPs is different, so the prices cannot be equalised to the last cent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, can the Minister confirm that the differences will only be in cents and not in dollars, or tens of dollars for each prescription?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am asking for these details because any price differentials will be a disincentive for Singaporeans from switching from polyclinics to family doctors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that Healthier SG aims to encourage residents to enrol with a family doctor by "narrowing the difference" in drug subsidies across polyclinics and private clinics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, how much can drug costs be brought down, without subsidising private GPs' profits, given that GPs also make a margin from the sale of prescription medication?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With all this in mind, it is my recommendation that residents who currently prefer seeking outpatient medical treatment at polyclinics should not be compelled to enrol with a private family doctor.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They should, however, remain with a polyclinic in the same healthcare cluster, so that their medical records can be shared with whichever doctor is attending to them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If, eventually, most residents enrol with private family doctors, can the Minister elaborate on what will be the role of polyclinics under Healthier SG?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government continue to build more polyclinics or will there be a reduction in polyclinic capacity as Healthier SG gets implemented?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A research study on childhood obesity published in the International Journal of Obesity found that early life risk factors increased childhood obesity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These risk factors included the father's obesity at 24 months after the child was born, the mother's pre-pregnancy obesity and excessive weight gain during pregnancy, short duration of breastfeeding and early introduction of solid foods.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The study found that early life and preconception intervention programmes may be more effective in preventing obesity if they concurrently address these risk factors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Another study by local researchers published in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth found that women interviewed had poor knowledge of the child health consequences of maternal obesity and were often unaware of reliable sources of health information.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is MOH looking to take a more preventive approach to maternal and child health?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, family doctors could take a more proactive approach in advising expectant mothers and young parents on healthy dietary habits for themselves and their children.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Healthy 365 app could also be used to provide more continuous guidance from healthcare professionals to women who are planning, undergoing and recovering from pregnancy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many habits are developed from a very young age and persist for the rest of our lives.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The benefits in terms of cost savings and health outcomes of preventive health initiatives for expectant mothers and children could, thus, be tremendous in the long term.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would now like to discuss more about the health outcomes under Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am glad to see that the White Paper has listed some short-term and long-term metrics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Without targets, these metrics hold much less meaning.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to the Minister's reply to these questions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The achievement of these targets should be closely monitored, so that adjustments can be made to better achieve them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given the huge investment in Healthier SG, the public should expect an improvement in both the short- and long-term metrics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Family doctors that accept enrolment should also be held to a high standard of quality and transparency.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They should publish their prices, bill sizes and clinical outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will allow residents to make informed decisions when choosing or switching to their enrolled family doctor.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Other non-clinical metrics should also be used to gauge them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These include the adoption of IT systems that make it easier for patients to make and change appointments, reducing waiting time and sharing of clinical data with other healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Good service quality would encourage patients to more regularly seek preventive health services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Last week, I received a phone call from a market research firm doing a survey on behalf of the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The pollster asked me to state the extent of my agreement: from strongly agree to strongly disagree, to statements like "Singapore is heading in the right direction", "the Government is managing Singapore well" and "I approve the way the Prime Minister is running the country".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This was not the first time I was surveyed this way.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But this time I was also asked a series of questions about healthcare financing, which was an uncanny coincidence given that it was only a week before today's debate in Parliament on healthcare.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The questions revolved around whether I was worried about being able to pay for my family's healthcare needs, currently and in the future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I must admit that the questions made me ponder about my own family's healthcare expenses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Individual healthcare expenses are unpredictable, and a large chunk of the costs are likely to come in the final years of life as a result of chronic conditions, many of which are preventable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Preventive healthcare aims to prevent illnesses, detect specific conditions early and encourage the promotion of good health.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Regular health screens, testing and healthy lifestyle counselling are but common features.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Globally, the incorporation of preventive healthcare in national plans is not new.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The United States, for instance, publishes 10-year Healthy People masterplans, five iterations now, to identify public health priorities to improve the health and well-being of the Americans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The latest is the Healthy People 2030 plan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But well-written plans may be, many people in the world, including the US, are still afflicted by poor health.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For the Healthier SG vision to come to pass successfully, we need to get the planning assumptions, strategies and execution right.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have several concerns to which I seek Ministry's consideration and responses.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, on mobilising a network of family doctors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The family doctor will consult, will develop a health plan, will conduct annual check-ins and help residents achieve their health goals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But, in practice, most residents only see a GP when they are ill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If GPs are the first to be tapped upon, then their transition from the role of a GP, just addressing someone's immediate needs, chop-chop and go, to that of a family doctor or physician – this transition, this journey cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Would there be prerequisite skillsets and dispositions that need to be considered?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Other than their intrinsic motivation to want to do good for their residents, would the financial incentive that Minister spoke about be sufficient to cover their time and their costs?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many Singaporeans also visit polyclinic doctors as their first port of call.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Working Singaporeans also tend to consult their employer's panel of doctors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How do these doctors become one's family doctor, if they may not be the same doctor who regularly attends to one?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These questions need to be answered and looked into.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Developing health plans for enrolled residents is one thing, but following up to ensure outcomes is another.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The White Paper correctly states, I quote, "while doctors can prescribe activities, it will only work if residents take personal ownership of their health and their lifestyles, and follow through with their health plans." The same challenges were also voiced by residents in the White Paper, quotes were given and validated also by many of our own lived experiences.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The move to take personal ownership for one's own health is far more complicated than just developing a health plan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are many theories of behavioural changes from time immemorial.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If not thought through carefully, the Healthier SG vision would really just remain a pipe dream.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What could be a highly effective combination of "inside-out", or intrinsic, and "outside-in", extrinsic intervention measures to address the needed change in mindsets and behaviours of residents?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How does the Ministry intend to address the first target group who are the senior residents above 60, who may be even more rigid in their mindsets and their behaviours?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Why is there little mention of upstream interventions when one is younger, such as those in schools, because that is when behaviours and mindsets are shaped?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Surely, upstream interventions in schools, through proper eating, proper exercising and emotional management are an important part of developing good health habits for life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And then, for the even more vulnerable, what is the Ministry's recommendation for younger Singaporeans who are disabled, who have special needs and who are prone to earlier onset of chronic illnesses due to a lack of education and care?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are best served by healthcare professionals who are a bit more aware, who are more trained of their conditions, such as, for example, Dr Chen Shi Ling and her doctors at Happee Hearts Movement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Who and how does the Ministry propose to include this group of residents and to fund doctors like Dr Chen?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Thirdly, on activation of community partners such as the HPB, Agency for Integrated Care (AIC), PA, SportSG and National Parks Board (NParks).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I agree totally with the White Paper that "patients' social, mental and physical well-being, are best achieved through community assets and services." My own lived experience on the ground, trying to coordinate all my well-intended service providers, for example, for the seniors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My experience is that although the different parties are all good community assets, with good hearts, many of their efforts are usually not well coordinated and they are not quite motivated sometimes to really work together.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They sometimes even "compete" for the same clientele.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Situations of, example, elderly residents being repeatedly served, because they are the ones who are more forthcoming, some are under-served or not even served.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will they, as integrators, better organise ground efforts without losing the passion and the resources of these precious community partners, for a Healthier SG?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, on setting up enablers for Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To justify that, I seek more clarity on the following levers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What would be needed to facilitate residents, as Dr Tan just mentioned, who are not tech-savvy, to use apps like Healthy 365, so that this group indeed is not left behind?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On performance indicators – the selection of performance indicators – whether process or outcome indicators, whether lagging or historical or leading indicators – this selection is never an easy task, even in the world of usual management and leadership.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What gets measured gets done, as they say.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But what gets measured and paid for, gets done even more.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Badly selected measures lead to unintended bad consequences.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I urge a further scrutiny and discussion on the White Paper's proposed key indicators.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many countries have done it, many developed countries have tried with varying degrees of success.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have raised issues and concerns from my own lived experiences trying to coordinate ground efforts and from those who are serving in healthcare and the community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope the Ministry will seriously consider my inputs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But I believe that if any country can succeed in nurturing a healthier people, Singapore would be the one.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The plans announced are ambitious and are meant to address the long-term well-being of an ageing Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As always, the actual execution and implementation of these plans and strategies bear scrutiny and discussion, along with the effect that they will have on our doctors, healthcare workers and most importantly, our residents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such a shift in approach to put preventive health and our family doctors front and centre of our efforts to improve our population's health and to integrate our care systems in the heart of our communities, requires that a multi-faceted set of issues are tackled.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My Workers' Party colleagues have and will over the course of this debate, share our thoughts and positions on important topics relating to financing changes, preventive care, patient responsibility and how we can better integrate the primary healthcare system with our Intermediate and Long-Term Care (ILTC) and social care systems to reduce the burden on care workers, patients and families as we set our foundations to navigate the new golden age of an ageing society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will speak today on the measurement of success for the new Healthier SG approach, on ensuring that our family doctors are set up for success and finally, on some care areas that I believe need more attention.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, an observation: the White Paper most often refers to increases in life expectancy as a measure for good healthcare outcomes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, this obscures the quality of those long years of life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, we must look at other indicators, such as healthy life expectancy, or the proportion of life spent in poor health, that are more telling of the situation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government has alluded to this, attributing the rising costs of our healthcare budgets over the years partly to the increased impact of chronic disease on our population.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our population is living longer, but not necessarily more healthily.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope that these other metrics start to form the backbone of how we measure good care outcomes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And today, as we debate a Motion that will see our health and social care systems shift towards placing family doctors at the heart of our care system, I cannot help but remember Dr Goh, who provided exceptional primary care for me and my family from when I was five.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is because of his gentle humour, patience and smiling countenance that doctors' visits never felt stressful – whether it was for a flu infection or a routine follow-up.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And his practice nurses too eventually got to know our entire family – including my two ageing grandmothers – well enough to automatically pull out our patient cards without us having to provide our registration details and to chat with us about the latest family updates.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As my father was often away for work, I know that it was a great comfort to Mom to know that she had a trusted team that she could call up and ask quick questions over the phone, whenever she had any medical or even quasi-medical concerns, especially when they related to her two young children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also remember him nagging Dad to get the usual tests and health checks done, despite Dad's aversion to all things medical.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Of course, I recognise that we lucked out in having Dr Goh and his team there for us, and indeed we hope that more – if not all – of us in Singapore will have the chance to have such excellent care through our various life stages.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the White Paper notes that just three in five Singaporeans have a regular family doctor and that most relationships between doctors and patients are still largely transactional in nature, with most interactions only happening during acute illnesses or episodes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The current system does not allow much space or resources for the care team to be able to support a patient's health more holistically and to develop and work out a long-term approach to each patient's care.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is therefore good that we are moving towards institutionalising and formalising that important relationship between family doctors and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, as we work on getting Singaporeans more familiar with registering with a family doctor, we must also ensure that this new shift does not end up unfairly burdening family medicine and GP practices and their associated ecosystems and that care workers do not end up bearing the brunt of well-intentioned but unintended consequences, even as family doctors – and I quote the White Paper – "do much more".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It also must be noted that in order to deliver the objectives outlined in the White Paper, the paradigm shift in care would mean that family doctors will inevitably end up spending more time with each patient and this would mean longer hours, the number of patients being equal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And could we look at lowering the barriers for foreign-trained Singaporean doctors to come home to practise and serve communities back home here in Singapore?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, it was not so long ago that our care systems were heavily strained by the COVID-19 pandemic and many of us would have experienced long queues in clinics and our hospitals, when GP clinics were so overwhelmed that they became unable to answer phone calls from worried patients.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And this is despite many Public Health Preparedness Clinics (PHPCs) extending their opening hours to cope with the surge in demand for medical care.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Doctors, nurses and practice staff generally come under extreme stress and pressure, and while grateful, we cannot afford to take this for granted in the future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, most of our care workers will tell you that they continue to feel the strain today of continuing to work under challenging circumstances and a generally tight manpower situation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it is true that the pandemic was a "black swan" event, our experiences in the past couple of years in particular have taught us the severe risks and downsides of operating extremely lean and "efficient" infrastructures, ranging from healthcare to housing and "just-in-time" supply chains.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is therefore an opportune time for us to consider how we can best prepare for such instances and spikes in demand and to ensure that increasing the role of family doctors in a Healthier SG, does not end up placing too much strain and burden on family doctors, nurses and allied healthcare workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The danger then is that it not only becomes unattractive for potential new doctors and health workers looking to serve in primary care, but may also end up, meaning the existing workers will resign.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is particularly important during the transition period while both patients and care workers are still getting to know the new approach and as we wait for the efforts of our preventive care programmes to bear fruit.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the Singapore Medical Journal in an article in 2020 stated that, I quote – "The nature of the (GP) work can predispose them to developing burnout, which in turn impacts the physician-patient relationship and patient care." In short, we must not forget to care for our care workers, to ensure that they are not burnt out while they care for us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, concerns about the amount of administrative or paperwork that doctors need to fill in, both to enrol in the programme, and also for each patient visit, need to be adequately addressed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Coming back to the capacity of our primary care system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that we are now in the final quarter of 2022, this is an ambitious target.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While MOH and its various partners will undoubtedly put in much effort to ensure that more will start choosing family medicine as a vocation, efforts are also hampered by what is traditionally seen to be the "lesser status" of family doctors.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I recall a former classmate feeling particularly down when the time came to choose specialities, as she had "only managed to get on a family physician track".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At the time, we discussed why she felt this way, despite knowing that being a family physician is, in itself, a speciality and requires a very specific skillset and years of training that may not be any less challenging compared with that of a consultant working in a hospital.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The sentiment that family doctors may not be as well remunerated compared with consultants – particularly in private practice – is also exacerbated by the high costs of setting up a private practice in the first place, when compared with the career option of a senior consultant working in a hospital.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Directly addressing and removing such concerns, would be essential in meeting the aims being debated here today and I hope that these are issues that we quickly overcome, to ensure that our very best and brightest medical students and even mid-career doctors see training to be a family physician as a career choice, or even "the" career of choice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Support for family doctors and their colleagues also needs to go beyond the obvious.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
