text: Family doctors and particularly solo practitioners are also often effectively running a small business.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of them operate in the heart of our communities but are also beset by increasing costs, such as increasing rent and higher utilities bills.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Solo or smaller practices surely would also end up seeing their financial situation strained in the current environment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, on to the important role that the primary healthcare system will need to play in our nation's efforts to improve mental health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A study of Singapore from 2017 found that those suffering from mental health conditions was the second biggest cause for ill health that debilitates residents without necessarily killing them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For our youths in the 10- to 19-year-old age group, in particular, this rises to first place.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Not having adequate treatment or support while suffering from mental health conditions has an impact on all aspects of one's life, ranging from economic output to physical health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, it is important that our plans to address mental health illnesses are firmly anchored within the primary health care system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While designing the mental health care protocols for family doctors, I also hope that attention can be paid to the intrinsic complexity of the field and that a "one size fits all approach" will not work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, how a practice nurse may approach a 20-year-old patient suffering from schizophrenia would likely need to be very different from approaching an 85-year-old showing signs of depression.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Because mental illness still carries stigma, aside from the different spectrum of mental illness symptoms, adjustments must also be made for different attitudes and cultural nuances that may be applicable to the situation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must ensure that the doctors and their staff are adequately trained and supported to deal with patients who suffer from ill mental health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The referral system must also not be overly complicated and doctors, nurses and other allied care workers need to have easily accessible references to know what resources are out there available out there to their patients.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially important in the context of our ageing society where the burden of care is without doubt only going to increase.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleague, Mr Leon Perera, who unfortunately is currently isolating at home after a positive COVID-19 diagnosis, in his Adjournment Motion earlier this year called for differentiated indices for health and care outcomes, and I would like to reiterate that call here.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, a 2020 European study on active ageing constructed an individual-level index of active ageing from people aged between 50 and 90 years old and found that gender-differentiated outcomes are pervasive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Like many other previous studies, it points out that women may live longer but are more likely to suffer from chronic and disabling illnesses and also score higher on levels of pain and depression.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The study also pointed out how problematic gender-blind active ageing policies are as they do not adequately address the different challenges men and women face in old age.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As I mentioned during the April Women's White Paper debate, the gender health gap is also a phenomenon observed here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While Singaporean females do have longer life expectancies, a sizeable portion of that extra time is spent in ill health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It was also a finding by a 2011 study in Singapore that it appears that we too suffer from the gender health-survival paradox of women having more morbidities despite longer life expectancies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus far, it appears that we can do more detailed studies and data on this phenomenon in Singapore, and we must make sure that this paradox does not grow, especially since we are still trying to tackle the negative economic effects on women brought about by COVID-19, the gender wage gap and an increased burden of higher CareShield Life premiums.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I, therefore, hope that more research and data can be collected on the nature of this phenomenon in our local context so that policies and targeted measures can both be taken and to allow the success of tackling it to be measured.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The other point I brought up during my speech earlier this year was that research, healthcare systems and treatments and diagnoses have historically tended to leave women out.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When it comes to gynaecological issues, it is further compounded by stigma and culturally-ingrained embarrassment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I, therefore, hope that these issues can be tackled sensitively and effectively by our primary care providers and that the necessary training and resources are given to support the providers to address these areas of concern together with their patients.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, it is imperative that we quickly address any areas of concern with a positive mindset and start to evolve a national conversation around health that is multi-sided.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It must not be a top-down, patronising approach where experts tell us what is good for us and that we must follow their approach.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, it should be a partnership between doctors, nurses, allied care workers and their patients and families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Good holistic care takes time and the right investments, as does our shift in approach.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope that this is something we will afford to both our patients and especially our care workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Statistically, the elderly is more likely to fall sick or suffer from disabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If left untreated, high blood pressure and high cholesterol will lead to significant health problems.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Shifting our approach from reactively caring for those who are sick to proactively preventing individuals from falling ill is an applaudable move by the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is understandable that we first focus on onboarding the elderly with regular checkups and promoting healthy lifestyle choices.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we must not forget the other age segments of our population and address lifestyle habits that are also of growing concern.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the March sitting last year, I asked the Minister for Education on the number of vaping cases that has been reported in schools since the ban on e-vaporisers in 2018.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also asked how we can educate our youths on the dangers of using electronic vaporisers and what action can be taken against those who supply such items to our school-going children.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unfortunately, there is no specific data point for vaping amongst students and the Ministry replied that it will continue to monitor the trend.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Though we do not have specific data on hand, conversations and anecdotal sharing all point towards a worrying rising trend on the use of these illegal electronic vaporisers with our school-going youths and young adults.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of our Pasir Ris-Punggol resident volunteers shared that it is prevalently used by her schoolmates in polytechnic and it is not uncommon to hear cases of students in secondary school possessing illegal vapes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When CNA did a special on teenage vaping a week ago on 23 September, confiscated vapes were sent to Health Science Authority for lab testing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The results of the chemical content in the liquid were shocking.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: According to the CNA report, Dr Aneez Ahmed, senior consultant surgeon for thoracic surgery at Mount Elizabeth Novena Hospital says he is starting to see cases of teen vapers with inflamed lungs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite its ban since 2018 and its harmful effects, vapes continue to be popular and is accessible even to our young.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: According to the report, one of the teenagers, Kelly, who started vaping at 16 years old, explained to the interviewer that it was simply much easier for her to get hold of a vape than to buy cigarettes from a shop as she is underage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Anecdotal conversations with youths disturbingly surface the ease in which they can obtain vaping instruments online or through Instagram chatrooms, with the product delivered within an hour to a day upon order.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although it is illegal, our youths still have access to it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While Healthier SG focuses on inculcating proactive preventative care and healthy lifestyle choices for our elderly and rightly so, we should not turn a blind eye to other emerging worrying trends too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must do more to educate our youths on the dangers of vaping, and prevent and enforce the illegal sale of vapes, especially to our school children.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the ease of purchasing vaporisers, the anecdotal evidence suggest that our youths are exposed to this unhealthy lifestyle habit at a young age which may be detrimental to our vision of long and healthy lives for Singaporeans as the Motion exerts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There may also be other unhealthy lifestyle habits that we need to be aware of.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Strong partnerships amongst stakeholders in the community can help to promote healthy lifestyle habits and choices instead.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This brings me to the second point on building strong partnerships within the community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Funding model will shift from a workload-based model to a capitation-based model where clusters receive a pre-determined fee for every resident assigned to them on geographical boundaries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure the clusters reach out to its residents effectively?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Being able to reach out to residents should just be one of the metrics for healthcare clusters to consider.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What other metrics will be given to healthcare clusters to ensure that they are successful at engaging the residents and able to drive significant changes to reshape health and lifestyle choices amongst the residents?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the White Paper, while we have explained the role that residents, family doctors and community partners such as ActiveSG and PA can play, one community partner that is significantly missing are employers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Getting the involvement of employers is very important, considering we spend a significant part of our day working.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other than employers encouraging their company panel doctors to participate in the Healthier SG enrolment programme, how can employers also be incentivised and recognised for participating in the Healthier SG programme?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is there scope for employers to be incentivised to provide healthier meals at the workplace, for example, or even provide healthier lifestyle options such as weekly or hourly time off for exercise breaks?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the best ways to incentivise and encourage healthy lifestyle habits is to have family members supporting each other.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Dieting, exercising and visiting the doctor can be a lonely and challenging task for many individuals, especially when it is done alone.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Different family members may also be at different stages of their health transformation journey and at times may accidentally do things that may not exactly help one another.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am sure many of us here have tried to be on a diet and have had a good day of controlling food intake, but the achievement is short-lived the moment a family member invites you to have a late-night supper or offers you that delicious plate of nasi lemak, nasi rawon or char kway teow which you simply cannot refuse!

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the heart of Healthier SG is the relationship between family doctor, patient and the health plan.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can Healthier SG adopt a family-oriented model and place family support at the core of motivating individuals?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Ministry consider allowing or encouraging family involvement in reviewing and following a prescribed health plan?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we also look into ways we can increase family engagement as part of Healthier SG, perhaps find a way to introduce gamification where families score points when they take part in an activity together?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we look towards our vision of long and healthy lives for Singaporeans, I would like to briefly touch on the support for dementia patients and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A nationwide study in the Well-being of Singapore Elderly (WiSE) found that one in 10 seniors above the age of 60 suffers from dementia.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a recent visit to Apex Harmony Lodge in Pasir Ris, a home specialising in dementia care, I was thoroughly impressed by the level of care for our dementia patients in the home.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The home, led by Chairman Mr Gan Boon Jin and CEO Ms Soh Mee Choo, has invested in upskilling its staff and introducing new technologies to provide the best care for its patients.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, such healthcare for dementia patients does not come cheap.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the lodge, more than 90% of the residents enjoy subsidised care, some even fully subsidised.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, Apex Harmony Lodge has a current capacity to accommodate 200 dementia patients, which is really a small fraction of the expected 90,000 elderlies with dementia by 2030.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How are we preparing to provide sufficient healthcare support for the growing number of dementia patients in the future that require either full board or day care services?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   By 2030, one in four Singapore residents will be above 65 years of age, up from one in six today.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Statistically, the elderly is more likely to fall sick or suffer from disabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, 32% of our population has hypertension and 37% has hyperlipidaemia.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If these conditions are not treated at an early stage, it will lead to significant health complications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a community, we must give more focus towards preventive care and tackle health issues and lifestyle choices before it is too late.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, we must certainly focus on the elderly, by encouraging them to watch their diet, for instance, by reducing their salt and sugar intake, exercise and to also stop smoking.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, as we focus on our seniors, this does not mean that we can allow other worrying trends to become prevalent amongst our youths.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have often heard about how easy it is to get e-cigarettes, also known as "vape" and there are those among our youths who partake in this unhealthy habit.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must do more to educate our youths on the dangers of vaping and prevent the illegal sale of vapes, especially its sale to our youths.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Building a healthier Singapore will require the participation of all levels of society, especially families, which must form the core support that ensures Singaporeans make the best health and lifestyle choices.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More can be done to encourage and support active participation of our family members to take good care of their health.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Community partners will continue to provide support, and together, we can all become a healthier, happier and thriving community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Notwithstanding the points and clarifications above, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Each family doctor will develop an appropriate health plan for each enrolled resident and would also administer the appropriate health screenings and vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Needless to say, any doctor would be familiar with his or her regular patients over time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I believe there are already many Singaporeans who have the habit of seeing the same GP over a long period of time each time they fall ill or need prescription and appreciate the benefits of a GP who is familiar with their medical history over time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have known my current family GP since I was in secondary school.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The proposed requirement of a family physician having to develop an appropriate health plan for each enrolled resident and having an annual check-in with each enrolled resident, to find out how the resident is doing in terms of his health or how he or she is adhering to his or her health plan should be a significant departure beyond the current common practice of only seeing the doctor when we do not feel well or when we require prescriptions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I agree with these proposals, but the devil is, of course, in the details.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The health plans, screenings and annual check-ins will, hopefully, provide a sufficiently regular opportunity for the doctor to be able to help us to pick up any signs of any health issue earlier before it manifests into something serious or chronic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That said, it is important that such health plans are appropriately developed for residents of different age groups and dealing with prevention of a range of diseases and health conditions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The White Paper also mentioned that mental health and end of life will subsequently be covered.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that mental health will certainly not be at the end of the queue, but some priority be given for its earlier introduction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The White Paper itself gave a "special mention" of mental health at page 52.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The family physician will, certainly, be ideally positioned to help residents with regular checks on their mental health and, importantly, early detection of any problem.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the task force help to integrate the family physician's new role alongside other resources and stakeholders which are already part of the task force's efforts to date?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Everyone must be willing and able to accord it priority alongside other demands of their everyday life and treating the plans and the appointments with the family doctor seriously and taking full advantage of them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the hustle and bustle of modern living, I am not sure everyone may be able to do so.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I do hope MOH will have an appropriate public education campaign not just to encourage enrolment, but to encourage enrolled residents to take this programme seriously and be diligent in adhering to the health plans and recommendations and advice of their family doctors, and to make full use of what is provided under the programme.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am aware that many Singaporeans currently visit GPs or clinics which are on the panel of their employers' corporate medical insurance plans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These GPs are often not their usual family GPs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Would MOH also engage different stakeholders, including both the medical practitioners and the insurance industry, to see how corporate medical insurance plans can be tweaked to enhance the Healthier SG objective of having more people stay with one family physician?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are also many people who have regularly gone to see GPs in polyclinics, ostensibly for reasons of cost and subsidy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can MOH give an indication of the size of this group of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Following the introduction of Healthier SG, how does MOH see the role of GPs in polyclinics with respect to primary care and would MOH be reviewing the role of GPs in polyclinics?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Healthier SG also proposes to allow for a change of family doctor once each year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I understand there may be a need for some flexibility, for example, when a resident changes his or her place of residence or even changes his employment, allowing changes of doctors within a short period of time may not be conducive for the greater goal of Healthier SG to get more people to have one family doctor to manage their health.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I welcome the above, but I do see that this must come with additional manpower as well as IT resources.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More assistance may be required by both stakeholders in managing the additional responsibilities as well as ensuring that all interventions, screenings and other measures recommended by the family physicians are well coordinated.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is not an easy task for the eldercare or senior activity centres to reach out to all seniors within their designated cluster and try to ensure that the seniors are in good shape and that help can be given if required.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The response of our seniors may vary between individuals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While many are happy to know of the support they can reach out to and many also get involved in activities in eldercare centres and welcome being connected to such centres, some seniors may not be open when eldercare centres try reaching out to them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some may not want to keep in touch with their eldercare centres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some keep to themselves and may not socialise with others.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some of these seniors live by themselves and may not have family members at hand to keep an eye on them in their homes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am concerned that for this group of people, the family doctors under Healthier SG may also experience difficulty in reaching out to them or ensuring their committed participation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope MOH can study how outreach efforts can be improved to such seniors so that all can actually benefit from these programmes under Healthier SG and, most of all, their health and well-being can be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I understand the White Paper may focus on chronic care management and prevention of chronic disease, dental health is important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Good dental and oral health can also enhance our overall health and prevent complications to other areas of our health, including prevention of certain chronic or other diseases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moreover, there is some overlap in similar lifestyle factors causing problems to dental/oral health and to other aspects of our health, for example, consumption of sugary products.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Still on the topic of dental health, recently, a resident provided some feedback to me about the cost of dental treatments not covered by MediSave.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Payments through MediSave can only be made for treatments where surgeries are involved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Dental clinic treatments like tooth extraction, root canal treatments and affixing of crowns, while not necessarily regarded as under the category of surgery, can be relatively expensive to many people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For retirees, the outlay in cash for dental treatments can be a burden, especially if they have recurring issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If need be, the Government can look into including more measures to deter possible abuses by minority practitioners.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Under Healthier SG, family doctors have new responsibilities towards the care of residents enrolled under them, regardless of age.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And how are the doctors expected to cope with the additional work and responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I support the recommendations in the Healthier SG White Paper that every Singaporean chooses a designated family doctor to provide medical services and manage their overall health.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To implement Healthier SG smoothly, we must ensure that the participation of the majority of Singaporeans and that participants have a positive attitude towards the health plan set for them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In addition, I hope that the mental health aspect mentioned in the White Paper will be given priority and included into Healthier SG as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These centres will take on more responsibilities and services and work closely with GPs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that the Government will provide more manpower, technology training and other resources for the various parties to support this new model of cooperation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At present, apart from ensuring the health of the elderly and providing them with assistance, eldercare centres also need to reach out to and communicate with the elderly in the area in different ways.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many seniors are glad to learn that the centres are able to provide the necessary assistance and are happy to participate in the activities organised by the centres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, there are still some elderly folks who choose not to contact the centres or participate in activities organised by them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This trend will pose some challenges to the Healthier SG programme.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, how GPs can effectively engage and persuade this group of seniors, especially those living alone, to participate in the programme is an issue to look at.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that MOH will look into improving outreach to this group of seniors so that all Singaporeans can benefit from Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that oral health will also be included in Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, notwithstanding the concerns I raised, I support the Motion.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The rising cost of healthcare is a threat to our Government budgets and to our economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is, in a word, unsustainable for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is unsustainable for Singaporeans like my Woodlands resident, Mr Z, whose wife suffers from diabetes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Mr Z comes to my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS).

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He has problems – how to cover the cash co-pay for her next hospital visit, how to pay for the bags and other consumables that are not paid by MediSave, how he is going to push her in her wheelchair to the NKF centre for her dialysis treatments, these days, often in the rain, when the growing arthritis in his bones sends waves of pain up his legs and back.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is for my resident, Ms N, who has worked hard to build her career.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But one illness to her aunt who lives here on a Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP), has wiped out a huge chunk of Ms N's savings, and continues to take a chunk out of her take-home pay every month.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is why my resident, Mr T, refuses to go for check-ups, let alone screening. "If they find something, I do not have the money for treatment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, better do not know", as Minister Ong said.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And, at this point, I want to react to the comment by the Member Ms He Ting Ru who stated that we are living longer but not healthier and that MOH tends to look at life expectancy rather than more healthy indicators.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For this speech, I did look at that data.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I just wanted to give the credit to MOH that our hospitals do a great job at treating the sick.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But could we have done more to avoid people getting sick in the first place?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Could we have done more in taking more decisive, holistic actions on preventive care, on a national focus on population health, that permeates everything we do in our daily lives, from the food we eat, the exercise we do or do not do, the amount of screen time we allow our kids that might have helped us prevent the rise of chronic diseases – diseases like diabetes, hypertension and lipid disorders?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, for these reasons, Mr Speaker, I say that Heathier SG is not just a good idea.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: More people are getting sick and living with chronic illness.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They are getting sick earlier in their lives and will require medical care for a long time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Add to that an ageing population and rising costs and we have no choice but to make this work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: HPB has worked hard to promote healthy living, but HPB cannot do this alone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is time we recognise and ensure that incentives, norms, practices, data analytics and policies must be aligned to the behaviours we want to drive across the system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Not only behaviours of the doctors, nurses, hospital administrators, everyone in the healthcare delivery system, but also of the community, of patients and currently healthy citizens, to take charge of our own health.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are many things to like in the Healthier SG White Paper – mobilising GPs, removing co-pay, free vaccinations, cheaper drugs at the GP, social prescriptions, leveraging community assets and solutions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But before I go into the enablers, I would like to frame them in the context of what it is that we are trying to achieve.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The ultimate objectives must be better health outcomes, at lower cost.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And indeed, this is the objective of healthcare reforms around the world, towards a model commonly known as value-based healthcare.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But when we look at the key performance indicators (KPIs) for Healthier SG, many of the KPIs, especially in the near term, are process indicators, things like enrolment rates, screening rates, vaccination rates and health plan completion rates, while health outcomes like disease prevalence and control, mortality, re-admission rates, frailty, start to figure only later.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Patient-reported outcomes includes measures of quality of life, for example.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Do they feel pain, their ability to perform activities in daily living, sense of control, their moods, loneliness?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Quite simply, it is because without measurement and transparency of outcomes, we would not know whether what we are doing and paying for is having an impact and how much.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Doctors and clusters would not have the data they need to make better decisions and drive innovation, teamwork and best practice sharing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need outcomes that are measurable, effective and standardised across clusters.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It takes time to identify, find ways to measure, and to show the value to everyone in the care delivery chain so it is not simply administrative overhead.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is not something we can leave to the clusters.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is very true that there is a big risk in a transformation as fundamental and complex as Healthier SG to expect too much too soon.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the evidence from successful value-based healthcare systems has shown that meaningful health outcomes can, in fact, be achieved sooner, but for defined patient segments, particularly at the intersection between primary care and the secondary and tertiary space, such as at the point of discharge from hospital.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, a general nutrition education takes a long time to payback.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But Oak Street Health, a relatively young and innovative US primary care provider, found that making sure elderly patients with diabetes are eating properly when they are first discharged from hospital is very rapid payback in terms of lower re-admission rates.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Another example, in Sweden, the Stockholm County Council launched a value-based payment programme for hip and knee replacement in 2009, led to a rapid shift of care from acute care hospitals to cheaper specialty clinics.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When a patient is diagnosed with diabetes early in primary care, and has regular GP visits forthwith, their diabetes journey is much more likely to be managed over time in the community setting.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In contrast, when the diagnosis is done later and in a hospital setting, and he does not engage much with primary care, this could result in poorer management of diabetes and increased re-admissions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is data that we can act upon and do something about.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The common thread in each of these examples is "think big but start small" – focus on a specific population group and patient segment, for example, people over 60 with diabetes and identify a subset of outcomes for that patient segment, and set the system to work to track and improve those outcomes and make this visible.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And I stress to focus first on managing and tracking and doing something with it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am a little bit more ambivalent about the suggestion by the Member Mr Gerald Giam to put a target on every KPI, especially with some of these KPIs, as the Member Ms Denise Phua said, it is very easy to achieve them, can set some perverse incentives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is important is to identify the right KPIs, measure them and actually use them to make our system better.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I urge MOH to consider a real push to measure health outcomes from the beginning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And with this lens of focusing on outcomes, I turn now to what it is going to take to make Healthier SG work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, healthcare financing, an area that will undergo significant reforms in Healthier SG, with a move towards capitation funding.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The drawbacks of our current model of a fee for service are clear.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It motivates doctors to take on more and more patients, even if they do not have time, to order that extra MRI, even if it is not necessary, to prescribe the most expensive drug instead of a generic that does the job.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It feeds off a very human trait – love, the love that makes us willing to try anything, spend anything, if we believe it might keep our loved ones alive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And trust me, I know how that feels.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But, Mr Speaker, more expensive care is not necessarily better care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Capitation, in particular, gives healthcare providers a powerful incentive to manage total systems costs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Most capitation systems are geared to encourage providers to focus on prevention and early detection and intervention.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Then, it is up to the insurer and its provider partners to figure out the best way to invest that money to provide the care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Insurers, such as Humana, have built their own or partnered provider networks to help them create more value-based models.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Oak Street Health, which I mentioned earlier, is one such Humana partner.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Oak Street clinicians are given the autonomy to do whatever drives best outcomes for the patient.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Working in multidisciplinary teams of GPs, nurses, specialists, nutritionists, they take input from the patient and caregiver, and also consider the patient's social determinants of health, such as food security and social support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This holistic approach often drives new insights and innovation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, if the patient needs a surgery to be healthy, they will make the referral.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If he needs food delivered to him to make sure he eats healthy, that is what they do.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Or if it takes a house visit to make sure that the home does not have hazards – a stray rug or slippery tiles that could cause him to trip and fall, that is what they do.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Or if they think the most meaningful thing is to have someone put their arm around him to be comfortable with his life situation, that is what they do – and they are achieving good outcomes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Another example is Kaiser Permanente, also in the US, where transparency about outcomes and costs encourages the clinical teams to avoid low-value care and right-site care within its integrated network of hospitals and primary care providers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A system of incentives encourages clinicians to work together and share best practices and always driving continuous improvement.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will there be bonus payments for achieving better health outcomes?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will health outcomes be shared across the delivery value chain to encourage people to work together?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How much autonomy will be given to the clusters and clinical teams to do what they believe is right to deliver better care, informed by care protocols and outcomes?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can there be participation payments for tracking and reporting health outcomes?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will adjustments be made at the backend when someone uses healthcare services outside his or her own cluster?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The enhanced National Health Electronic Records system under Healthier SG is much needed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We should not need to tell every new doctor or specialist we see about our medical history or our prescriptions or to have to repeat expensive tests and x-rays or to repeat information needed by our medical social worker at every hospital you or your child goes to.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Digitising and automating processes, leveraging mobile apps like MyHealthHub and Healthy 365, all these make sense, though implementation is non-trivial, as some colleagues have raised.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The hon Member Tan Wu Meng has made the point that digital solutions must be easy to use and reliable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To change behaviour though, doctors and patients alike must be excited and willing to use these tools.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Here is where the lens of outcomes pushes us to go even further and, that is, data – clinical data, pharmacy data, health screening data, health app data, cost data, but also data about the individual and how he likes to be engaged.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can we use all that data and analytics to identify risky individuals for whom we can have the right conversations and make the right targeted interventions in order to make a meaningful impact?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can we engage patients and physicians, not only with apps and technology and tools but with data – data that tells them where they stand in comparison to others and advises them with personally relevant information of actions that they can take, including, of course, working with community partners?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I think the role that data and analytics can play in driving outcomes for Healthier SG is incredibly interesting and I would suggest doubling down on the capabilities to do this.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have spoken a number of times in this Parliament on the adequacy of healthcare manpower, including the shortage of nurses and the need for healthcare manpower transformation in preparation for a future that is much more focused on value-based care and prevention.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For Healthier SG to work, we not only need more nurses, we need enough good family doctors, nurses, allied health professionals, pharmacists and care coordinators.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They must be comfortable dealing with a wider range of complex conditions, working with data and technology, working in multidisciplinary teams, including specialists, and new ways to engage patients.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need everyone in the healthcare delivery system to be rewired around prevention and putting care in the right place.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, they are not trained in that way, they are not compensated in that way, and let us face it, their intellectual respect – our intellectual respect – is not for prevention.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our intellectual respect is for the surgeon who pulls off a complicated surgery.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, we need to respect family doctors a lot more.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If Healthier SG is to succeed, we have got to get this rewiring right.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I believe that, for most clinicians, the language of health outcomes is an inspiring and powerful one versus administrative tasks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It can underpin the enormous change management effort that will be required.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To put our healthcare system now on a more sustainable footing and to get a healthier Singapore and Singaporeans – for Mr Z, Ms N, Mr T and millions of other Singaporeans like him – we cannot fail.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I propose to take a healthy break now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 5.21 pm until 5.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I just want to make a clarification to Ms Mariam Jaafar.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: She mentioned that she was concerned about setting targets to accompany the KPIs because she mentioned that the hospitals could game the system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I just want to clarify if that is what she said, because the KPIs that I mentioned were all KPIs that were mentioned in the White Paper.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, is Ms Mariam Jaafar saying that we should not set targets right now even though we have the KPIs, or is she suggesting that there is a certain time frame later on that we should set the targets and so when will that be?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I think we would need to look at different KPIs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I cannot say when the right time is to measure it, but I expect that will come in future once we have more data, I think it is important to do this based on a good fight, based on data.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: First, let me declare my interest as a member of the medical profession – I am a practising ophthalmologist in the private sector.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: You know it is a good paper when many, many Members suddenly rise to the occasion and start to claim credit for it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, everybody would quote their own previous Adjournment Motion, COS debate and so on.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: A paradigm shift because most of us, most of the patients, only when they are ill, will they see a doctor.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If you are not ill, you should not see a doctor at all.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Most of the doctors will only see patients when they are ill.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If the patients are well, they do not see the patients.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am not sure if we should even call them patients in the first place because now, they are not ill at all.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Maybe clinics will have to change their name, they should not be called clinics, they should be called wellness centres, because they are there for wellness, they are not there for the sick.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: To have a paradigm shift, you have to change the mindset of both patients, as well as the GPs, as well as the population.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think that is the enormous task that MOH have now, ahead of them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: First, let me just congratulate MOH for taking this very bold step, one small step ahead, but it is bold step for the nation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I totally agree with the White Paper and support the White Paper.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: All those proposed initiatives are commendable, but there are many areas of concerns, like my Parliamentary colleagues have raised.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The details are always in the execution and the problems are always there.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Like many of my Parliamentary colleagues, I do have my family doctor, Dr Tan in the Nee Soon Clinic that looked after me and my family when I was young.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That one GP clinic looked after my entire extended family – my grandmother, grandfather – he was the one who came and signed the death certificate for my grandfather, and for my grandmother as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I think we are quite familiar with the relationship of one good GP to a family and what a good family physician can do.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But our current GP practices now are no longer like those which were in Nee Soon village.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Most of them are in group practices now.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, they are big group practices whereby doctors always change.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, you may not see the same doctors all the time.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If the scheme now is to be attached to the clinic, then does it defeat the purpose of this White Paper, in the sense that you do not build a relationship between the doctor and patient, but it is just between the clinic and the patient.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I am not sure how that changes the paradigm.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is very similar to the current polyclinic system now, whereby my residents always complain that when they go to the polyclinic, they see different doctors all the time.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The only thing that held everything together is good medical records.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is to make sure that the medical records are seamless so that patients do not need to repeat everything, doctors do not need to look through a lot of other records in order to find out how to manage this particular patient or resident.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In established healthcare systems in developed countries like the UK and Switzerland, access to healthcare starts from a regular GP or family doctor.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: When doctors have a good long-term working relationship with their patients, they can harness the power of these relationships to solve problems beyond what may be too complex for other healthcare professionals, such as those pertaining to social and lifestyle challenges as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As a doctor with regular patients, I can certainly attest to the effectiveness of such working relationships where both parties have mutual respect, trust and confidence, which is the most important.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As I mentioned earlier on, many GPs are now in group practices.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If patients are enrolled with a particular doctor, they may find it very difficult to reach this doctor at the preferred location on certain days or certain times.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Under such circumstances, of course, the patients would be attached to the clinics instead.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If the enrolment is based on the clinic and patients see different doctors, then the question, of course, is what is the value of the doctor-patient relationship?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some patients would prefer doctors who are not in their health cluster – not within their area of residence.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think the Minister has mentioned that they can switch GPs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If the patient can switch GPs, can they also switch cluster?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is important as patients may want to exercise more choice over their preferred specialists.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The reverse is also true, in the sense that with specialists, can they refer patients now to GPs or polyclinics within their health cluster for step-down care?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If the patient requests to go to their preferred GP, will this cross-referral and transfer of medical history be conducted seamlessly?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will cross clustering further complicate funding of the programmes as it is funded by clustering?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Then, there are the patients who go to their company's medical group to utilise their company's medical benefits.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Employees these days are spending fewer years working with the same company.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This means that it would be very difficult to forge the long-term relationship that we hope to achieve through this "One Resident, One Doctor" scheme if they are switching doctors every few years under the company's scheme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How does the Government plan to counter this?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The enrolment of one-to-one GP will still allow patients to use their CHAS card at other GP clinics and this does not allow for "stickiness" to one GP and patients will still go GP-hopping.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is the feedback that I got from my GP colleagues.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There will be GPs that are very popular.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am afraid that when this enrolment starts, the very popular GPs will be all fully booked out.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Just like the good schools, MOH may have to start a balloting system for patients to book their favourite GPs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last of all, can GPs choose their patients?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are they allowed to reject patients who choose them in the first place?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If that is the case, then, yes – by right, GP groups and GPs can cherry-pick.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They can choose patients who are well, who do not need so much care, who are much more cooperative, compared to those who are not so cooperative.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As for the age of entry, disease prevention, especially for chronic diseases, is the focus of the White Paper.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I was wondering why the Ministry choose 60 and above as the entry age for the programme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, 60 and above is where chronic diseases start.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: At 60 and above, like what my Parliamentary colleague Sharael Taha just mentioned, one out of 10 will be having early dementia.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If you want to prevent dementia, you should encourage them to start walking at 40 years old.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If you walk 4,000 steps a day, it reduces your risk by 20%.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If you walk 10,000 steps a day, it halves your risks straightaway.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In that case, you do not need to build so many expensive dementia management centres if you start the programme early.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, the question is – of course, ideally – that the implementation age should be 40 years old and younger – not older.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The earlier you start, the easier it is to manage chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, we are here not to manage chronic diseases, but trying to prevent chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: By the time you hit 60, you are actually managing chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The essence of the White Paper is to prevent disease from forming.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Of course, we also want to make sure that chronic diseases are well managed, they do not progress to become more serious in the first place.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Free medical checkups and vaccinations are, undoubtedly, attractive for boosting participation, yet there will be residents who are unconvinced.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Even for our free COVID-19 vaccination programme, which it comes to their mind, there are people who will refuse the vaccination.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are also regular functional medical screenings via Project Silver Screen that is held in the heartlands, free for seniors over 60.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I have older folks who do take care of their health through good lifestyle habits like regular exercise and eating healthily but there is an aversion when it comes to asking them to go for medical screenings or seeing a doctor, especially when they are not feeling unwell.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Preventive healthcare does require commitment on the patients' part.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is unlike a simple medical consultation where patients see the doctor because they have symptoms.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: After they have their symptoms seen, they get treated, they go home with a medical prescription and that is the end of the transaction, whereas preventive healthcare is a long-term journey.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What else can you do, as a Government now, to encourage the active participation of the population in preventive healthcare because it is really a big paradigm shift for all our residents.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I shall talk a little bit on remuneration for GPs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This, I must, first, not take credit for myself.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I must credit my GP colleagues who have emailed me when I asked them for their feedback on the Healthier SG White Paper.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The first thing they asked me was, "How is the funding model?" Many GPs are concerned about the remuneration model as they believe that the new scheme will add considerably more workload for them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think the argument on what KPIs to set, how to measure, has already started in this House.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: A younger patient who is more receptive to advice will naturally make more progress than an older patient with more chronic health problems and who may be more resistant to changing their lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can the Ministry provide a clearer outline on how GPs will be remunerated?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While I believe that most doctors want to make a difference to their patients' lives.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, if they feel that they are not compensated reasonably for their time and effort, some will choose not to participate in this particular scheme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In short, my concerns are how do we empower GPs and how do we make sure that GPs do not cherry-pick at the end of the day?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That is the tough part, the tough balance that you have to make.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That is one feedback that I got from most of the GPs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I also want to voice the concerns from my GP colleagues about the IT-enabler for GPs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While clusters can help him and his patients to connect to the social and community partners, he still has to see patients in an efficient and timely manner and ensure outcome indicators as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This can be a daunting task for many GPs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They will not receive payment for their work right away, it may be a year later.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, we need to walk this journey with the GPs and scope this launch very carefully.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The next topic I want to talk about will be the participation from the healthcare clusters.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I note that the three healthcare clusters will be involved in keeping the resident population healthy and will be step up as regional health managers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I echo some of my Parliamentary colleagues here.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the UK's National Health Service (NHS) system, GPs form the bedrock of their entire healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The healthcare journey for every patient starts with the GP first.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, GP practices across the UK face significant and growing strains with the declining number of GPs, rising demand and struggling to recruit and trying to retain staff as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This translates into longer waiting times and poorer service for patients.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: According to data from the British Medical Association (BMA), the overall number of GP partners has been on the decline in recent years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Since 2017, the number of GPs working full-time hours or more in GP practice-based settings has been steadily decreasing.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: More GPs choose to work part-time as they have better control of their hours and workload, to improve work-life balance and reduce stress and burnout.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Besides loathing the heavy workload and long hours, NHS GPs have expressed their unhappiness with how their contributions and abilities have been undervalued, compared to specialists.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They also face increasing abuse from patients as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We must learn from these countries with similar models and recognise the benefits but see how we can avoid the pitfalls.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For the shift in our healthcare policy to be successful, we need adequate GPs to be working regular and reasonable hours to minimise burnout and to ensure that all our patients will be able to receive timely and adequate care.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will there be a support channel for both patients and GPs to share feedback?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is not to encourage patients to complain, but for MOH to seek meaningful feedback and to provide necessary support if the clinics are facing difficulties coping.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The last thing we want is for the national care standards to drop and patients to be left in the lurch.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will MOH now require GPs enrolled under this scheme to operate a certain number of hours on specific days or specific times of the day?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are clinics that are open only half a day on certain days of the week.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many do not operate on weekends and public holidays.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What will happen to patients who require medical care when their GP clinic is closed?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the contingency plan if the GP is away for an extended period of time, be it for professional or personal reasons?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are enrolled clinics required to have more than one GP?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Would they have to hire a standby and inform MOH if they will be away?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will there be a backup – a first-line GP and a second-line GP?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Instead of appointing one, you have to appoint two, which means that one is on standby.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: To get a clearer picture on the GPs' interest in the "One Resident, One Doctor" scheme, we need more statistics.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Currently, how many GPs are practising on a part-time basis?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These GPs may not be able to accept major cases or cases requiring commitment for long-term follow-up.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How many GPs are participating in the Primary Care Network?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What percentage of GPs nationwide does this constitute?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Responsibility for health should be a collaborative effort among individuals and the society that we live in.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We all have to look after our health.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, many may not be well-versed in healthcare matters and would greatly benefit from having a healthcare professional by their side to walk them through this healthcare journey.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We cannot put this plan into execution without strong support from our GPs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: During the pandemic, widespread burnout caused an exodus of healthcare staff around the world.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Singapore experienced our highest turnover rate of healthcare workers over the past two years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Yet, even before that, healthcare workers have voiced their discontentment with long, inflexible working hours, and the abuse and disrespect they faced from patients.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The pandemic has pushed the stress faced by healthcare workers to a breaking point.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As we recover, we must ensure that Singapore continues to be a safe, conducive and inviting place for all our healthcare workers, including our GPs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With that, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I support the White Paper.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: MOH has been actively engaging the College of Family Physicians and the SMA; and is aware that doctors broadly support this move.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We support the shift in emphasis from treating disease to prevention and to strongly support the individual's health in primacy care via the family doctor and community support.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I speak now to raise specific concerns and hope that these will be considered as we embark together on Healthier SG.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am a general surgeon who has worked in several restructured hospitals, before stepping out to private practice as a breast surgeon three years ago.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: And, as Dr Lim pointed out about wellness, I am registered as "Breast Friend Surgery and Wellness" because I advocate strongly for prevention of breast cancer.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: During an administrative briefing many years ago, I once saw patients described as "clients" and doctors are called "service providers".

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: That is when I decided – I will do what I can to reclaim back the doctor-patient relationship, for all of us.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It is demeaning to think of healthcare purely as a business, or a transaction of payment for services rendered.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Those of us who have enjoyed good doctor-patient relationships – and I have been on both sides – understand the world of difference it makes.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Having a good family doctor provides that strong anchor – to look after you and your family, and in turn, refer you to the necessary and relevant specialists for additional care.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In real life, the difficulties and limitations of logistics, insurance panel restrictions and personal preferences will affect the flow of care.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I have spoken on the problems with the Integrated Shield plans previously and I am glad to report that there has been some progress made.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: What other broad challenges exist now for healthcare workers?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The newspapers have reported on the national downtime affecting electronic healthcare systems in restructured clusters and this House has had updates from MOH on investigations.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As SMA President, I received feedback on the struggles that healthcare workers face on the ground.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Complaints and angry patients aside, what we are more worried about is the potential lapses of care, as back-up manual paperwork is done during downtime, and then healthcare workers have to stay back to load the relevant information back into the electronic system.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Duplicate documentation – can you imagine how many man-hours are wasted, rather than focusing on actual patient care?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As much as we understand the need to make things electronic, most healthcare workers are wary and cautious of the roll-out of the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR).

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I also propose that there should be education and encouragement for patients to take ownership of their own health records in HealthHub and to actively share relevant information with their attending doctor.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I, personally, would like some of my medical information to be private.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Just, as an example, if I had a previous miscarriage and abortion, mental health issues, I would not like every healthcare worker to know about them.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I will choose to inform my attending doctor on what I feel is relevant, or, if they ask, I will question, is this information going to make a difference to my current condition?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In conjunction with Healthier SG, let us remember to educate individuals on the importance of personal care and responsibility.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Next, manpower issues may not be solved just by hiring more healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just the number of staff but the experience of each staff.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Look to the retention of staff – for senior, trained doctors to stay in public sectors; for experienced nurses and allied health to want to stay in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It is good that there are more training and new hires for Singaporeans and for foreigners, but how do we actually retain them?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Exit interviews should be taken seriously to evaluate systemic problems or work culture differences.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: For my own exit interview some years back, the schedule was changed a few times and eventually, it was a new HR staff who met me to take back the staff pass and sign some papers as a formality.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I hope MOH continues to engage all stakeholders on a regular basis and take our considered feedback.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The Tripartite Committee looking in the welfare of our junior doctors is a positive step.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Why are the foreign nurses, who have worked and trained here for years moving on to work in other countries?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Is it purely about matching the salary, or struggles with setting up a family and their childcare needs?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: What are the subsidies available for foreign staff in the childcare centres?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I take note that certain kinds of leave are eligible only if the child is a Singaporean Citizen.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: How may we help them to find a home and be willing to be here long term?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The feedback from senior specialists in restructured hospitals is that, should there be a decrease in the number of complex cases, it will affect the training of our younger specialists.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the average layperson does not quite understand how complex the healthcare system is.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In having team-based care, with nurses and allied health taking on so much of the healthcare needs, it should be recognised, by having the patients know that these are all professionals, who are trained to deliver specific interventions and health outcomes.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As an example, I perceive that sometimes, patients do not understand the importance of physiotherapy after surgery and neglect to keep the range of movements, resulting in a frozen limb, and then, wrongly blaming the doctor for bad surgery.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: For patients who come to the hospital for the first time ever with end-stage organ failure; I am deeply saddened.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Was it a lack of awareness or lack of resources?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: How about the role and responsibility of the immediate family in reminding the elderly loved one to go for regular check-ups, advise compliance with medications and to take active steps to modify this.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: On the one hand, we see some patients who have chosen not to know anything about their own bodies.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, we also see some people who Google non-stop and take bits of information with inadequate context, even to the extent of arguing with healthcare professionals about what is correct medical care.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Establishing a good doctor-patient relationship and having mutual trust in each other gives much better patient outcomes and satisfaction.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The rise of badly-written Search Engine Optimisation articles is severely detrimental to the doctor-patient relationship.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: So many articles share half-truths and myths, even fear mongering.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As a council doctor of the SMA, I will continue to advocate for this public education and allowing doctors to do our work well, with adequate support.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Each and every one of us here has to play our part well, in taking responsibility for our own health.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have a number of questions on the funding model and manpower requirements, which I hope the Minister can provide answers to.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I welcome the change in funding model to incentivise efforts towards preventive and early intervention measures and better health outcomes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I note from the White Paper that MOH is still in the process of working out the KPIs for the healthcare clusters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Apart from KPIs based on the performance of the healthcare clusters at the regional level, I hope to also see KPIs based on outcomes at the national level as well for the regional clusters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will provide incentives for the regional clusters to cooperate with one another for a better outcome at the national level.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, the outcome at the national level is of greater importance to us and the KPIs should reflect that.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Apart from KPIs for the healthcare organisations, the performance appraisal and reward system of key personnel should also be revealed for the same reasons.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would there be any financial reasons for GPs or healthcare clusters to lean more towards one group?
