speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I have some questions on the manpower requirements.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How does MOH intend to reach those numbers?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would it be via an increase in enrolment in relevant courses at our universities, polytechnics and other training centres?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, what is the planned enrolment for these courses in the next decade?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many is expected to be via recruitment from outside Singapore?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And does MOH plan to change the terms and conditions of these healthcare professionals to attract and retain them?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also have some questions on chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The White Paper showed that the rate of diabetes has fallen slightly, while that for obesity has risen slightly.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the rate of high blood pressure and high blood cholesterol has risen sharply.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unbalanced diet and low level of physical activity were cited as reasons.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These two reasons would, however, cause rises in all four categories.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And since the magnitude of change is so different, could there be other contributing factors apart from diet and exercise?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, would stress levels and poor work life balance be contributing factors?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can MOH also provide more details on what ways is our diet unbalanced?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The White Paper also mentioned that the prevalence of chronic diseases have risen across many age groups including the young.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can MOH provide the prevalence rate with breakdown by age?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, I have a couple of suggestions for the Minister to consider.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have raised this before and I will raise it again.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MediSave can currently be used for hospitalisation and limited outpatient treatment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have heard anecdotes of how some people chose inpatient treatment for something that can be treated as an outpatient and at a lower cost, because the former can be paid via MediSave while the latter require cash outlay.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, demand is skewed towards the more expensive inpatient treatment due to MediSave rules.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we find ways to make healthy food less expensive compared to unhealthy food?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One option to consider is a tax on unhealthy food that goes towards subsidising healthy ones.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I welcome the announcement of the Healthier SG White Paper.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The push toward preventive health is an area that I have advocated throughout my career, from being a Physical Educator and now, through research and programme design.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am supportive of the plans laid out by the Ministry, which have been on the agenda for many years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And now, with the fundamentals in place, we are taking this necessary step to improve our healthcare further.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How does MOH intend to engage and support them?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, I was encouraged by the efforts on the ground to visit the elderly who are less mobile to provide vaccinations for them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that similar efforts may be made to engage and support them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thirdly, the elderly may take a longer consultation time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How does this impact the GPs daily workload and operations?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And collectively, how will this impact the quality of support for the elderly?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My fourth point revolves around the caregivers who selflessly tend to the elderly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This would allow the doctor to plan a more holistic and inclusive approach for both of them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Nevertheless, some are concerned with how fast technology and apps have evolved.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Moreover, the thought of being scammed, too, may hinder their usage of digital support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This would be more pertinent when Healthier SG is rolled out to the younger generation, who are more open to mental health issues and understand the importance of mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Issues like dementia or depression due to social isolation remain pertinent issues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, concerns like whether there would be enough mental health trained GPs and, if so, how would these GPs engage and manage consultation time, bearing in mind that consultation times may differ in complexity, require deeper attention and may take a longer time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe Healthier SG is an opportunity to address the issues that I have raised previously related to accessibility and screening.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I was unable to find the roles of IHLs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Practice-based research efforts are expanding and courses that provide lifelong learning regarding public health have grown.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: IHLs play an important role within the public health system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To educate and train; conduct basic and applied research in disciplines pertinent to public health; and engage in the community and professional service.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Of course, IHLs are not the only institutions that provides education, research, and service.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, it would be useful to tap on IHLs as additional resources.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   In my English speech just now, I touched on several matters that I hope the Government can clarify.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In Jalan Besar GRC, for instance, where many of its residents are senior citizens, I am concerned about their health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And I hope that they will make full use of the Healthier SG initiative.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that MOH can provide some clarification on the issue of resources, both in terms of doctors and community partners, who are able to support our seniors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that the quantity and quality of these resources will not be affected.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, for senior citizens who are less mobile, frequent visits to doctors may prove to be challenging.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, how does MOH intend to engage and support them?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, I was grateful that many of our seniors, who have difficulty getting around, could be visited by doctors and get vaccinated.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that the same effort can be made to support them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, consultations for senior citizens may require a longer time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, I am concerned about the impact on the quality of support for our seniors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Fourth is about the caregivers of the elderly who have worked wholeheartedly and tirelessly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope they are allowed to register the elderly under their care.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will enable doctors to prepare a more holistic and inclusive health plan for both of them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My final point is related to the use of digital devices.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our seniors have gone a long way in preparing themselves digitally.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, some are worried about the rapid advancement of technology and applications that continue to evolve.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition, many are also anxious and afraid of online scams.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, how does MOH plan to address their concerns?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that the Minister can elaborate on the role of mental health in the Healthier SG initiative.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): Madam, please allow me to end by sharing a personal anecdote.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Last December, I had a health scare and I conceded that at 43 years old, I just could not catch up with my children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I consulted a doctor friend and after analysing the results, he assured me that I was just too exhausted but highlighted that it is time I put my sports science knowledge into practice.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I started the New Year with a simple goal of being more active, having a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The first lesson is looking okay or feeling okay, does not mean one is healthy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, the importance of screening cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It not only gives me a peace of mind knowing the results of my screening, but nudged me towards preventive health too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My initial commitment to physical exercise and increased physical activity then manifested into other aspects of health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, I became more conscious of nutrition, cutting down on salt and sugar and eating more vegetables.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I also began to be conscious of my overall well-being, like cutting down on screen time and making sure I have enough sleep.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, lesson number two is health is not just about physical health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A holistic, balanced, sustainable approach to self-care, based on the numerous dimensions of health and wellness, is important – like mental, social and spiritual health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Notably, the people around me became the catalyst and motivation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Family members, friends, colleagues and even my grassroots leaders, were more receptive to my healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, simple things like a healthier food spread, more family activities at the park and shorter meetings in the evenings, makes a lot of difference to our health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These allow me to maintain my newfound healthy habits and encourage others to pick up healthier habits too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, lesson number three – it is always better together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that MOH and community partners like PA plan activities for all the communities – activities that revolve around families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Studies have shown the elderly who stay connected to the family and participate in regular recreational physical activities benefit from a longer life expectancy, better immune system and better mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In this regard, an individual's commitment and the whole community must move towards a healthy lifestyle and make preventive health happen.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I do hope that the plans laid in place will nudge and ease Singaporeans to control and begin a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Those who enjoy good physical and mental health, report high levels of well-being.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: An effective health infrastructure is critical for sustaining per capita income.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Poor health keeps people from fulfilling their potential." That was a quote by Baroness Philippa Stroud, CEO of Legatum Institute, a thinktank in London.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), a well-functioning healthcare system requires a steady financing mechanism, a properly trained and adequately paid workforce, well-maintained facilities and access to reliable information to base decisions on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, as reflected in Figure 1 in the White Paper, Singapore has been able to achieve good health outcomes, improving our healthcare system, without incurring substantially higher levels of healthcare expenditure.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is not by chance that Singapore has been able to come out of the COVID-19 pandemic with relatively low deaths.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How we have emerged from COVID-19 reflects the resilience of our healthcare system, of our institutions and most of all, of our Government and our people.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Kudos especially to the generations of healthcare professionals and policy-makers who have strategically enabled us to more than survive COVID-19, and to emerge from COVID-19 stronger together.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Healthier SG White Paper, which is being debated in the House today, is timely.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is faced with a rapidly ageing population, and we can expect, therefore, an increase in the proportion of people living with diabetes, hypertension and other chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As the saying goes, "Prevention is always better than cure." We need to shift our emphasis from reactively caring for those who fall seriously ill, to proactively preventing individuals from falling ill.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, health screening, a healthy lifestyle and education are the key pillars to disease prevention.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we need to sharpen our focus on the value of care, recognising that there is a cost to care.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Brent James, a renowned clinician and Doctor of Medicine who was the Chief Quality Officer for over 30 years at Intermountain Healthcare and a senior advisor with Health Catalyst as well as co-author of a book, "To Err is Human", suggests that Value of Care =   divided by cost.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Prevention and going upstream has been proven to be the best way to improve clinical outcome.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The community also plays a part in the reshaping of our healthcare model toward one that involves every resident and not just when they become a patient.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to share two initiatives where I personally witnessed the community in action, and the impact on the health and well-being of the seniors as well as the volunteers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Makan at Block 52 Marine Terrace is a programme by Caritas' Montfort Care Family Service Centre (FSC).

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Seniors in the neighbourhood are encouraged to come together at the GoodLife!

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Makan community kitchen to prepare, cook and share their meals with one another, and more importantly to listen to one another's stories and to learn and support each other.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SHARE A POT® is another community initiative which brings seniors together around a pot of hot nutritious soup for them to enjoy, and also to rally each other to grow stronger and live well with broth and brawn.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: During COVID-19, SHARE A POT® went online and did its part to help seniors to stay connected.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These kinds of initiatives can become a part of the Healthier SG community partnership.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I applaud Healthier SG for the comprehensive holistic approach that it has taken.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is a lot to be done but we will need the whole of Singapore to be committed to act for a healthier Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Continued dialogue with all stakeholders to clarify issues and collaborate on solutions as we take this forward will be imperative.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For the rest of my speech, I will cover three areas.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: First, going upstream with resident and family physician relationship.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For example, at Intermountain, they incentivise the Primary Care Network to keep people out of hospitals as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Healthier SG is enlisting the primary care providers to play the central role in this healthcare model.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This will cement the place of family medicine in delivering holistic and coordinated healthcare to all patients, reduce doctor and clinic hopping and have the potential to ultimately improve rationalisation of specialist care by public hospitals.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone I have spoken with agrees that this is certainly a step in the right direction, but cautions that as in all things, the devil is in the details.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How to implement and to implement it right from the start is the big question.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Here are some of the questions which we hope MOH can clarify.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While it is good for a patient to come under a fixed doctor or clinic, it may not always translate in practice.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For example, patients seen at polyclinics often do not get to see the same doctor at every visit.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can a resident be enrolled with more than one GP so that there is a second opinion or a back-up doctor in case the enrolled doctor is on vacation or at a conference?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How does the enrolment work for the family paediatrician, the family dental surgeon, the eye doctor and others?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: By the way, will health screening include regular eye screening and dental screening?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What happens to the residents who do not enrol?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will it work for residents with company provided or insurance provided panel of doctors?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can the employees consider the GP clinics of the healthcare partners as their enrolled GP?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think it is good also for research – comparing the different groups, how they adopt and enrol themselves into such a programme.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next, the plan to use technology to help implement this programme is laudable and should be explored.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I love the idea of using the HealthHub app as a digital reminder to patients.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To close the loop, there can be digital reminders in-built into the electronic medical record system, which prompts the doctor to check on the progress of the healthcare plan and ensure timely implementation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To take it one step further, appointments with relevant care team members can also be considered to be implemented online.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, the IT system, the health communications network and the National Electronic Health Records system are critical for the successful implementation of this initiative.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: MOH has done very well as it is in this space but will need to continue to invest as more still needs to be done to ensure system up-time, efficient sharing and update of the patient's health records while ensuring data is secure and personal data duly protected.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There will also be a need for trained doctors, nurses and staff to engage, educate and support the patients in the enrolment and transition journey.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What help and support will MOH provide to help the GPs and clinics transition to the level of digital that will enable them to perform their role in this healthcare model?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: According to Dr David M Eddy, the father of evidence-based medicine, it is now well studied and clear that "complexity of modern medicine exceeds the capacity of the unaided expert mind.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Solo reliance on the craft of medicine is scientifically untenable." It has been found that the best way forward is to develop evidence-based best practice protocol, blend it into clinical workflow, embed data systems to track protocol variations and strongly advocate that clinicians apply the protocol but subject the protocol to continuous improvement based on patient need, and thereby improving the protocol in a continuous loop applying Deming's Lean Six Sigma principles.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Clinicians globally have found this approach to improve clinical quality and drive better clinical outcomes over time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I read from the White Paper that our Singapore medical and clinical professionals are exploring such best practice methodologies and I applaud it.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In spite of the best efforts of the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), GovTech and their volunteers, there is still a large group of seniors who may not be digitally savvy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Will we consider similar initiative like they did in Japan where the neighbourhood postman becomes the point of contact for this group of vulnerable seniors?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For vulnerable elders, will home care and support for end-of-life be part of this programme?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We will need to enable the caregivers and the elderly themselves to transition with dignity and with comfort.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In summary, the initiative is an excellent one.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In the long run, it would lead to Singaporeans leading healthier and more productive lives.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Whenever she is asked, "What is your secret, Auntie Lily, for a long and healthy, happy life?", Mom's answer is "Use it or you'll lose it." Mdm Deputy Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The last time MOH published a White Paper was 30 years ago.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That paper was on affordable health care and it was a landmark paper that went on to define the development of our healthcare system over the last 30 years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This White Paper shows how urgent and important our challenge of bending the healthcare cost curve is.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I had two key considerations in mind as I prepared this speech.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, because the challenge before us is so important and so urgent, we must take a thorough and critical look at every piece of the Healthier SG strategy and leave no stone unturned.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I will make quite a number of points in my speech.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But second, I will focus only on the strategy – and the key strategic pieces – and set aside for now questions that are of a more operational nature, even if there are a number of these.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: With this preamble, let me lay out my views on the White Paper on Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, Healthier SG must be inclusive because it goes to the heart of our social compact, and our social compact must, in turn, be for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On this point, I have three key questions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How do we ensure Healthier SG is inclusive socio-economically?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We know the lower-income segment has poorer health outcomes and a lower propensity for health-seeking behaviours for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, I wished the White Paper had included specific mention of how we plan to support our lower-income segment through additional, differentiated measures to remove the particular barriers to health-seeking behaviours that this segment faces.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For example, because travelling distance may be an especially salient barrier for this segment, do we need to be particularly deliberate in ensuring proximity of family doctors in both GP clinics and polyclinics to our rental communities?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How can we improve seemingly basic things like nutrition, sleep and smoking cessation through targeted interventions for this segment because these things may not be basic for them?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How can we help this segment find time and cognitive bandwidth to exercise, when time and cognitive bandwidth may be particularly scarce for this group?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because the social needs of this segment are especially high, how can we be particularly deliberate in enabling GPs to work with community partners to address such social needs?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How can we better bring Social Service Offices and social service agencies into the framework of healthcare clusters and Primary Care Networks so that we strengthen and tighten the nexus between social services and health for the low income?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Who will have primary responsibility to pull all the assets together to wrap around the enrolled person?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I wish the White Paper had provided some insights to these questions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The second question that I have is how do we ensure Healthier SG is inclusive digitally?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But we know that a number of seniors have dropped out of exercise groups when these groups went onto Healthy 365 for the sign-up and bidding of slots.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They dropped out because they did not know how to do this on Healthy 365.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Seniors have also given lots of feedback about polyclinics and their recent shift towards more and more of an appointment-based system in lieu of walk-ins.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Seniors wonder how they go about booking polyclinic appointments online or on mobile?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If they call the hotline, what number should they call?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How long do they have to wait for their calls to be answered?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The White Paper further mentions HealthHub as the second "digital front door" for every individual's health action plan.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But each of the three healthcare clusters also has its own app – its own "digital front door".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, put together, these could add convenience to users but they may also confuse them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The point is: while digital is essential and we must have digital channels, we have to also preserve traditional touchpoints.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, we must provide optionality in the key touchpoints of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Optionality by providing both traditional and digital options rather than substituting the traditional with the digital.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need optionality as a core design principle of key Healthier SG touchpoints.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The third question I have is, how do we ensure Healthier SG is Inclusive for All Healthcare Professionals?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The word "doctor" was mentioned more than 160 times in the White Paper, unsurprisingly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Compared to "nurse" and "nursing", which were mentioned 22 times, "pharmacist" was mentioned six times and "allied health", seven times.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, the doctor appears overwhelmingly to be the centre of gravity in the Healthier SG strategy, but what about the roles of a nurse, a pharmacist and an allied health professional?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Is there room for more equal roles, more co-leadership to shape preventive care in the community?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because, let us pin the flag squarely on the mast.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, it is not complex medicine per se, but medicine that is person-centred, relationship-driven and certainly high-value.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And in this respect, nurses are very good at titrating medication and at engaging, motivating and cajoling.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These are key activities in preventing chronic diseases and in managing chronic diseases, that nurses can be very good at.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And in comparison, what is more exclusive to doctors is the gestalt to diagnose diseases and to provide prognoses of disease trajectories.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I wish we had a fuller articulation of the vision for nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals, including medical social workers, in the overall Healthier SG strategy – all practicing at the top of their respective licenses in the community, alongside doctors, to prevent and manage chronic diseases across our population.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I think we also need a mindset shift in our population, from a doctor-centric view to one that respects all healthcare professionals including nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals, and what they can do.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In summary, my first broad point: our Healthier SG strategy needs to be inclusive socio-economically, inclusive digitally and inclusive for all healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My second broad point is that manpower planning will be key in Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The most natural question in this regard is how many family doctors, nurses and so on, would we need to fully realise the strategy, but I prefer to leave this to MOH's COS debate next year.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think that would be the best time to discuss manpower numbers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Today, I would like to raise some other points about manpower planning.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, for the public healthcare sector, we need stability to become a key principle in manpower planning.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Family doctors and physicians in our public polyclinics will take on a significant portion of the Healthier SG workload even as we enable GPs to step up and to do more.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, within the polyclinics, I would like to ask what happens to enrolment arrangements when family doctors and physicians within these polyclinics move, get rotated or cross-deployed, as they routinely do.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fundamentally, are Singaporeans going to be enrolled to a polyclinic or to a particular doctor within the polyclinic?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Currently, the healthcare clusters have principal responsibility for this strategic manpower function.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Taking this responsibility off the clusters and moving it to the Ministry level will ensure a coherent manpower planning strategy nationwide in support of national desired outcomes, and as importantly, this would free up strategic bandwidth within the clusters for them to step up to their very important new roles and responsibilities as regional health managers under Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Besides clinical manpower planning, we would need equally robust manpower planning for our cybersecurity and healthcare IT talent.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As the White Paper noted and many Members have noted, IT is a critical enabler and quite often a pain point.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the competition for tech talent has never been more intense and will probably intensify further.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, how does the Ministry plan to manage the competition and secure the healthcare IT and cybersecurity talent it needs to deliver on Healthier SG?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need to get this right, because this is about securing public trust in the protection of their healthcare data, and it is also about securing the trust of professional users in the usability and inter-operability of our healthcare IT systems.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In summary, my second broad point about manpower planning for Healthier SG: we need this to enhance clinical manpower stability in polyclinics, we need to free up strategic bandwidth for healthcare clusters and we need to secure critical IT talent.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My third broad point is: let us remember to integrate downstream even as we look to integrate upstream.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is timely and apt that Healthier SG emphasises upstream interventions, primary care, preventive care, collaboration between GPs and community partners to promote health.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: All this is good, but we also need to pay an equal amount of attention to integrating much more downstream.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, strengthening the integration between GPs and specialists that are based largely in our hospitals.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: GPs have spoken of the need to become more equal partners in care, vis-à-vis their specialist counterparts.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: GPs want to feel that after a referral is made to a specialist in a hospital, there is tight two-way communication and the loop is closed, and GPs do not feel like they are losing their patients to the system, and in the system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Of course, details about such integration between GPs and specialists ought to be worked out by the healthcare clusters but I wished the White Paper had made a stronger mention of our larger, strategic intent in this regard.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For Healthier SG to really tackle chronic diseases across our population, we need to integrate much more, both upstream and downstream, across the health and healthcare value chain and address all archetypes, including those with more advanced diseases and requiring more specialised care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I hope as we progress in this multi-year Healthier SG journey, we will keep pushing the boundaries on healthcare financing as a key lever to drive integration and what is currently described in the White Paper will not be become our eventual end-state.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My last broad point on Healthier SG: in certain aspects of the strategy, let us avoid optimising at the margins, only to blunt the tip of the spear.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Motion before us today has only three limbs and community-based programmes are one of the limbs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, the White Paper also emphasised that, "good health is sustained through everyday choices and habits, which take place outside healthcare facilities" – outside the clinic.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, community-based, health-promoting programmes are a centre of gravity of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These programmes in the community are what I would call "the tip of our Healthier SG spear" and as Minister mentioned in his opening speech, they occupy that space and the time between the visits to the clinic, to the GP, so they are really important.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They are the tip of our spear and we must keep it sharp.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Keeping it sharp means amongst other things, ensuring that there is adequate funding to this part of the strategy, and as importantly, we need to rethink how we measure effectiveness and efficiency of such funding.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If the purpose of these exercise groups is simply community programming, then I would agree with this approach because we need to be prudent.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But if such community exercise programmes are so important in Healthier SG, if these programmes are the tip of our Healthier SG spear, then we need a different approach.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need to have K-pop classes available in the mornings and evenings on weekdays and on weekends.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need to have Zumba and Stretch Band and HIIT classes equally available, mornings or evenings, weekdays or weekends.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Xie, you have one minute to round up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Indeed, we should welcome such redundancy and it could serve as a useful buffer.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: If we focus instead on optimising capacity and funding efficiency at the margins for these programmes, we will blunt the larger intended purpose of the programmes under the Healthier SG strategy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I will make one last point about the community and that is eating and food choices in the community.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: But this is precisely why we must do it, and we will do it together to secure a better and healthier future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This Motion clearly emphasises the need for and the importance of living healthily to start at a young age.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This will then pave the way for healthy daily living and mobility as we grow old to enjoy the fruits of our hard work during our early age.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, unions also want to ensure that our fellow workers can continue working beyond the retirement age, knowing that one of the criteria is about the medical condition of the worker.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: My speech today will cover the role of unions in strongly focusing on preventive care and building strong partnerships with community partners to support our fellow workers who are taking care of their own health and wellness.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While many may be aware of the workplace grievances handled and social benefits provided by our NTUC social enterprises and affiliated merchants, unions do so much more than that.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, we need to provide unique, value-added services to the remaining 90% of our members, one of which is to provide support and subsidies for our members in terms of health and wellness.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Unions continuously innovate to serve our members better because, for the unions, it is "Members First, Workers Always".

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to enlighten the House on the three different ways that our unions and our leaders have supported members and workers in the preventive healthcare journey.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This role is not new to the unions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Minimally, we encourage our management partners to provide regular complimentary health screening for our members and workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Regular health screening is critical to identify any symptoms of sickness that each worker has, and they could then be provided with the necessary early intervention measures before the sickness worsens.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While providing these complimentary health screenings looks simple, mobilising and encouraging workers to take part is never an easy task.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There were times when some management partners wanted to discontinue this, due to the low take-up rates, but our union leaders rejected strongly and worked with management partners, to maximise outreach efforts to increase and optimise participation.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to share some examples of two unions that have gone beyond what their management partners do for their workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: First, is the Union of Security Employees, in short, USE, which has set up a healthcare advisory booth provided by the HPB at their customer service centre for any member to walk in and request for assistance.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: These members take the opportunity to know and understand health advisories while waiting for their turn to be called up.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Another example is one of mine, the Union of Power and Gas Employees, in short, UPAGE.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We started this movement many years ago with one of our management partners.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are happy to share that most of our represented companies today provide basic complimentary health screening for our workers either at their workplace or at a designated healthcare or medical centre to provide that flexibility for the workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to this, UPAGE started to provide additional subsidy since 2018 to encourage our members to go for additional testing during their health screening.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are only able to do this because of our close partners' strong support and generosity for workers in the power sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Please note that this subsidy applies to UPAGE members only, not for all.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With so many support measures and subsidy provisions, I always believe that the union membership fee would be beneficial to all, if not many.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I would call on the Ministry to acknowledge and work together with the Labour Movement and our affiliated unions as one of your community partners to reach out, engage and encourage our fellow workers to strive for a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This will then align with the Government's vision of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to put forward four requests to the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: First, can the Ministry provide a guide on the kind of medical checks that everyone should prioritise for their own well-being at different age groups?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Next, can the Ministry provide more designated centres for our fellow Singaporeans to do their health screening?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   This Motion, that calls us to strive towards a healthier society, is the right move.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It will help us to achieve a healthier life compared to a situation where we have to suffer in pain, regardless of whether we are young or old.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Among the challenges that our society faces are diabetes and being overweight, just like me, which can lead to various other diseases.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, this must be changed from early on.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We must gradually change our eating habits that always crave for sugary drinks and fatty food, so that we will choose less sugary drinks and healthier food, as well as consume lesser portions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I have personally witnessed family members, relatives and friends who had to live in pain at a young age, as early as their thirties, suffering from various diseases, such as diabetes, high blood pressure and so on.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There is an Arabian proverb which says that every disease has its cure except death, but that does not mean that we should let ourselves go until we get sick, and then we start to get medication.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It is certainly very challenging to change our unhealthy habits into healthy ones.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must accept that this change is meant for our own good.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We also do not want to trouble our children when we get old, whereby, they need to take care of their sick parents and have difficulty leading their own lives.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let our old age be full of healthy activities, such as playing with our grandchildren and taking care of them, being able to walk to the mosque and so on.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: All these can be achieved by ensuring that we lead a healthy life from a young age.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It is true that death can happen at any age, but a healthy and active body and mind will be more beneficial for us.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not leave our twilight years to chance, but instead, we ensure that we remain healthy for ourselves and for our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The White Paper has set a bold direction and has completely redesigned the way we deliver healthcare – from one that is reactively caring to one that is proactively preventive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we are more user-led in solutions, we will be better able to identify patterns and similarities where solutions can be scaled up.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This White Paper shows our ability to turn a potential adversity of the silver tsunami into a possible silver lining.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We cater to our seniors first and eventually scale this to a nationwide system for those above 40.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In time, I hope this would be scaled up to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most importantly, Singaporeans now know that this Government will co-design a preventive health plan with them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This partnership will require every Singaporean to play their part in co-solutioning.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I rise in support of the White Paper on Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many are pleased with the preventive measures in place.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To enhance this White Paper, some came forward to share their opinions, which will be categorised into two main sections.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, I will share concerns from the perspective of the individual Singaporean, following which, I will touch on ecosystem partnerships that are required to scale up Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I will now touch on the ground sentiment from residents I have interacted with.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, would there be a need for Singaporeans to indicate a reason for wanting to switch clinics?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the increasing levels of tech literacy, Singaporeans are also turning to virtual doctor appointments and companies are offering such services as part of their medical benefits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whether it is changing GPs or being able to access virtual clinician services, it will be very important for this programme to allow Singaporeans to make choices at key life stages.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, while the GP would be the critical first touchpoint in this relationship, it would be ideal for individual Singaporeans to have a fitness coach who can journey with him or her on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A little exercise goes a long way and the new Singapore National Physical Activity Guidelines launched by national bodies Sport Singapore and the Health Promotion Board rationalise official guidance towards healthy activity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having access to fitness coaches would allow for a deeper collaboration between MOH with SportsSG, HPB and People's Association, especially with the vast range of community fitness centres that the Government has invested in for Singaporeans over the years.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By understanding that every Singaporean will need a fitness coach or ambassador or advisor nearer to where he or she lives to execute this preventive health plan, we keep our communities close to our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Much like the relationship between a resident and a GP is a personal one that takes into account individual preferences, so will the relationship be with a fitness coach.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To provide Singaporeans with greater choices, would MOH look into collaborating with private fitness service providers?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As these service providers are all across the island in different fitness centres and gyms, they are well-placed to provide community care.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: MOH could also consider engaging self-employed persons (SEPs) with domain expertise as Healthier SG ambassadors and health coaches.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such approaches will, in turn, encourage diversity of offerings to cater to different individuals and tap on expertise and knowledge in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It would be a missed opportunity if we do not harness the choice private sector and self-employed individuals provide to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will keep Healthier SG relevant to our citizens' preferences and also enable new innovative services like digital clinician services to participate.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the systems level, designing this programme to have high inter-operability with innovative delivery models will enable Healthier SG to tap on the private sector's ability to discover leaner and effective models of preventive healthcare.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will ensure longer-term success, especially with the backdrop of manpower constraints and rising costs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Next, I will touch on the ecosystem partnerships that are required to scale up Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As shared, employers are providing employees with medical care plans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Healthier SG's proactive, preventive approach needs to harmonise with employers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The strong support of the Singapore Business Federation and the Singapore National Employers Federation will be needed to help companies to remodel corporate health plans with this new approach.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many Singaporeans rely on the provision of medical benefits from their employers and are restricted to a fixed panel of doctors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, in some cases, such services are provided by corporatised clinics where doctors are less rooted to a specific clinic or location.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another added complication is when an employer changes healthcare providers or when an employee moves to a new company.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The area of interest of Singaporeans will be the co-payment or full payment by their employers under their existing employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers need to embrace Healthier SG so that every Singaporean feels assured that this is in line with their personal healthcare journey.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is all part of an evolving workplace environment and, as such, MOM needs to work very closely with MOH for this initiative.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another key ecosystem partner in the provision of healthcare is insurers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such preventive efforts need to be rewarded and if our insurance actuaries can understand the percentage of population making serious efforts to live better, their calculations of risks need to take this into consideration.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such co-related pricing will make our Integrated Plans relevant and useful.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would provide another incentive for individuals to take charge of their preventive health plan.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, on the micro level, let us place individual Singaporeans first in this journey by providing virtual doctors and fitness coaches by tapping on the private sector for more options.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, at the macro level, let us engage employers and insurers in recalibrating benefits, costs and incentivise them to better align with our model.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The easier we make this to follow, the more we can guide Singaporeans to a society where we can all keep costs sustainable, maintain a comfortable standard of living and, most importantly, age well in the decades to come.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This gives me an opportunity to share with them about healthy living, a key theme that I promote in Jalan Kayu besides sustainability and intergenerational bonding.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An apple a day keeps the doctor away – this 19th century proverb sounds simple, but it is not always easy to follow.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my COS speech in March, I spoke about my concern for the increased prevalence of chronic diseases, such as high blood pressure, high blood sugar and high cholesterol in our population, not just amongst our seniors but also in some of our younger people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recognise that our national Budget for healthcare will inevitably have to increase in order to create better health and quality of life outcomes for our people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I also suggested to manage the workload on our healthcare professionals by empowering Singaporeans to take more ownership of our own health and participate whenever possible with our healthcare professionals on our treatment or health plans.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I thus read the Healthier SG White Paper with great delight, that we are, indeed, embarking as a nation towards a much healthier way of living, with stronger emphasis on preventive care, building relationships and trust with our family doctors to maintain our health, supported by each of our own community, right in our neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a transformative healthcare policy, in my view.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will also require a transformative mindset from our people to fully reap the fruit of this healthcare policy breakthrough.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we can take heart that we will have our neighbours to walk the journey ahead with us together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For my Jalan Kayu residents, you have your Member of Parliament who will walk this journey with you.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All good policies can only be as good as how well they are implemented.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is when the tyres hit the road, so to speak.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will focus my speech on clarifications with MOH on three implementation considerations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One, awareness of subsidised preventive health screening; two, enhance community partnership and participatory approach to collective health; and three, enabling seniors through simplifying healthcare technology.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And what improvement does MOH aim to achieve under Healthier SG?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From my Meet-the-People (MPS) experience, whenever I asked my residents in need about their awareness of Screen for Life programme, I will usually draw a blank look.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the handful who may be aware, they would admit to me their fears of finding out illnesses that will cost them more to treat and affect their jobs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe for preventive health behaviours to improve significantly in Singapore, MOH must invest more in creating the right awareness and assurance of benefits of preventive health screening and a follow-through care that Singaporeans can expect.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This should be done in more mass media and vernacular languages, including even some dialects, to correct the misinformation that screenings will lead to more problems.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The White Paper proposed to rally a group of community care partners to support residents in leading healthier lives.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The White Paper mentioned the People's Association (PA), SportsSG and Agency for Integrated Care (AIC)'s Silver Generation Office (SGO) to help organise healthy living programmes for residents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It also mentioned plans to tap on the eldercare centres to serve as the community care connectors for seniors, to help them follow through the recommended lifestyle interventions prescribed by their family doctors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although I am fully supportive of this approach after speaking with a few GPs in my Jalan Kayu constituency since the release of the White Paper, I noted their concerns on the bandwidth to activate such community partnership to care for their patients who are my residents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There were also questions on seniors who are living in the private estates, such as those who are living in the Seletar Hills East and Jalan Kayu private estates where some of my older residents live.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The existing eldercare centres are usually located nearer to rental blocks of each constituency.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is good as we should always prioritise the health of our seniors first, given their higher risk of developing health challenges.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The White Paper proposed the HealthHub app and Healthy 365 app as the digital front doors of Healthier SG to encourage and nudge residents to adopt healthier lifestyles.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that the HealthHub app will have a digitally enabled health plan where residents can access and check their health outcomes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will be complemented by the Healthy 365 app which allows tracking of physical activities and diets, as well as supports their access to community activities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Like fellow hon Member Dr Tan Wu Meng, several studies that were published between 2020 and 2021 shared that there is lower interest in adopting mobile health applications and digital health services amongst seniors despite the convenience that it presented during the COVID-19 lockdown.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not only does this phrase demonstrates our understanding of preventive care, but it is also the core concept of the Healthier SG White Paper.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through preventive care, we can help every Singaporean improve their health and quality of life.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our ageing society, preventive care can also reduce the cost and burden on the healthcare system and individuals.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If you want everyone to be healthier, we must empower them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I strongly support the initiatives put forward in the White Paper.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, I would like to make three suggestions to the implementation of Healthier SG to help residents better accept preventive care measures to improve their health.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MOH currently has the Screen for Life programme which covers chronic illnesses and some common cancers, for example, colorectal cancer.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that MOH will further strengthen public education under Healthier SG, and even use Malay, Tamil or even dialects to reach out so that more Singaporeans, especially the seniors, will understand the benefits of preventive health checks.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the community, we should also have the regional health system to help identify common illnesses in each local constituency through the coordination of the three regional healthcare clusters, and work with Government agencies such as the People's Association and SGOs, as well as the residents, to organise healthy activities that benefit the residents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this way, residents will be able to take ownership of their own health, making it easier for them to accept preventive care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that when the seniors experience the benefits of using these apps, they will help promote Healthier SG through word of mouth.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): In closing, I would like to speak up for a group of healthcare professionals who have become my friends in my four-and-a-half years of involvement in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are the family doctors working both in GP clinics and public polyclinics.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are a group of highly intelligent, motivated and committed healers in our community.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The falling ill of one family doctor in a busy polyclinic can mean the rest taking up a much higher patient load for the day, sacrificing lunchtime or even any breaks in that day.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that MOH will continually invest in helping them reduce unnecessary administrative workload.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is no doubt that Healthier SG will take time – I think at least a decade – before we can see a healthier population coming to fruition.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nevertheless, as a strong advocate of healthy living and active ageing, I commend MOH for taking this bold step towards reshaping Singapore's population health.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the collective and united efforts of all Singaporeans, we will get there.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding my considerations raised, I strongly support the White Paper on Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All of us as individuals need to consciously take steps on a daily basis to minimise the risks of illnesses and diseases, with care and guidance from our doctors and their teams of support professionals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of the things we can do are quite achievable, though not always easy for some of us, such as taking the necessary medications on time, watching our diets and exercising.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Following up with doctors familiar with our health histories regularly will help to introduce some discipline into our lives, as we have to be accountable to them too.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I understand the intent of this clause, the reality is that there will be some patients who have difficulties being compliant and it is not reasonable to expect the doctors to control their patients.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will there be situations where doctors may choose not to continue with the management of very challenging patients?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another question is regarding the additional administrative and IT set-up and maintenance requirements necessary for this scheme.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Going forward, inputting data and maintaining the IT system in a clinic will need more manpower and IT knowledge, particularly to ensure a high level of cybersecurity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While MOH has stated that it will support the GPs in this aspect, what will happen if a patient's preferred GP chooses not to join the network due to the clinic's constraints?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yes, patients can select another doctor but it is not so easy, especially when a strong relationship has been built and, more importantly, the doctor's medicine works well for the patients.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would then mean that patients have to doctor hop before finding the right one that suits them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some residents are also concerned that more costs for the GPs will be involved and they worry as a result, the medical costs will be higher for residents who see GPs under this Healthier SG initiative.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, there may be some non-generic drugs which will continue to be priced above the limits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will patients be given a choice to opt for such drugs via personal top-ups and MOH to provide greater subsidies because these drugs work well for them?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last, I would like to ask about the role of TCMPs in the Healthier SG model.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: TCMPs have been playing a significant role in helping residents, particularly the elderly, to better manage their health over the long term.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) methods often emphasise holistic care and can be complementary to our current system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If the Ministry is concerned about the standard and consistent TCM healthcare delivery, how about setting up a system similar to our present Western medical framework and ensure its integration into our healthcare system?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Last, I would like to ask about the role of Traditional Chinese Medicine Practitioners (TCMPs) in the Healthier SG model.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: TCMPs have been playing a significant role in helping residents, particularly the elderly, to better manage their health over the long term.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: TCM methods often emphasise holistic care and can be complementary to our current system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If the Ministry is concerned about the standard and consistency of TCM healthcare delivery, how about setting up a system, similar to our present western medical framework, and ensure its integration into our healthcare system?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I concur that prevention is undoubtedly better than cure, not only because the former can be easier and more affordable as compared to the latter but also because individuals and their loved ones can minimise the risk of experiencing a lower quality of life that comes with chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is well understood that prevention of chronic diseases is achieved by addressing risk factors before falling sick whether through healthy living, better dieting or exercising regularly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although doing so seems simple and straightforward, these actions are easier said than done.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of us are used to long working hours, a sedentary work life, late nights and, for better or worse, various cuisines within easy reach whether day or night – all of which contributes to a less than healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With that said, it is possible to return to good healthy habits, but it will take some time, effort and some encouragement.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Similar to the Singapore Green Plan, I view the Government's initiations of Healthier SG as a whole-of-nation movement which seeks to rally bold and collective actions, to transform our healthcare system and to encourage all Singaporeans to come together and take steps towards better health.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The funding support from the Government and community partners will come in vital to kickstart this project and steer it towards the right direction.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition, this committee, with extensive community experience and networks from its members, can also provide useful guidance for healthy lifestyle clubs, thus further advancing the objectives of Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One example of how such funds can be utilised would be to encourage GPs to organise community outreach events to foster lasting relationships between residents and their family doctors.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The GPs can be the first line of support for many Singaporeans living in our heartlands.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of these neighbourhood GPs have served the community for years or even decades and earned the trust and reputation of being the resident experts in all health-related matters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Other funding support can go towards encouraging more community organisations to set up healthy lifestyle interest groups and for its champions to form strong, sustainable partnerships with the community to promote healthy lifestyle activities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, in my capacity as a community volunteer and subsequently as advisor, I have witnessed many inspiring examples of how healthy living has been promoted among residents through health awareness and wellness programmes initiated by the grassroots, such as the Northwest CDC's qigong, dance fit and brisk walking clubs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The provisions for support for these interest groups and their events will empower them to further enrich the lives of many of my residents in Woodgrove by providing a wider range of healthy activities to choose from.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition to that, allocating funding support for passionate and committed healthy lifestyle champions, such as instructors and coordinators would also help grant a renewed sense of purpose for retirees looking to making a positive effect.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These individuals are more than just active participants in their programmes of choice.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They also serve as the glue within their own communities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Through them, I have seen many friendships forged among the members and their trainers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even outside training, they will gather to organise potluck sessions, sharing healthy cooking tips.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Woodgrove, our active dance fit club members often help to bring more joy to events organised by the Residents' Committees, such as by choreographing a dance performance with them donned in special handsewn costumes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Picking up healthy living tips and sports can be interesting and enable the creation of more family bonding opportunities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One such example is the Woodgrove Badminton Clinic, which was jointly organised by our Woodgrove Community Sports Club and the Singapore Badminton Association, with support from Horlicks.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the event, apart from inviting our national team's shuttlers Crystal Wong and Jing Yujia to coach our little ones and their parents on badminton strokes, a health talk was also carried out by Horlicks, sharing tips on possible diets to follow before and after exercising.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Next month, Woodgrove will also be collaborating with ActiveSG to organise a community sports day at the Woodland Stadium, encouraging families to participate in various sporting activities such as air badminton, table tennis, Zumba and K-cardio.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In our Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC, the recent launch of the Healthy Living card game in Marsiling's "Living The Life Carnival" was also received positively by elderly residents and their families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this game, players are supposed to collect cards depicting good health habits in order to win.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Through playing the game, these cards will serve to inculcate players with these healthy living habits.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Good health habits begin at a young age.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a community effort, Woodgrove is working on expanding the reach of this Healthy Living card game by encouraging our youngest residents to play with their families, hopefully inspiring them to a healthier lifestyle while promoting family bonding opportunities at the same time.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One way to encourage healthier eating is to educate the public about new healthier alternatives.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One good example of this would be the recent introduction of the lower sodium salt campaign.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that the public may find it useful to learn more about the science behind these healthier options from credible sources, such as HPB, so that they may be better informed about the food choices to make.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Disseminating the information through mass media will be very helpful in this regard.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As such, in order to make the Healthier SG movement of success, there is a need to call for a mindset shift.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   Last month, Woodgrove division, in collaboration with Sian Chay Medical Institution, organised a free health talk, sharing with seniors tips on healthy living and post-recovery from COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many participants shared with me that they prefer to see a TCM doctor first when they are not feeling well.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The reasons vary, including cheaper consultation fees, for example, Sian Chay and Chung Hwa Medical Institution provide free or low-priced consultation and treatment.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To me, both Chinese and Western medicine offer benefits, integrating both would bring a win-win situation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For them a short trip to the MPS is, itself, a difficult journey.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As I learn more about their circumstances, I often ask myself whether the quality of their lives might have been drastically better if they have had the correct interventions and advice at an earlier stage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
