text: I tend to see this particularly in residents of less means.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On today's Motion on the Healthier SG White Paper, I wish to focus my speech on three areas: one, the potential of Healthier SG: two, clarifications around capitation funding; and three, to conclude with the importance of a whole-of-society buy-in.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A key thrust of the Healthier SG White Paper is that residents will be encouraged to enrol with a family doctor even when they are well so that they may benefit from advice regarding social interventions to adopt healthier lifestyles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is envisaged that the doctor will take charge of the overall well-being of the resident for a period of time, rather than to treat the patient on an episodic basis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This holds much promise for a healthier nation overall.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In moving the Motion yesterday, the Health Minister assessed that the returns of better health outcomes from Healthier SG would take maybe eight to 10 years before tangible results might be seen.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, on returns based on dollars and cents terms, there are encouraging experiences from overseas.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Prevention strategies have been shown to make economic sense as they are substantially cost-saving.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is well-known that it is preferable for healthcare systems to aim to prevent ill health rather than to subsequently treat it from a financial standpoint.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Five years ago, a systematic review was published, assessing the returns from investing in public health interventions such as promoting well-being and preventing ill health in society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although we do not yet know what returns Healthier SG might bring in dollars and cents, there is reason to be optimistic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From the healthcare system standpoint, it is vital that the focus of prevention ease the pressure on our acute facilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even as we debate today, residents experienced very busy A&E departments in public hospitals in the past months, with patients sometimes waiting more than a day at A&E before being allocated a ward bed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If achieved, these reductions will bring relief to patients and staff at acute facilities and contribute to better care for those most in need.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I have two further observations; first, to seek clarifications on the move to capitation funding and how healthcare outcomes will be safeguarded; and second, to conclude with the importance of a whole-of-society buy-in to the plan.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At Chapter 5 of the White Paper, it is stated that to fund Healthier SG, the Government intends to roll out capitation funding first to family doctors and then to the geographical healthcare clusters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are scant details in the White Paper about how this will be implemented and the Minister yesterday did give a few more details.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As stated in the White Paper, capitation funding will be a shift away from the current funding model based on services provided, commonly called fee for service or FFS models.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry has pointed out that capitation funding is in place in healthcare systems in other countries, such as in Europe, New Zealand and the United States.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yesterday, the Minister pointed out that general practitioners (GPs) here are also not new to the concept.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For Healthier SG, the Minister stated that besides the annual servicing fee paid to healthcare providers, there would still be separate subsidies for patients' medicines and screening.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If successfully implemented, it will go some way towards reducing healthcare inequality.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, capitation funding has been the subject of research in many countries, particularly on whether such funding has led to healthcare providers to function as economic agents, that is, instead of focusing on the patient's best interest, healthcare providers look at the financial bottom-line and behave in certain ways which may not be in the patient's best interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is often not clear whether this was a result of capitation working well by cutting down unnecessary treatments and waste, or whether, on the other hand, patients were, in fact, underserved, that is, not getting adequate treatment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also goes without saying that the level of funding is key.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If capitation funding is pegged more generously, the quality of care would generally be better.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some studies focus on doctors' own assessments of whether the way they treated patients was different and under capitation funding compared to FFS models.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There were indications that some physicians believed that funding had affected their choices of treatment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There has also been concern whether capitation funding would lead to healthcare providers cherry-picking their patients.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other words, with a fixed annual servicing fee, it might make economic sense to choose healthier patients rather than, for instance, older patients with health problems.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Each of us needs to make adjustments to our daily lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate the possible difficulties and inertia, please let me share a personal anecdote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As they continued to order local favourites, such as char kway teow, fried Hokkien mee and others, I asked them whether they had heard about the Healthier SG plan which would be debated in Parliament this week.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They gave me a quizzical look and, without blinking an eye, continued to order more of the same.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides having incentives to consult family doctor regularly, there will also be a need for a supportive infrastructure and to change mindsets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On infrastructure, the Government has built sporting facilities and beautiful park connectors for Singaporeans to exercise in.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides that, healthier food needs to be affordably priced so that less privileged Singaporeans can afford to make healthy choices daily.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Whatever the case, in the final analysis, changing people's deep-seated habits might be the most difficult of all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Motion to focus on preventive care as a key thrust in healthcare should be supported.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It holds the promise of meaningful and fulfilling lives for Singaporeans into old age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And, if implemented well, can help reduce healthcare inequality.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Ministry will clarify in due course how the funding model will be implemented so as to minimise any compromise on health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   I thank MOH for further expanding the role that our clinics and family physicians can play in universal healthcare.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Years ago, some of my Parliamentary colleagues and I proposed to the Government to allow residents to visit neighbourhood clinics instead of polyclinics, while benefiting from the lower outpatient service fees charged by polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since its implementation, the plan has been welcomed by residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also shared feedback from residents at that time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In many cases, residents often perceive that their family doctors were more cordial, reliable and trustworthy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Residents do not need to go to the polyclinics to queue for outpatient services.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They can easily go to the family doctors in their neighbourhoods for treatment and follow-up consultations, hence prevent the deterioration of chronic illnesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, they can obtain early and proper treatment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the last session of Parliament, I talked about "the best doctor", that is, prevention is still the best medicine.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, this White Paper is the best form of medical practice.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is farsighted and looks to the future so that Singaporeans can age in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that under this scheme, residents will have more flexibility to change clinics or GP, if the GP has transferred to another clinic or has left.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Deputy Speaker, Sir, I fully support the excellent proposals in the White Paper on Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This preventive care model is yet another step in our journey to help Singaporeans achieve and maintain their best health and live more good years.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The proposals in this White Paper will further strengthen the role of GPs in the national healthcare framework.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a superior strategy and deserves our full support.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have always believed that our family doctors play an essential role in this endeavour.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Residents find it comfortable to have family doctors with whom they are familiar with to look after their healthcare issues.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe it can be technically done to have all GPs to have online access to patients' records.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we must recognise that there is a need to balance patients' confidentiality and operational efficiency.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some patients may ask for more than necessary, as generic medications are generally more economical.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will patients be given a choice between new and generic medications?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Patients may still find it a burden regarding the choices of new medicines.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope this plan can be expanded soon to allow residents to visit more than one GP at similarly subsidised rates for the management of diseases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some GPs may be more experienced and skilled at managing certain diseases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is because certain GPs may have individual competitive strengths or specialties.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, each patient may like to have a principal GP doctor in attendance and be assisted by such specialists upon referrals.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am concerned because the White Paper has stated that this new model will be outcome-based.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Ministry will not penalise the doctors in charge as these patients should be the ones responsible for their own health.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many GPs clinics, especially those in mature estates, are already overwhelmed with patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some popular clinics, the wait for the face-to-face onboarding health consultation may take days to weeks.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another concern is regarding the use of Healthhub to choose preferred clinics and enroll in Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will assisted support on-site and via helplines be available at the clinic itself or at CCs?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As many seniors are non-IT savvy and some may be illiterate, they will not be able to use the apps after enrolment to monitor their health progress.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They may require simple printed materials to do manual recording.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means that the GPs will have to manually key in the progress reports into the available system to enable monitoring.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is additional work for GPs if they have many of such senior patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For this group of seniors, they will not know how to use apps like Healthy 365, ActiveSG and OnePA to book and pay for activities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They may have to ask the doctors to teach them during their first consultations or even subsequent consultations and this will take up the doctors' time, which could be better used in treating patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another concern is about patients who are not enrolled into Healthier SG at GP clinics.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The clinic assistant will have to remember to charge correct prices for patients under the Healthier SG and non-Healthier SG schemes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the popular clinics, the clinic assistants may be overwhelmed, resulting in longer waits for all patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For residents who do not have chronic diseases to follow up at the GPs, the face-to-face consultation after enrolment via Healthhub will probably be the first and only visit to the GPs under Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I doubt anyone with no sickness would want to see a doctor regularly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If a healthy person sees the GP for their first health consultation under Healthier SG or subsequent follow up, will they be given a medical certificate (MC) or memo to excuse them from their work?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Not long after I landed on US shores for my doctoral studies – a week after 11 September 2001, as it turned out  – I had to confront the behemoth that was the US healthcare system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One of my earliest tasks on arrival was securing medical insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because I was a graduate student, I was enrolled in a plan managed by the university.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The amount was non-trivial, especially for a student confronting US dollar exchange rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in exchange, I was able to see the doctor at any time without paying any fee, including for routine illnesses, such as cough or fever, while also enjoying fully-paid dental and access to world-class hospital facilities and surgical procedures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I was only 25 then, of course, and like most pre-chronic-condition 25-year-olds, I thought I was physiologically invincible and I would never need a doctor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, the insurance plan was mandatory and so I reluctantly signed on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After spending a dozen years embedded in the US medical system, I have come to understand just how painfully convoluted the system was.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The University of California healthcare plan, which I had previously been under, was, as it turns out, a relatively good one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, many plans are far less generous in their terms and costlier to boot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If one were to lose one's job, one would automatically lose one's health insurance – a painful double-whammy of being both unemployed and uninsured.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast to my free-of-charge visits to the university health centre, most insurance plans charge a co-pay per visit, which could amount to $30 or $40 – the amount that I would pay out-of-pocket for any doctor in Singapore, even without insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because I used to think that the Singapore system – where we were assured of world-class medical care at a fraction of the cost – was an amazing healthcare policy success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore managed to contain costs, all while generating impressive and still-improving health outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We appeared to have cracked the code of healthcare financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the global level, our healthcare costs do remain admirable, prompting the New York Times to question in a fawning article as recently as 2017, "What Makes Singapore's Health Care So Cheap?" I had often attributed this miracle to a combination of Asian veneration of doctors as a calling, our scholarship-bond system that kept junior doctor salaries compressed for a half-decade out of medical school and the dominance of a largely single-payer, publicly-run, broadly universal healthcare system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But over the years hence, our model has begun to edge ever closer toward the mixed system that characterises the United States and I am not entirely certain that this has been a positive development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The solution our people face today must go beyond the Healthier SG initiatives, as laudable as they are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Healthcare costs are escalating, are doing so rapidly, and look to continue to do so in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even without greater attention paid to prevention, we must not limit ourselves to outsourcing yet another initiative to the end user without simultaneously tackling issues inherent to the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Including subsidies, this increases, but not by all that much.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The upshot is that, beyond the 3Ms plus subsidies, we cover a significant amount of expenditures directly out of our own pockets and savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But even though out-of-pocket expenditures, as a share of total health expenditures, have fallen, the absolute amount we have had to pay has steadily risen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Over the period, increases in healthcare costs outstripped inflation at the rate of 2.3% per annum to 1.5%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps more worryingly, other independent sources peg much faster price increases in the future, between 7% and 10% per annum in more recent years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such spending was as much as families set aside for education and more than communication, clothing, footwear and recreation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, this share has been growing for the least fortunate among us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While dedicating a little bit more than 5% of each pay cheque to health is surely a wise investment, the concern is that this could continue rising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Spending a few hundred dollars monthly may still be manageable, but this becomes much harder to bear when the amount begins to approach $1,000 every month or more than $11,400 a year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I hope so, but it is worth noting that American households currently fork out an amount comparable annually and they used to pay our current share as recently as 15 years ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The issues of how informational asymmetries are endemic in markets for healthcare and health financing are well understood by members of this House and I shall not regurgitate them here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The main takeaway is simply that we cannot expect healthcare markets to function in a similar manner to other markets, which necessitates some degree of Government intervention.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One important corollary of this result is that while we may very much wish to harness market forces to contain price increases, we need to be very judicious in our application of such mechanisms because introductory economic principles may give rise to counterintuitive and perhaps even counterproductive outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will document several examples of such outcomes when I deal with potential solutions later in my speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another important corollary is that any policy that increases the distance between the patient and the payee may also lead to perverse outcomes because this distance separates agents – patients, in this case – from the cost implications of their choices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could be on the part of healthcare providers – if doctors are primarily making treatment decisions, with little input from the patient – or from healthcare financiers, if health insurers are defining available options or covering all costs involved, with little feedback from the insured.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While some gap is inevitable – I would have no idea how to choose between one treatment regimen versus another – but the more information we put in the hands of patients, the better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The suggestions I will detail also account for the importance of keeping this distance, as far as possible, to the minimum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, public healthcare often coexists with a vibrant private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As the pandemic has reminded us, public health is, in and of itself, a valuable public good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the private market for healthcare often plays an important complementary role in the overall national healthcare system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In developing countries, the emergence of a parallel private system is what often prevents an outright collapse of overstretched public systems altogether.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In advanced economies, the private system can plug gaps in care that the public system is unable to meet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Managing the COVID-19 pandemic would have been much more challenging in the absence of private healthcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, while there is seldom an "optimal" division of the proportion of healthcare provided by the public versus the private sector, resource limitations in the former usually means that it tends to ration by time, either a longer wait before an operation in a public hospital is scheduled, or a shorter time spent with the doctor at the polyclinic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the latter, the private system, controls demand by price, which is why one tends to pay for the privilege of speed and attention when seeing a private doctor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These differences are not problematic, per se, as long as we recognise that there are the essential trade-offs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, we should never allow these trade-offs to become a synonym for quality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, many of my doctor friends, including those in private practice, suggest that complicated procedures could well be best performed at a public hospital in Singapore, because they are endowed with the latest technologies and tend to see a greater volume of complex cases and, hence, acquire familiarity and expertise in dealing with them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Promoting competitive forces are often a positive and a means of containing costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, we want to exercise care when we apply regulation in service of promoting greater competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, price fixing or collusion is typically frowned upon, because this allows suppliers to coordinate on a price target, which would otherwise be unsustainable in the presence of genuine competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But such prohibitions may only make sense when the competitive landscape itself is characterised by few players in possession of substantial market power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When there are many suppliers, coupled with free entry, firms are much more likely to compete on product differentiation rather than price.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this case, even when doctors can freely set prices, excess profits are no longer assured, at least in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What remains is to have all prices cross-referenced to these benchmarks, so that incentives to adopt them will remain compelling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Benchmark ranges should also not be to drift too wide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To prevent a proliferation of procedures, fee ranges should be posted just for the most common ailments, not surgical procedures, since the latter are often less relevant to the typical patient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These should be prominently displayed at all registration counters, not just in hospitals, but in clinics and medical centres as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such restrictions are inherently anti-competitive, since panel membership is restricted by definition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And as SMA has stressed, panels short-circuit the patient-doctor relationship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To contain cost escalation, insurers can simply agree to pay out amounts between the 40th and 60th percentile, leaving patients a choice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Those who wish to do so may top up any of the excess charges at their own expense.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should also be sensitive to how more players in an industry, especially in health insurance, need not automatically give rise to the most competitive prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, competition may also be the most effective at containing costs when there is simultaneously a dominant player, in this case, the Government, operating through MediShield Life, who takes on the role of the price setter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This requires MediShield Life to be even more proactive in negotiating and bargaining for lower prices for procedures and medications that it covers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, since the 3Ms account for less than a tenth of total healthcare spending, the value of these publicly mandated components of the healthcare system must rest in the ability of the public sector to either coordinate players, or signal the direction that the system should follow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such negotiated pricing is common in single payer systems worldwide, including Canada, France, Germany, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, MOH should also scrutinise the face value of public charges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There have been anecdotal reports that pre-subsidy prices of some public health providers are now significantly higher than their private sector equivalents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I believe that the public sector still bills less than the private sector overall, it is important that the regulator keep an eye out for unwarranted public sector charges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, when the typical patient will only be concerned with his or her actual, unsubsidised fees, it falls. therefore, on MOH to police price escalation "on paper" since these are benchmarks for the private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Fee Benchmarks Advisory Committee should expand its scope to not just examining the overall fee schedule, but also interrogate any persistent or accelerating divergence in public-private fees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More than one doctor we spoke to stressed that the industry-wide need to raise prices was premised on increases in rental costs at private hospitals and that this elevated benchmark was, in turn, first set by the precedent of Mount Elizabeth Novena.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here, higher land sales costs have translated into higher medical charges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The need to adapt to rising costs, of course does not fall solely on the medical profession and medical facilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Insurers often find it easy to pass along costs, which allows them to stack additional layers of paperwork to access insurance payouts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I am not in favour of interfering with how private firms run their businesses, additional administrative burdens undeniably lead to fee bloat, while also adding distance between the patients and the treatment they receive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here, the Government can leverage information technology to roll out a central insurance claims system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MediShield Life claims are already directly submitted by CPF at the moment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, IP claims are still independently processed by the respective insurers, this adds unnecessary steps and increases administrative costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is currently an effort underway to develop an integrated claims platform across insurers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since there is already, presumably, a common claims system for MediShield Life, MOH could enfold this proposed claims platform under the same umbrella, into an expanded, public-private partnership platform.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But my bottom line is simple, we allow the private system to grow, sans public sector leadership and strong regulatory guidelines, at our peril.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My actionable takeaways are that we include greater cross-referencing of prices to benchmarks that are limited in range, that we allow insurers to pay out within this narrower range.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if we believe in the justice of covering pre-existing conditions, the Government should play a coordinating role in mandating such coverage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Government should be more proactive in bargaining for lower prices for procedures currently covered under MediShield Life, while also auditing excessive discrepancies between public-private fees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And as the price increases in other inputs, such as real estate, should be managed, since this can spill over into healthcare costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am sure we have all heard stories of how we have experienced long wait times for admission into our hospitals lately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Ministry takes the question of wait times seriously, yet researchers from the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health note that despite "measures to reduce waiting times… the problem and the concern persists." I will conclude, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I was just going to remind you that you have nearly breached your 20 minutes full complement, that is your right; so, could you wrap up, please?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This White Paper has naturally gotten a lot of attention amongst my senior residents and GPs in Yio Chu Kang, which is a mature estate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Having spoken with them, I would like to raise feedback on several areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I will discuss Healthier SG from my residents' point of view.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My residents are generally happy with the Healthier SG benefits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many patients also like to get a combination of Western and TCM treatments for their ailments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some elderly patients prefer to get regular acupuncture treatments at registered TCM clinics for their aches and pains, rather than to rely on pain medication.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, how will compliance and success be measured?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Measuring health is unlike exercise, where we can determine participation and progress through counting the number of steps taken, heart rate and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the GP and the wider healthcare system assess adherence and compliance?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we measure the impact on the individual at the personal level?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For patients who refuse to follow the prescribed health plan, how can we then determine whether the overall programme is effective, or even whether the GP is proficient?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Having a good number of sign-ups is a favourable start.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, this does not necessarily guarantee in-depth participation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is more important would be compliance to a single GP or the Primary Care Network (PCN).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we discourage the practice of GP hopping?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be penalties for either the patient or GPs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is this a key performance indicator and who is it directed to?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe we should be more ambitious, especially considering that chronic illnesses can start in the 40s.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One way to do this is by allowing family members to enroll in the programme together with the senior.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, if an individual is 60 years old and his wife is younger by a few years, can they both enrol at the same time?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They can motivate and accompany each other for consultations and screenings, and adhere with exercise plans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our GPs have been very helpful with our efforts to build a dementia-friendly community in Yio Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They shared with me some useful insights on Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, how adequately are our GPs trained in managing chronic diseases?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A GP who wants to manage more complex health problems must begin their training from medical school.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In big countries like Australia, there may only be one doctor serving one or even a few towns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The GPs there are trained through medical school and postgraduate courses, with the expectation that they will function as the only doctor in the town and would, therefore, be equipped as such, with skills spanning from common ailments to more complex chronic conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, because of how accessible our tertiary healthcare institutions are, many of our GPs focus on common ailments and function as referrers for more complex and serious conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, how many GPs are enrolled in our PCNs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This may give some insight on GPs' willingness to participate in Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do we have the majority of GPs on board the PCN initiative?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What more can we do to get their buy-in to provide effective care in the neighbourhood?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government has gone to great lengths to reassure us that the drug cost parity between prescriptions from GPs and polyclinics is reduced.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will this be done through restricting the brands of drugs brought in?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What happens if a patient opts for "branded medication"?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As drug sales constitute a large part of GPs' incomes, how will drug cost parity affect a GP's willingness to sell generic drugs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does this also extend to the cost of ancillary services, such as blood tests, X-rays and other related services provided by GPs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The White Paper also mentions a team-based care approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will this be similar to the PCN where backend support for care coordination and other ancillary services are provided to the GP?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would GPs have to hire additional manpower or to pay for these services?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, how many more staff are required to deal with the additional administrative workload and to handle social prescription?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Under Healthier SG, we expect GPs to provide advice on lifestyle and dietary activities but such social prescriptions can involve a longer consultation session and probably over an extended duration of time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the meantime, GPs still have other patients' ailments to tend to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the GP count on the care team to help out or will they have to hire additional staff if they are unable to manage?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is more so in solo practices and goes back to my previous point on getting more GPs to join PCNs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In tertiary healthcare institutions, typically, you would have a nutritionist speak to a patient on diet and then there will be other healthcare professionals and programmes to deal with smoking cessation, weight loss and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With many GPs still practicing solo, would they have the time and resources to do so?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This gives them adequate time to holistically review a patient's clinical and lifestyle needs, including making adjustments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, it is, generally, a numbers game.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The more patients a GP sees, the more money a GP makes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would only be natural that the GP would want to earn more by seeing more patients.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could include frailty and mobility issues, which are common with old age.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Delaying the onset of such problems is critical in preventive care and will greatly help to improve the quality of life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes encouraging them to do Advanced Care Planning, or LPAs, at the opportune time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These conversations are best started by people like GPs who know the patient best and ideally understand the patient's family and social context.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is these meaningful conversations that may need to take place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is not so much to "bend the cost curve", though it might, but it helps people prepare for the inevitable and for families to be at peace with their decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I will now talk about the role of community care providers in Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The White Paper mentions leveraging on physical spaces in ECs to conduct activities like health screening, early detection of dementia risk and other healthcare initiatives for seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, GPs are also expected to conduct screenings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Regular opportunistic screening systems may make screenings more widely accessible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, they could be confusing and overlapping in intent, thus resulting in excess costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It shows that Singapore continues to grapple with long-term issues, such as low total fertility rate and the ageing population.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The responsibility of caregiving for older family members will rest on fewer shoulders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If all of us can take better care of ourselves and be more independent in our silver years, we can help to reduce this caregiving responsibility for our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At the systems level, this means reduced fiscal funding on healthcare so that the money can be better used in other areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But what matters most is for the individual.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I recently spoke with Mdm C, a senior living alone in Yio Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I often see her around in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Most of the time, I see her at the weekly exercise class in the park or at the market after her exercise for her breakfast with her exercise kakis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I asked her what she thinks is a good life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She told me that, being in her 70s, she does not ask for much.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She said as long as she can eat well, sleep early, exercise and meet up with her neighbours and her friends, she would have lived a fulfilling life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the benefits of Healthier SG, such as having an assigned GP who knows her well and having a proper health plan to keep healthy, I am certain she will be active and can enjoy her silver years for many more years to come.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The focus should rightly be on health and not on healthcare, and to stay healthy in the community for as long as possible and not in the hospital.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, I would like to take this opportunity to encourage all eligible residents listening in to sign up with Healthier SG as soon as the opportunity avails.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us all do our part to take responsibility for our own health and build a healthier Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my Budget speech in 2016, I brought up coordinated care, about GPs playing a more prominent role in the overall well-being of our people.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I was told the ratio has improved since.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope that with the focus on primary care, we can look forward to stronger GP-patient rapport.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has showed us the importance of reducing our load on public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Often, this trust overlaps generations and is passed between family members.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This trust transcends doctor and patient and goes into areas of digital privacy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my 2016 speech, I mentioned I was surprised to see the GP in Australia pull out the x-ray and surgical records of the next patient from his computer and it really made me ponder on the importance of coordinated care.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The availability of our healthcare records will empower our GPs to make informed care decisions for us.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to trust our doctors with the data and that the systems that hold our healthcare records are safe from bad actors, hackers and lapses.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In 2016, I also mentioned that isolation is one of the biggest problems for seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: During the pandemic, due in part to the Seniors Go Digital programme, many seniors learnt to harness the power of technology and stay in touch with their loved ones.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They were taught communication skills like video calls, connecting to WiFi and basic cybersecurity.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: These have helped thousands of seniors remain connected and engaged through the most difficult times of the pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We should continue with the momentum to enrich their lives for them to stay connected, not isolated and yet not addicted.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is a small issue of addiction to gadgets which may aggravate isolation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some of you know I am very close to my nephew.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am very conscious about children's gadget time.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am even more concerned about my senior residents' gadget time.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many of them have learnt to download movies and dramas and are hooked to them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My volunteers and PA staff work hard to create programmes to draw them out of their homes to have a healthy and active social life.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Programmes must be targeted at pre-retirement age so that they will continue their active social life post-retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For the not so socially active seniors, I was heartened to read The Straits Times article on 28 September 2022 on retired timber worker Lim Thiam Teng who warmed up to volunteers and is now an advocate of care centres.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The auntie who started walking to the centre before she went blind so she could familiarise herself with the route.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Her meals were provided for in our centre and she could listen to the news in the afternoon, amidst other activities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The auntie who no longer needed plasters after daily exercises at the centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She also found someone there who loves singing Cantonese songs like her.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Most recently, we had our youngest dementia client in her early fifties.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: These allow our elderly to age in place, with their family and in familiar surroundings.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I remember my first referral as a new Member of Parliament.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: During our regular house visit, the auntie said the flat is occupied by her and her husband who had suffered a stroke.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For the past seven years, she was his only and main caregiver.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I asked her if she was okay and the tears just rolled.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I cannot even go to the market for too long." Her eyes brightened up when I explained the respite services at our day care centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She was happy she could get a couple of days off to go and meet her friends and have a walk, just like she used to.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I was reminded of its importance of care centres during the pandemic when a resident approached me at a Tampines East vaccination centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She said, "My brother-in-law is in your centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was so hard for us when the centre was closed.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He seemed to understand and was in a good mood and went to bed readily.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The centre is a great help to our family." Often, our mild dementia patients, our clients, will call me "teacher" and say they will go back and tell their "parents" about their day.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am not sure if they would remember to but we go with the flow on good days and manage their bad days.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I want to take the opportunity to thank all day care and nursing home staff for their contributions to the many families.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Recently, a dementia client was supposed to be discharged from our centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Her daughter cried when she picked her up on her last day at the centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They were supposed to check into a nursing home that weekend as her condition has deteriorated.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is hard for some to send their loved ones to a nursing home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They will try and manage with some help from the Government.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our Tampines GP, Dr Leong, even contacted us when he had extra flu vaccines that had some months left to expiry for us to ask our staff and clients if they would like to take the flu jab for free and many did.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, while some families hire caregivers and have helpers to multitask with housework, children and seniors, it lacks the exercise and activity elements that senior activity centres or day care centres provide.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One morning, we visited their senior day care centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I decided to spend the day there and what struck me was the heart and effort the staff put in in caring for the elderly there.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For instance, one staff tried to feed a resident using a spoon.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She tried three times before she switched to tube feeding.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She explained that she did that so that the resident would still retain her ability to swallow and not just rely on tube feeding, which will aggravate her decline in her physical state.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When the day ended, their families picked them up in a trolley sort of wheelchair as they could not sit up straight.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some thoughts went through my mind such as – with this condition here, they will be in a nursing home or with a dedicated caregiver at home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Several of these topics are intertwined and the White Paper has done a good job in articulating these areas to address.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is why, as part of the Healthier SG strategy, it is important to build an ecosystem and rally the community as part of that ecosystem to facilitate healthy living, making it easier for us to make better, healthier choices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Today, I would like to address various Members' questions related to preventive health and encouraging healthy lifestyles in the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our efforts can be summarised with the acronym "HEALTH". "H" for harnessing existing health initiatives, "E" for enhanced suite of health programmes, "A" for active collaboration with community partners, "L" for looking out for caregivers, "T" for tracking health activities via technology, and the last "H" for health-related lifestyle nudges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The first "H" is for harnessing existing health initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Currently, there are a wide range of national initiatives to support us in adopting and prioritising healthy living.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To promote physical activity, there are self-directed programmes such as the National Steps Challenge – where you can participate at your own pace anytime and anywhere – to virtual or on-ground MOVE IT leisure-time physical activity programmes for those who prefer guided exercise sessions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Good nutrition is also a key component of living healthily and we actively encourage Singaporeans to adopt a healthier diet, particularly by reducing sugar and salt consumption.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Hazel Poa and Ms Sylvia Lim had spoken about this earlier, in particular about improving affordability of healthier food choices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Hazel Poa had gone so far as to suggest taxes on unhealthy food.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan had sought clarification from her yesterday during his speech so the specifics of her proposals are not clear.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In any case, let me share about our ongoing initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some of you may also have heard that we are working with retailers to introduce lower-sodium alternatives which are healthier than regular salt.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, HPB supports food manufacturers and suppliers to develop healthier products through the Healthier Ingredient Development Scheme (HIDS), and partners food and beverage establishments, including hawker centres and coffeeshops, to offer healthier meal options.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: HPB also works actively with supermarket chains to introduce more Healthier Choice Symbol (HCS) products to increase the variety of HCS house brand products which are typically more affordable than branded alternatives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MOH also has a multi-pronged strategy to reduce the prevalence of use of tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In his speech, Mr Sharael Taha highlighted the issue of vaping.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To address the use of vaporisers, we are working with various partners to strengthen enforcement measures and public education efforts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will step up enforcement at borders, social media platforms such as Telegram and public areas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These are just some of the many initiatives we have and I am happy to note that they have impacted the lives of our residents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One such resident is 84-year-old Mr Louis Loh.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Diagnosed with diabetes 10 years ago, Mr Loh remained largely sedentary.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: He only grew more motivated and began exercising regularly after joining National Steps Challenge Season 4 in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Brisk-walking became his everyday routine and this enabled him to accumulate a daily average of 60 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Keeping active has helped Mr Loh achieve a healthier body mass index (BMI) after losing about 10 kg in the last three years and his health conditions are now better managed and controlled.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Loh's improved health outcomes have encouraged him to keep to his walking regime even outside the Challenge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Today, he continues to track his daily physical activity for the benefit of his health.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: When her family members were diagnosed with diabetes and hypertension, she realised the importance of having good health and decided to take steps towards a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To encourage healthier eating habits, Madam Rahimah cooks healthy meals at home and packs them for her children to bring to work.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The HPB's Healthier Choice Symbol made it easier for her to choose healthier ingredients and the information on how to cook healthier meals have also been useful.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She opts for wholegrains such as brown rice and brown rice bee hoon.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: When making desserts like "bubur kacang" for the family, she uses low fat milk instead of coconut milk.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In her cooking, she uses healthier oil and includes more vegetables, as well as using healthier cooking methods such as grilling and stir-frying instead of deep frying.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Besides eating healthily, Madam Rahimah also incorporates physical activity in her daily routine to stay active.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She is more energetic and does not feel tired easily.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Loh and Madam Rahimah took ownership of their health and harnessed existing health initiatives to improve their lifestyle.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This includes not only recommended health screening and vaccinations, but also lifestyle adjustments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Your doctor can also recommend existing health-related activities and services in your community that will be suitable for you.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, "E" refers to enhancing our existing suite of health programmes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will collate community partners' programmes and house these on the Healthy 365 app over time to cover the range from self-directed programmes to targeted weight management interventions for residents with well-controlled chronic disease and practical nutrition workshops on preparing a well-balanced healthy meal.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan called for a wider variety of community programmes so that every local community is abuzz with exercise groups and health-promoting activities, catering to different needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We do want a vibrant and robust slate of programmes but not all programmes need to be HPB- or MOH-driven programmes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To optimise resources, we will have to channel resources towards programmes that are well-received and impactful.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, we encourage community partners to play a part in this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is heartening therefore, to hear Ms Hany Soh share about the ground-up initiatives in her constituency.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ground partners can supplement existing health promotion efforts and programmes, and I would like to thank Ms Hany Soh for her ideas in this area.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We hope these efforts will continue to bloom and add to the existing suite of offerings that residents can tap on to sustain healthy lifestyles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, we will explore how a more comprehensive range of physical activities may be made available to residents across the island through collaborations with private partners such as physical activity providers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: HPB's Healthy 365 app will be the lifestyle application that you can use to easily access lifestyle programmes offered by community partners near you.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I agree with Dr Tan Wu Meng's and Ms Denise Phua's comment on the need to assist seniors or those who are not digitally savvy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With these features in place, you will be able to easily access and select suitable programmes that support your health and lifestyle goals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Next is "A" for active collaboration with community partners.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Over the years, we have worked closely with the community to extend our preventive health efforts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One example is the formation of the Malay Community Outreach Workgroup (MCO), which comprises of Malay community leaders with wide ranging experience, including PA MESRA, MUIS, Mendaki under the M3@Towns committees, and Muslim Health Professionals Association (MHPA).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At this point, please allow me to say a few words in Malay.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: (In Malay):   We have been working closely with the mosques for several years, to encourage congregants to lead an active lifestyle through the JKJU programme (Look After Your Health, Look After Your Community).

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: HPB will continue to expand the JKJU network by involving more organisations apart from the mosques to develop healthy lifestyle programmes and culturally-nuanced healthy lifestyle messages for the Malay community.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: This initiative aims to encourage more Malay/Muslims to stay healthy through community-led interest groups.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: These groups can design their own local health programmes by leveraging on the various healthcare facilities and services provided by community bodies and Whole-of-Government organisations.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We hope to nurture at least one community-led interest group in every M3@Town.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We will also continue to enhance existing programmes and support the Malay community with various health programmes, to encourage them to lead a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: (In English): In her speech, Ms He Ting Ru touched on the gender health gap for women.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The feminisation of ageing is a well-recognised phenomenon, where women face a greater risk and duration of loneliness as those who are married tend to live longer than their husbands.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: They also have greater financial insecurity than men and carry a greater budget of the challenges and stresses of caregiving.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: In fact, I chair a Women's Health Committee which comprises community partners championing for women's health issues.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Together with our partners, we will continue to increase the awareness of women's health issues and promote healthier lifestyle practices amongst women.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sustained education efforts and support for women is important in addressing this long-term phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The efforts of the Committee will complement Healthier SG in supporting women in their preventive health journey so that they may live longer, healthier.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I agree with Ms Ng Ling Ling's point on the importance of adopting a community participatory approach under Healthier SG and this is in line with our plans.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Under Healthier SG, we and our healthcare clusters will continue to work closely with agencies to explore these suggestions and we look forward to the support of all our partners to achieve the vision of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Moving on, we have "L" which stands for looking out for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: As we seek to empower fellow Singaporeans to stay healthy, we recognise that some of our seniors are already frail, living with dementia, or approaching end of life.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: These seniors and their caregivers also need our support.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Second Minister for Health, Mr Masagos Zulkifli, will speak more about our commitment to enabling seniors to live and age well in the community.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Over the years, we have enhanced our support for caregivers, with a range of initiatives under the Caregiver Support Action Plan and the White Paper on Women's Development.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ground-up community efforts can also let caregivers know that they are not alone in this journey.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: For example, peer support networks under the People's Association's WIN Caregivers Network and Project 3i empower caregivers to learn skills and receive social-emotional support.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We recognise that caregivers also need even more support as their loved ones approach the end of life.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Palliative care comes in here to provide not just physical, but also emotional, psychosocial, and spiritual support to patients and their families.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: In their speeches, Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Hany Soh touched on enabling caregivers to better support their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Currently, nominated caregivers can already conveniently access the health records and appointments of their loved ones in HealthHub.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I would also like to acknowledge Ms Janet Ang's point on leveraging digital technology to engage caregivers and we will continue to work with partners to engage caregivers through various channels, including digital channels.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So far, I have covered how the Government and community can play a role in supporting our healthy living journey.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: For my last two points, I will cover how technology can be used to empower and motivate you to take charge of your own health journey.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The letter "T" is for tracking of your health activities.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: In between visits to your family doctor under Heathier SG, you can access relevant, up-to-date advice via the Healthy 365 app and the HealthHub app on your personal devices.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Healthy 365 enables easy tracking of different lifestyle behaviours such as physical activity, healthier food purchase and consumption.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: You will also be able to share your lifestyle data by showing the app to your family doctor, enabling the doctor to have a holistic view of your progress and discuss what lifestyle goals and programmes can help you.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: There will also be ways to support those who are not digitally fluent, for example, by enabling patients’ caregivers or family to assist.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: At the heart of Healthier SG is empowering residents to choose health for themselves while the system supports them.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We know that lifestyle behavioural change is a long-term journey requiring both strong motivation and regular participation.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: While we may interact with our family doctors once every six to 12 months and participate in community activities a couple of times a week, personalised recommendations and nudges delivered via digital technology can be a constant support to help us stay engaged on our healthy journeys.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We will enhance Healthy 365 to deliver more personalised nudges, such as through recommending suitable lifestyle activities, achievement of health goals and improving adoption of healthy lifestyle behaviours.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Many private companies have been developing such technologies and some have built deep expertise in nudging health behaviour change.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We will continue to explore collaborations with them to harness technology and insights to help us all take better ownership of our health.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We have also made healthy living rewarding with HPB Healthpoints.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: You can earn Healthpoints under programmes, such as the National Steps Challenge.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We will continue to improve on this and encourage all of us as we choose better health.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: With Healthier SG, it will be easier for everyone to start and sustain healthy living.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: As Madam Anna is overweight and has high blood pressure and pre-diabetes, her family doctor recommends that she attends the “Live Well Age Well” programme to stay active and pick up nutrition tips to avert diabetes.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: She is also automatically registered for the “National Steps Challenge” and “Eat Drink Shop Healthy Challenge” where her daily healthy lifestyle activities help her earn Healthpoints to exchange for vouchers.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The Healthy 365 app will also remind her to clock more steps, complete more moderate to vigorous physical activity (MVPA) minutes and offer other suitable activities to add variety.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: During Madam Anna’s next half-yearly check in with her family doctor, she proudly shares that she has become more active and has reduced her caloric intake by using the Healthy 365 diet logging tool to monitor her meals.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The family doctor notes that Madam Anna has lost two kilogrammes in the past six months.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Her high blood pressure is also under control.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: If Madam Anna continues to sustain her healthy lifestyle and manage her chronic condition well, the family doctor may consider reducing her regular medication at her next health consult.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Although Madam Anna is a fictional character, as demonstrated by Mr Loh and Madam Rahimah in my earlier example, it is possible to start and sustain a healthy lifestyle and Healthier SG would make it easier for you to do so.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: In the meantime, you may download and explore HealthHub and Healthy 365 to access a wide range of preventive health resources and programmes.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Thus, as the Government strengthens support for preventive health under Healthier SG, I would also like to urge all of us to make a conscious decision to invest in our health.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Let us strive towards living healthier and better lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   As the saying goes, "prevention is better than cure".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore's public healthcare system has always placed a greater emphasis on treatment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From the allocation of Government funds to services provided by civic organisations, there is a clear bias towards the treatment of patients.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even in the eyes of the general public, to be a specialist is better than a general practitioner.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This attitude inadvertently affects the choice of students when they choose their course of study, hence has an impact on our talent supply.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It also affects the perception of the public with regard to public healthcare.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, when people are sick, we have to treat and take care of them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Like a parent, the Government should not only provide quality medical care for Singaporeans, but also give subsidies to reduce the financial burden from medical expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Against the backdrop of an ageing population, it is even more important for the Government to provide quality and affordable healthcare.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, when people fall ill in their twilight years, they may find it hard to enjoy life even if they own a mountain of wealth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence it is often said that health is wealth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Because if you are healthy, you will have the energy to travel around, play with your grandchildren, pursue unfulfilled dreams and scale new heights in life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this way, seniors will not be counting down to the end of their lives, but will be anticipating every new day.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, from a long-term point of view, preventive public healthcare will only bring benefits.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, good health helps to improve our quality of life, and a good quality of life helps to improve our happiness index.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, a healthy and strong population means a prosperous country.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With good health, one need not fear about the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Earlier, I heard Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's speech and I have some doubts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He talked about listing out consultation fees at private clinics.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe benchmarking fees against market standards and listing out consultation fees at private clinics are already in practice.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Is he looking for greater transparency or better consistency of consultation fees?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From what I heard he seemed to suggest that more medical services be included in MediShield Life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can he elaborate on what additional medical services he is thinking of?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, we are debating the White Paper, does he expect that certain preventive care services be included in MediShield Life?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
