text: If so, how will that affect the premiums of MediShield Life?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How do we help Singaporeans deal with the increase in premiums?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can Assoc Prof Jamus Lim clarify on these points?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My general feeling after listening to Assoc Prof Lim's speech is that he still plays a greater emphasis on treatment, but the Healthier SG White Paper is focusing on preventive care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Does he also agree that the preventive medicine is better than curative medicine?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the long term, I feel that preventive care is a better option.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Now, I would like to return to my original speech.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Bai Juyi once said, "feel how other people would feel with your own body and heart".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When we rollout Healthier SG, we must pay attention to both the body and mind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At present, if we ask Singaporeans whether they should live healthy lives and take preventive care, the answer must be "yes".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ask if they support it, the answer will surely be "yes" as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And whether they will translate it into action, the answers are not so clear.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, unless we are sick, we tend to have the mindset that "it will not be me".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Health checks or healthy dietary habits are often not on the agenda.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, in the White Paper, it is right to emphasise the role of GPs in inculcating good habits among Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Building on the existing CHAS network, I hope that all GPs will heed the call and join the Healthier SG initiative to benefit more Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For these reasons, I support the Healthier SG White Paper.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The White Paper's analysis is meticulous and the measures put forward are suitable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, in some mature estates, there may be more elderly people living alone who are old, frail and financially disadvantaged.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What they need is not just recreational activities, but also social and financial support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How can the Government ensure that every community, whether it is old or new, rich or poor, provides equal services?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: After all, one can get chronic illnesses regardless of one's status.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But one's financial ability affects one's choice in life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, I am happy to see that the Government agrees with the importance of mental health.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope that the Government will also step up its efforts in the mental health area.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is a high stress environment and mental health cannot be ignored.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During the pandemic, many older Singaporeans have become accustomed to staying at home or avoiding the crowds because they have lived at home for a long time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This inevitably aggravates the psychological challenges that they face.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, I think mental health is an issue that we have to deal with sooner rather than later.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I understand that it is a reply to the clarification asked of you.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And thank you that I got a little more air time today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I will just quickly point out in response to the two specific questions that were raised by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first was Ms Tin suggested that I was saying that more fees should be published, right?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is not, in fact, what I said.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second point, Ms Tin mentioned about what I was suggesting be included into MediShield Life in terms of procedures that were not covered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Again, I think she may have misheard what I said.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The reason is preventative care – which is, of course, the focus of this Motion – is insufficient if we wish to contain costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We have to address the demand side, in terms of how much people are demanding medical care but also address concerns from the supply side, those insurers as well as medical providers that are providing said care.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, is there a response?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Please allow me to congratulate the Health Minister as well as the team at MOH for this progressive strategy.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The shift from being a reactive to a strategy that promotes preventive healthcare makes perfect sense.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Quite frankly, it is high time that we make this move.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: On engaging with the sports, fitness and wellness community, I am happy to see that the White Paper asserts that improving health goes beyond the doctor's visit and encourages residents to adopt a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This reinforces what sports and fitness practitioners have long believed.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This has a significant impact on populations, more so on economies like Singapore which depend heavily on its people.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is good to see that there are plans to activate community partners, such as SportSG and the People's Association (PA).

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It would be better to see more engagement with private sector entities that provide relevant and structured programmes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these programmes are customised to the requirements of our seniors and persons with chronic diseases.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Partnering such private sector entities would give SportSG and PA greater options and relevant programmes to communities that require specialised programming.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Sports has a large part to play in getting Singaporeans active.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In the last National Sports Participation Survey (NSPS), swimming, walking and jogging are the only activities that consistently rank amongst the top five most participated activities across all age groups ranging 13 to over 60 years.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Physical health and mental health ranked amongst the top motivations for participants in these activities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: From my own experience, I can tell you ploughing up and down a swimming pool by yourself is not the most exciting nor the most social activity.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: But when you come together as a group, complete sets, set goals and throw in a little competitiveness, sports can be a fun and it can be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Which is why I believe National Sports Associations, private sports clubs and academies have a part to play in in the Healthier SG White Paper.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Structured, competitive sports and games should not be limited to just a person's school years, but for life.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: He said, "Our sports events can be more veteran-friendly.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: One is never too old to participate in sport and there is ample medical evidence to show that one can benefit from exercise, even if one starts late." I agree with Dr Tan and we can do more to design programmes which are "veteran-friendly", modifying games, adjust training intensity, make it fun, such that physical activity is a way of life.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Physical activity promotes optimal health and is integral in the prevention and treatment of many medical conditions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Which brings me to my second point on education and certification.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In the Healthier SG White Paper, a doctor will be able to keep track of an individual's health conditions, detect health problems early, work with the individual on a care plan and refer the individual to suitable activities or programmes in the community.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Knowledge of disease care is as important as knowledge of disease prevention.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Exercise is Medicine strives to make physical activity assessment and promotion a standard in clinical care, connecting healthcare with evidence-based physical activity resources for people everywhere, for all abilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Physicians and other healthcare providers should be encouraged to include physical activity when designing treatment plans and to refer patients to evidence-based exercise programmes and qualified exercise professionals.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Training a young athlete for peak performance is different from training an adult in his or her 30s and 40s, and is different from training a senior with chronic disease.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: However, many coaching and fitness certification courses do not address the physiological differences in depth.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, such courses can be delivered through CoachSG and PA.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In Primary school, we all went through health education.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In Secondary school, we went through physical education.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Such information can be bespoke based on data and information collected on wearable technology and pushed through an app.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my next point which is leveraging digital technology.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As our population ages, a concern is mental and cognitive health.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, with wearable and mobile technology being more accessible, we can explore how gaming and virtual reality can help diseases such as dementia and Alzheimer's.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Researchers at UC San Francisco described that an immersive game called Labryinth-VR, where players wear a head-mounted virtual reality display and navigate through "neighbourhoods" of increasing size and complexity and run errands.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Players walk through a place and move their bodies as they navigate the game, gaining physical exercise that can increase cerebral blood flow associated with improvement in general cognitive performance.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We live in an amazing time, where technology can bridge the physical and virtual worlds.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: During the pandemic when physical activity in groups was limited, we made do exercising from home.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Technology played an important role in connecting our physical activity done at home to an online community.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us took part in virtual races and activities and where we logged distances walked, swum and cycled.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I remember even doing a push-up challenge with Speaker to raise funds for the Community Chest.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Platforms like Zwift enable us to compete in real-time in virtual reality, connecting with people from all over the world.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Gamification creates a stickiness and technology connects and gathers data for us to make educated decisions on our health and physical performance.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The potential to connect and activate is boundless.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: However, the strength of our strategy is only as strong as its weakest link.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Healthier SG is an ambitious strategy and by no means a simple matter.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It requires an immense level of coordination from various organisations to make it a success.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Together, we can look forward to greater quality of life in our senior years.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Hazel Poa, I understand you have a clarification or want to respond to one.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yesterday, I understand that the hon Member Xie Yao Quan sought a couple of clarifications from me.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, with regards to my suggestion of tax on unhealthy food, he asked for specifics.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And also, the second part is whether imposing such a tax adheres to the spirit of the White Paper.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As to the specifics of the tax, one specific example would be the sugar tax that exists in many countries and cities, including places like UK, France, India, Thailand, Malaysia and in certain cities in USA, it is is quite common.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it has been proven to be effective.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As to whether imposing this text adheres to the spirit of the White Paper, I do believe so.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, I do not see any contradiction.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, if the Member disagrees, perhaps, he can share why he feels that it does not.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, in same spirit, I would also like to ask the Member whether he thinks that our current tax on tobacco and liquor adheres to the spirit of the White Paper and does he think that they ought to be removed.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I see Mr Xie Yao Quan and Minister Ong Ye Kung's hand.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister Ong and then perhaps, Mr Xie can decide whether he wants to respond thereafter.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have been very reluctant to look into a tax like that.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The principle is not wrong – having a "sin" tax is the policy of this Government.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When it is cigarettes, it is something that is harmful, we do tax it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The question is sugar causes diabetes, should we tax sugar?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I assume if you extend it further, you can also tax salt or oil, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Sugar is commonly consumed by so many people and so, you will add cost.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And also, we consider the equity of the tax.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because sugar is found in fruit juices, sugarcane, the pearls in bubble tea.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, you start to make such comparison, it is not going to be so easy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam talked about the Nutri-Grade labelling.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once we announced Nutri-Grade A to D, if you have high sugar content for canned beverages, you will be graded D, immediately, the beverage companies reformulated.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I stand in support of the Motion, which seeks to empower individuals to take charge of our own health and wellness and help Singaporeans live longer and healthier lives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The strategies proposed within the White Paper on Building a Healthier SG provide significant steps in the right direction to provide better quality healthcare in a more affordable and convenient manner.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my speech, I will talk about how Healthier SG will benefit our workers who work hard, work long hours and more often than not, also work in stressful environments and offer suggestions on areas where we can and should do more.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During the NTUC's recent #EveryWorkerMatters Conversation, many workers raised concerns about the steady creep in healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Concerns were understandably more pronounced among our mature workers, who are deeply worried about being able to afford treatments for their chronic illnesses such as diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Employers too are affected by the rise in healthcare costs for their ageing workforce as they have to spend more for their employees' medical benefits.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to the United States' Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, some job roles can result in workers becoming more susceptible to chronic illnesses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, four out of the 10 most costly health conditions for US employers, which include chest pains, high blood pressure, diabetes and heart attack, could be attributed to work stress and physical inactivity caused by prolonged hours of sitting at the work desk.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This relationship between certain job roles and chronic health conditions is unlikely to be unique to the United States.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond general chronic illnesses that Singaporeans are susceptible to, we should also consider whether certain types of work predispose us to certain chronic illnesses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As I have alluded to earlier, spending long hours sitting in front of the computer or in a driver's seat, among many other repetitive job tasks, can result in various forms of chronic illnesses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Examples include arthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome and hypertension.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, employers must put in place a work environment that prevents job-specific chronic illnesses from forming and to adapt the workplace and work processes to help workers who are suffering from chronic illnesses, in particular, our mature workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a 2017 Swedish study, which examined the challenges involved in encouraging an ageing workforce to continue working productively, the researchers found that workers with chronic conditions can continue to work meaningfully by changing tasks and having proper physical aids to assist them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, the study also observed that these changes often come at the workers' initiative, rather than the employer proactively doing so.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As our population and workforce ages, employers must be cognisant on how to adapt the work environment to help their workers remain productive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will reduce the need to visit the doctor just to get an MC and reduce medical bills too.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While some employers are already doing this – for example, workers in our healthcare clusters are given up to three days of non-MC sick leave – I urge all employers to do the same.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This benefit should also be provided to all workers, including those in the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement has been pushing for this as early detection and intervention can help prevent chronic illnesses and infection of diseases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, the National Taxi Association, the National Private Hire Vehicles Association and the NTUC's Freelancers and Self-Employed Unit have been working with the Health Promotion Board (HPB) to encourage gig economy workers to go for quarterly health screening and health coaching sessions, to get active and to stay in shape.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Third, companies with staff canteens can promote healthier eating options.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The canteens operated by the National Transport Workers' Union have been offering brown rice at subsidised rates, to encourage our public transport workers to take up this healthier option.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Instead of a sugar tax, the canteens rolled out promotional discounted prices for our kopi o kosong and teh o kosong to encourage workers to cut down on their sugar intake.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We are working with HPB next on a low salt campaign for our public transport workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that all companies with staff canteens can follow suit and nudge their workers towards a healthier diet.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: More than half of respondents said that they were struggling with their workplace mental health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I therefore fully agree with the White Paper that taking a preventative approach in mental health is aligned with the objectives of Healthier SG and I note that the scope of Healthier SG will eventually widen and include other complex chronic conditions such as mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would just like to ask the Minister when that will be.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The bottom line is that mental health conditions should be given the same priority as all other chronic illnesses and it is in everyone's interest – employers, workers and the Government – to ensure that we have a mentally healthy workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that MOH and the Inter-agency Taskforce on Mental Health and Well-being can prioritise the roll-out of preventative mental healthcare for the next review of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While the strategies outlined in the White Paper on Building a Healthier SG will help us achieve a higher quality, affordable and convenient healthcare ecosystem, we can all lean in and do more.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I encourage employers to play their part in tackling job-specific chronic illnesses at the workplace and putting in place a structured healthy workplace programme for their workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Workers too should also do their part to go for regular health screenings, partake in regular exercise and eat healthily so as to remain healthy, productive and employable.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, I hope that the next review of Healthier SG will include a strong focus on preventative mental healthcare.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.57 pm until 3.25 pm.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This means that on average, we spend about 10 years in ill health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our chronic disease prevalence rate has also risen.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We want to reverse these trends and empower residents to lead active and healthy lives, surrounded by people whom they love and can support them in their journey towards better health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must not let our health be determined by medical care alone, even if there are plentiful experts who can provide it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In fact, the way we live, work and play, and the environment we put ourselves in are as important, if not, more so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: From young, Singaporeans participate in activities in schools, such as physical education (PE), and go on to participate in programmes and activities in their workplaces and in the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: During our engagements, residents have told us that they are better able to sustain healthy behaviours if it is social.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, some find joy in going brisk walking with their friends.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Others are motivated to stay healthy so that they do not burden their family members.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One resident said "Exercise and sports, I do a lot of that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: If I am not playing games, I am going for walks with my friends." Another resident said "If a doctor recommends for me to do something, I would convince him that I rather do it with my friends." Like both residents, we are more motivated to exercise if our friends and family encourages us to do so or better yet, to do it with us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Healthier SG acknowledges the importance that we place on participating in activities we enjoy, with our loved ones and friends.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In support of this, community partners will provide a range of lifestyle programmes and activities to attract different profiles, and bring them closer to residents' homes, especially for our seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam has touched on HPB's support for this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: People's Association also has a wide array of health and wellness lifestyle activities, interest groups and courses catering to a broad range of preferences and interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Those who prefer more structured support can start with Sport Singapore's network of Active Health Labs and Coaches.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Active Health Labs will help residents get started and stay on their health regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Residents will receive regular health and wellness coaching and advice on exercise customised to them, in order to meet health goals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This includes residents who are at risk of developing chronic conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Even before Healthier SG, we are and will continue to be inclusive in promoting health to all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Mr Mark Chay asked about MOH's plan for persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Enabling Masterplan 2030, which was just published in August, sets out our approach to enable persons with disabilities to live healthier lives, supported by quality healthcare.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about MOH's upstream efforts on child and maternal health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have already started on this, in parallel with planning for Healthier SG.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The inter-agency Child and Maternal Health and Well-being Taskforce that I chair focuses on improving health outcomes for our women and children, starting from as early as the pre-conception stage and during pregnancy, to give every child a good start.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Expecting and postpartum women can access educational information and resources on Parent Hub, which can be found on HealthHub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ms Denise Phua also asked about upstream interventions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will continue to inculcate healthy habits from young by making health more prominent in schools and preschools and have started a review with MOE and MSF on this so that we can better support the health and development of our children.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I have heard your concern for care and outreach to seniors participating, including males.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling suggested to partner family doctor with community partners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These suggestions are important as we shape Healthier SG.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will need to ensure family doctors are plugged into relevant community level information so that they are familiar and can refer residents to these programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But more importantly, we hope their doctors can help them follow through on their health plans and show how these can achieve good health outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, we will strengthen coordination and support across partners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: First, Healthy 365 as the entry way for all residents to easily access lifestyle programmes offered by community partners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling suggested making it easy for more seniors to use Healthy 365 and HealthHub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Help is available at our community centres, eldercare centres or through our Silver Generation Ambassadors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There are also about 230,000 seniors above 55 who are using HealthHub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will reach out to more seniors and ensure they will be able to easily navigate the apps and locate the information they want.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Second, our healthcare clusters, as regional health managers, will step up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Mr Sharael Taha asked about the role of regional health managers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They will build relationships, coordinate activities and support across community partners and tailor programmes specific to the needs of the population in their regions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over time, healthcare clusters will gain in-depth understanding of their residents’ needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They will work with partners to strengthen the environmental and social support for our residents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Agency for Integrated Care, a trusted partner of many community partners, will support this effort, integrating care across partners to better support residents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng expressed concern that there may be duplicative efforts in screening by community partners and primary care.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will be sharing the care protocols that will guide screening done by family doctors and their care team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In addition, our healthcare clusters will guide supporting initiatives in the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over time, we hope to minimise duplication and target population segments that need more help.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These partnerships will make it easy for residents to live healthily in their day-to-day lives and help connect residents to relevant programmes and services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are committed to enabling seniors to age and live to their fullest potential in the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Ministerial Committee on Ageing (MCA) adopts a whole-of-society approach towards making Singapore a better community to age in.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is one instance of a whole-of-society approach in health which Member Sylvia Lim said we should have.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am glad to share some key achievements from the Action Plan and the latest initiatives on how we have built communities of care around our seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Today, active ageing programmes exist in every neighbourhood.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our seniors have opportunities to learn new things and meet new people close to their homes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We provide targeted outreach to those who need it through the Silver Generation Office (SGO) and with intermediate and long-term care (ILTC) partners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Since April 2022, in their door-to-door preventive health visits to seniors, SGO looks out for seniors’ frailty status and level of social support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They will intensify outreach to seniors identified to have higher health and social risks so that they can be referred to the right services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Dr Wan Rizal will be glad to know that we have been enhancing our care infrastructure and capacity to support the growing needs of our population, helping seniors to age in community, including those that are less mobile or immobile.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Transport is provided to seniors who need it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Healthier SG will extend to all seniors, including those who are lower-income earners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I appreciate Mr Xie Yao Quan for raising concerns about the lower-income in Healthier SG.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Preventive care is not only for those who can afford personal trainers and coaches.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With Healthier SG, we are making preventive care accessible to everyone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are collaborating with GPs and polyclinics to help residents stay healthier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are activating community partners to support them to live healthier lifestyles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Healthcare clusters have been working with SSAs and MSF’s social services offices (SSOs) in their regions to jointly address the health and social needs of the residents, particularly those from the lower-income households.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, there are community nursing posts co-located with many SSAs and SSOs to make health services more accessible at these community touchpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With Healthier SG, we will facilitate partnership and shared care of individuals across health and social agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will also work through PCNs to strengthen the collaborations with Healthier SG GPs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: All hands must be on deck to enable our seniors to remain physically, cognitively and socially engaged, as well as maintain and improve their health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MCA ran a series of engagements with more than 5,000 residents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We found that many seniors continue to have aspirations even as they age, whether it is to volunteer in the community, care for their grandchildren or even start a business.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have concluded our recommendations and are finalising the report which will be launched early next year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For the Care thrust, seniors will be supported through preventive health, active ageing programmes and care services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: On Contribution, seniors will have opportunities to contribute their knowledge and expertise to the community by volunteering, continuous learning and employment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Through our Citizens’ Panel on Contribution, many seniors have told us that they also wish to contribute to society by mentoring our youths.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As suggested by Ms Hany Soh and Mr Sharael Taha, we will increase opportunities for families to provide the support system to help our seniors live healthier lives, strengthening intergenerational relationships within the family.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Action Plan Refresh will focus on interventions in the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and SGO help seniors to be more confident in using technology to stay healthy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, our eldercare centres have been collaborating with IMDA to hold digital literacy workshops for seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Seniors Go Digital programme also helps introduce use of Healthy 365 and HealthHub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Housing monetisation options like the Lease Buyback Scheme are also available to support seniors to age in community while boosting their retirement savings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Eldercare Centres will be further strengthened as the key node for seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: ECs will be the go-to points for all seniors’ health-social needs, including connecting them to social and lifestyle activities and monitoring simple vitals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Today, ECs provide support for seniors from different ethnicities and backgrounds and many of them participate regularly in activities and programmes at ECs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We welcome more stakeholders and community partners to come together in this endeavour to build a society that empowers seniors to contribute, be socially engaged and achieve their aspirations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Before I conclude, let me summarise my speech in Malay.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: (In Malay):   Healthier SG aims to empower all of us to take care of our own health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Family doctors will work with residents to improve our health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But beyond healthcare, we acknowledge that social and environmental factors are also important.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Under Healthier SG, community organisations will also be involved to provide various programmes close to homes to facilitate participation in programmes and activities to stay healthy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will help seniors age in place and live to their fullest potential within the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ultimately, every individual must be responsible for their own health and therefore take active steps to stay healthy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Let us all make use of the resources available to live a healthier life and support one another to do the same.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: (In English): In closing, the shift to leveraging community support for better health is a significant move.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Everyone – families, individuals, community partners and the Government – must and will do their part, I hope.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Together, we can help one another sustain healthier lifestyles, live and age well and be a Healthier Singapore.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Masagos also spoke about many hands on deck.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that is the correct direction to go.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am very supportive of these initiatives in Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: One, I am hearted to note that these efforts to reduce cost of healthcare amidst the ageing challenges is to mitigate institutional healthcare costs, which is by de-institutionalising care.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I believe the Government is already embarking on this with various "Ageing in Place" efforts, like Minister Masagos has said.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I personally think that the pilot for Queenstown's Health District pilot is very commendable.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is really good to see the concerted efforts by both MOH and MND to do so.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To supplement the infrastructure design and development of care within the vicinity of people's homes, we also need to build up what we call the "soft infrastructure".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As my hon colleague Denise Phua brought up yesterday, what is there in between GP visits to ensure that people follow their health plan that is recommended to them?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To that, I would like to propose that we harness and strengthen the community's capacity to be the peer influencers and peer enablers for each other.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: First of all, we need to harness our people, our citizens for mutual support to be influencers as well as facilitators.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For the past two years since being a Member of Parliament at Nee Soon, I have worked closely with Yishun Health and gotten to know and see the very good efforts they created in neighbourhoods as part of their community health outreach efforts.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am very inspired by their approach and model towards health, which is to decouple it from sickness and to emphasise instead empowering the agency within the individual for wellness.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They started initiatives like Share A Pot, which Nominated Member of Parliament Janet Ang mentioned yesterday.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is a programme that taps on seniors to gather together with other seniors.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They are cooking and sharing bone broth together to strengthen their bones, to decrease their risk of frailty and risk of falls.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The other notable project is called Repair Kakis, where a group of elderly uncles come together and they provide handyman services to their neighborhood.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It was actually started by a gentleman who suffers from Parkinson's disease.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The Yishun Health team discovered that he was an aircon serviceman before and he possesses the technical knowledge and mechanical knowledge to repair appliances.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They encouraged him and he started this group.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And now, weekly, they create a session where they welcome neighbours to bring their faulty home appliances for them to repair.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I think what is really beautiful about this initiative was that it harnessed the strength of an individual, created a ripple effect and it built up this man's sense of dignity in being able to contribute to his community despite his medical condition.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I think the self-esteem that he got and the wellness that he got from such an initiative and being a contributor really, really showed him to be a positive role model amongst his peers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I also heard from the Yishun Health team that amongst these groups, there were successful cases where elderly gentlemen saw a friend of theirs pass away due to lung cancer from having been a chronic smoker.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: That prompted them to decide that they would also want to quit smoking.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In these examples, we see that it is actually the power of social relationships that worked wonders.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Often, people do not need an expert to come and tell them what to do.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: People can make good choices for themselves when they are inspired by the stories and people amongst them.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As much as I am very glad for the current plans by Healthier SG that focus on physical health, I would like to encourage MOH to work closely with other Ministries such as MSF because the social determinants of health are equally, if not even more important in upstream efforts.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Our efforts may go to waste if we neglect this critical piece.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As Woodlands Health Campus' Chief Operating Officer (COO) once shared with me a few years back in my then capacity as the executive director of Daughters of Tomorrow, many of the hospital's "frequent-flyer users" come from the lower-income segment.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They also avoid seeing the doctor because they are in jobs that are daily paid.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They work long hours or are mentally overloaded with too many chronic stresses to make healthy lifestyle choices.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Under these circumstances, the mindset that they are often beset with is, "I cannot" or "It is too difficult".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such asset-based community development initiatives help to uplift wellbeing from lifting the self-esteem and social connection of people and contribute to their socio-emotional health – a key dimension as well as determinant of physical health.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can scale up such efforts by involving and enhancing the capabilities of PA to do similar.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We already have so many grassroots activities, interest group activities, brisk walking" and so on.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But we are looking at in the A-B-C-D model is to enable residents to initiate and own the programmes themselves, thereby increasing their sense of ownership and their personal sense of agency.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Ong mentioned that the community plays a big part in this plan.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I think this would help effect a very important transformational mindset shift from our people being at the receiving end of services to them being the enablers for change in the community and within themselves.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My next point: how can we better distribute care in the system so that it is not concentrated in formal settings, which are costly to provide?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The good news is I believe we leverage the very good momentum that the COVID-19 pandemic has provided, where we see that in many parts of Singapore, neighbours are already helping neighbours, whether it is buying food, helping to fetch groceries when their neighbours are in quarantine and so on.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These acts of kindness and helping and care are already happening sporadically in a rather organic manner.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The question is – how can we be more intentional about it and grow such mutual support and care within the community more systematically?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With the team there, they have created a list of care tasks and micro-errands that do not require medical expertise for people to help with.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We are enrolling volunteers from the community to step up so that discharged elderly from the hospital can be adequately cared for and caregivers can have more support and more respite.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As we worked on this pilot, along the way, I met other initiatives in the form of social enterprises and ground-up groups that are doing the same or attempting to do the same.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Initiatives like SG Assist by amazing Singaporeans like Adrian Tan and Greg Tan as well as Denise Tay and Michelle Lau, who founded KampungKakis.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They are doing great work to excavate and pull together the human power for mutual support and caregiving in the community.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to grow the efforts of these leaders and champions for community care.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These are social entrepreneurs with hearts that care and a commitment to pledge their careers to creating solutions for society.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We should support, harness their strengths and invest in them.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I have some specific suggestions to support social enterprises to provide capability building in community care so that we can help to accelerate the de-institutionalisation of health and healthcare.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can do this for as long as before they show any positive monetary returns or profits.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Ground-up initiatives have closer experience on the ground.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Often, their interventions and services are designed with personal experience of founders or beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They can plug the last mile service gap much better than Government agencies can.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In summary, I would like to wrap up my speech to emphasis this point that aligns with the Ministry's intention for Healthier SG, which is that as individuals, we can do more to own and to take charge of our health.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To do this, we need to harness the capacities, strengths and assets of individuals amongst residents.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to invest in and grow the capacity of leaders amongst our citizens.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In so doing, we can truly bring the power of the community together and build up our citizens' agency and health by facilitating their initiative and their pioneering spirit through mutual sharing and caring activities that they start.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There is a Chinese saying, "百花齐放" – a hundred flowers bloom.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can seriously consider these proposals to nurture and fertilise the flowers to bloom in this community health and community care space.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And so, I urge MOH to set up a dedicated work group that includes MSF and MCCY to help drive Healthier SG because the social determinants of health are key if we wish to see the outcomes we want.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Hopefully, we can create, through these collective efforts, a virtuous cycle driven by the will and initiatives of our people.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The more we care and share, the healthier we get.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This a good move but there will be challenges during the implementation stage.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The general practitioners or GPs are critical to the success of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: After the release of the Healthier SG White Paper, I managed to communicate with a few GPs, including GPs who are practising in the Nanyang division.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In general, the GPs are very supportive of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While some GPs operate in residential areas and in clearly family clinics, others practise at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Those GPS who practise at the workplace are concerned that some residents or many residents would not appoint them as the primary family doctor, especially those residents above 60 years old, who are not working.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: On the other hand, some popular GPs may be overwhelmed if too many patients want them to be their primary family doctor and they have to turn people away.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Minister Ong alluded to this in his opening speech.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For Singaporeans, securing a family doctor should not be a competition.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For instance, would they take into account factors like whether the patient had visited the clinic before, or how far away the patient lives from the clinic, or on a first-come-first-served basis?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: What exactly are the factors they would have to take into account and is that a priority?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Such GPs also have questions on the need to be qualified as a family physician.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I would like to ask, does it mean that the family clinic with only doctor, the sole doctor would have to be qualified as a family physician?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, this may have profound implications for family clinics run by solo doctors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If GPs are to oversee the end-to-end journey of caring for a patient, it would be helpful if they can work with partners to deliver this care.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: According to an article from the Harvard Medical School, such GPs, who are also called primary care physicians, work in teams to keep patients at the centre of all diagnostic and treatment activities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: These teams often comprise medical assistants, nurses, pharmacists and social workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Likewise, in the Netherlands where the GP is the central figure in Dutch primary care, GPs employ salaried nurses and primary care psychologists, who can even provide mental health services.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The typical practice size is approximately 2,200 patients per full-time working GP and over 95% of the citizens are registered with one GP that they have chosen.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chronic care management is coordinated through care groups, which are mostly GP networks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: These care groups coordinate care from multiple service providers for certain chronic diseases, such as diabetes and cardiovascular conditions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Would MOH envisage the formation of such GP networks in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, would such networks be coordinated by the respective three health clusters?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Outside of the clinic, there are many touch points and community engagement opportunities with members of the public.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I heard from Minister Masagos that the healthcare cluster will coordinate with community partners and GPs to provide healthy activities for the residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: And to this end, as a Member of Parliament taking care of the Nanyang Division of West Coast GRC, I would be happy to leverage on my community partners to work with the healthcare clusters and the GPs in Nanyang to provide healthy lifestyle activities for the residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As with any change, it would take time for residents to embrace Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Preventive care requires more commitment from people to live more healthily, commit to advice from their doctors and spend time on regular health screenings.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many Nanyang residents I met and have spoken to after the release of the Healthier SG White Paper are very supportive of Healthier SG but they have also raised some concerns.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Many residents in Nanyang support Healthyier SG, but they also have some questions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: She has just changed her job, and the clinic is not on the company's list of designated clinics.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Hence, Mdm Tan cannot claim medical fees from the company for the cost of seeing the doctor at the Teo Clinic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For a common cold, Mdm Tan still needs to go to company-designated clinics.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This situation is just like what the White Paper has described on page 24.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If Mdm Tan has a choice, she would prefer to go to the Teo Clinic which she is familiar with whenever she falls ill, just like what the White Paper has recommended.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Another important aspect of Healthier SG is to encourage Singaporeans to take part in more activities that are good for their health, such as Zumba, brisk walking in parks and gardening.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To date, most of these activities are only attractive to women.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many men prefer to drink in coffee shops, eat and chitchat for a long time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It seems that we need to mobilise our men and entice them to move from drinking tables to table tennis and from eating to growing vegetables.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While this is not MOH's strength, it is an important factor in Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I hope the Minister will think about it and invest more in this area.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In English): Next, I would like to touch on another very important topic, which is the funding.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As mentioned earlier, healthy activities for the residents as coordinated by the respective health clusters are a very important component of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Earlier, I heard from Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam that they will make Healthy 365 as a very key component of the entire Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But we know that there are many other apps that are very popular with the residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, how would Healthy 365 interface with those apps that are very popular right now, like LumiHealth, so that they can be more coordinated and benefit more residents?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Ultimately, we can take inspiration from what is being done in other countries for preventive healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: A research study of primary care physicians in 10 countries including Australia, Norway, United Kingdom and Switzerland showed how patients that are managed by one primary care physician are able to view information from their medical records, and can even e-mail their doctors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While this could prove quite onerous for our GPs, it would certainly go a long way in building trust between patients and their doctors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is possible if all Singaporeans, all GPs, all Government officials and all community partners are ready to make Healthier SG as a priority for a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These include concerns on capitation funding, manpower issues across the healthcare landscape and the future evolution of the family medicine ecosystem as envisaged, amongst other points.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The upcoming changes to the healthcare system underwritten by the White Paper are significant, and in the main, the Workers' Party supports the Government's strategic shift towards preventive healthcare, important aspects of which were pre-emptively raised by Workers' Party Member of Parliament Leon Pereira in his Adjournment Motion on reviewing strategies towards preventive healthcare in February this year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My contribution to this Motion will be short and it covers an important but sometimes understated stakeholder in the public health care ecosystem, and that stakeholder are the Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) practitioners and others who are practitioners of alternative or complementary medicine.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the course of the debate, I have heard hon Members Ms Joan Pereira, Ms Hany Soh and Mr Yip Hon Weng also speak on TCM and how it interfaces with the Healthier SG White Paper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my speech today, I will make three suggestions to bridge TCM and complementary or alternative medicine as important community partners of a healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, successive health Ministers have raised hopes of alternative approaches to healthcare like TCM, which complement and integrate Western medicine.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some almost 30 years ago, in 1995, the Health Ministry accepted the recommendations of the Committee on Traditional Chinese Medicine and moved to begin regulating TCM.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Globally, under the Beijing Declaration adopted by the World Health Organization (WHO) in November 2008, Traditional Chinese Medicine was recognised as having an important role in the improvement of public health.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Acupuncture has in fact, been scientifically proven through trials recognised by WHO to be an effective treatment for more than 20 diseases and disorders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, TCM practitioners in Singapore are governed by the Traditional Chinese Medicine Practitioners Act and physicians are expected to abide by the ethical code and ethical guidelines for TCM practitioners issued by the TCM Practitioners Board which also comes under MOH.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2019, legislative changes were made to further professionalise the TCM industry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These included the introduction of continuing professional education and raising the maximum fines on errant practitioners from $10,000 to $50,000.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This hike in fines brought the TCM Practitioners Board's disciplinary powers in line with those in the dental, pharmaceutical and allied healthcare boards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is no different with non-Chinese Singaporeans resorting to TCM and alternative medicine as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, some TCM products have even been halal certified.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, as early as 2005, MOH allowed licensed hospitals and nursing homes to have full service TCM clinics, including acupuncture, tuina and herbal medicine services to be co-located on their premises on the condition that the TCM clinic was clearly distinct from conventional medical services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2018, an acupuncturist at Khoo Teck Phuat Hospital was quoted in the newspapers as saying that around 40% of her patients who sought acupuncture were non-Chinese and under the age of 25.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government, for its part, has previously allocated $3 million for the TCM Clinical Research Grant from fiscal years 2013 to 2018 to support research into chronic diseases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A further $10 million in research and development grants was also announced in 2017 as part of efforts to modernise the industry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Then Senior Minister for Health, Mr Chee Hong Tat, was quoted as saying: "After you come out of hospital, how do you help a person to get back as quickly as possible to good health?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think things like therapeutic massage actually play a very useful role." On 29 December 2020, in a significant move, MOH announced that it was extending means-tested subsidies and MediSave coverage under a pilot arrangement to support acupuncture for lower back pain and neck pain at specialist outpatient clinics in public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The pilot did not cover acupuncture used to treat other pain indications and other forms of traditional complementary and alternative medicine offered at public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the Ministry stated that it would review the expansion of the pilot to other settings in the longer term, taking into account learnings and data from this pilot.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Healthier SG may well provide the opportune platform and impetus to expand this pilot.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Suggestion one – extending use of MediSave to more procedures and allow TCM practitioners who offer them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In order to prevent abuse, a fixed and audited list of procedures and caps to limit the fees that can be charged for such procedures ought to be considered.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Additional subsidies can also be extended to Pioneer and Merdeka card holders for these procedures, many of whom resort to TCM as an important source of primary care.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Suggestion two – consider alternative and complementary medicine to lower costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, MOH should look into the cost of alternative medicine that substantively produces the same clinical outcomes as medicines and drugs disbursed by our public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2015, the then Head of the Traditional and Complementary Medicine Branch of the Primary and Community Care Division at MOH confirmed and I quote, "MOH constantly reviews the regulations and policies on TCM, taking into consideration the scientific advancements and rising standards of TCM." In similar vein and with a view to better manage costs, a review of commonly prescribed medicine which substantially produces the same clinical outcomes as complementary medicine should be undertaken on a longer-term basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be useful to understand if the Ministry or a relevant body like the Health Sciences Authority currently carries out such comparisons of clinical outcomes between Western and alternative medicine with the view to lower overall healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, I suspect more than a few in this House would have encountered cervical episodes for which traction and other specific thoracic mobility stretches are commonly prescribed through physiotherapy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, TCM also advances traction and certain stretching and mobility exercises as rehabilitative procedures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such rehabilitation is not usually just more affordable than physiotherapy sessions at many private and public healthcare facilities, but the convenience of having such options for Singaporeans within one's neighbourhood and perhaps right under one's block can ensure that patients complete their rehabilitation and live healthier and more mobile lives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Suggestion three – leverage on TCM practitioners to achieve Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In response to this, MOH arranged to meet all TCM practitioners to explain why vaccination was critical.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Like Healthier SG, prevention of long-term diseases is a core belief of TCM and complementary medicine.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And this does not start in one's senior years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Their treatment philosophy places an acute focus on prevention before a disease arises.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They advance the view that one's lifestyle is intimately related to health, which can be improved through effective mental health management, rest, a good diet and interventions based on a person's specific physical conditions, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By watching such indicators, one is well on his or her way to good health, regardless which economic strata of society one belongs to.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, the White Paper lists a number of community partners, such as AIC, Sport Singapore, the People's Association (PA) and the National Parks Board (NPB), that will empower residents to chart their own journey towards healthy and active lives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our journey to live more healthy lives, I would suggest that we should not underestimate the wide reach of the local sinsehs in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such an approach would also be consistent with the aim of successive Ministers of Health who had hoped to integrate Western medicine and TCM and alternative medicine as far as practicable, even as both branches of medicine operate in different cultural and professional milieus.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While progress in this regard appears to have been fitful so far, Healthier SG provides a new-found opportunity for TCM and alternative medicine to play a more active role in the primary healthcare space and in preventive healthcare.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For some, the reasons behind this may well be behavioural, peace of mind and more comfort dealing with a TCM practitioner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government is on record to say that TCM practitioners are an important stakeholder in Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry should consider concrete plans and strategies to include them in the country's strategic shift towards preventive healthcare as Healthier SG is fleshed out and operationalised in the months and years ahead.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry will not be starting from ground zero.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With decades of regulatory experience and periodic reviews of the TCM landscape undertaken by the TCM Practitioners Board, a dedicated effort must be undertaken, driven by the Ministry to draw on the treasure trove of alternative and complementary medicine that has been relied on by generations of Singaporeans for their well-being.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is an opportunity that should not be missed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will give a fuller response later in my closing speech.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some never even had close family members or friends to begin with.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For them, their final years can be harsh.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of them decide that in the absence of love, health is meaningless.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yes, loneliness can kill, sometimes, in the most undignified way.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But I have seen it with my own eyes that it need not be so.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The centre combines health and social care for the most vulnerable seniors living in that block of rental flats, most of whom are frail and without familial support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We took over four units of HDB studio apartments and we did up the void deck.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We got doctors and nurses from TTSH to review the health status of every senior under our care and to come up with a personal health plan.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By health plan, it means more than just doing monitoring their vitals or ensuring medical compliance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It also includes social prescription, getting them to join in regular exercises and activities, getting them to eat healthy meals together and getting them to join in the kampung downstairs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These social prescriptions were delivered by a few staff and seniors were given micro-jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We also have the assistance of community partners and volunteers from all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Both have consented for me to share their stories, but I will still mention them using pseudonyms.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, Uncle Paul, who is in the 80s.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: He has a heart that is functioning less than a quarter of what it needs to be.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: He was frequently admitted to the hospital, taking medicine was a chore because he felt hopeless about life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But when he felt the love and support of our volunteers, he decided to fight on.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With proper medications and regular reviews, his health has improved.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, even though he continues to be frail, he is energetic and cheerful.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Uncle Ong is a single, retired construction worker in his late 70s.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: He has always been independent, never troubling others for help and he never joined our activities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: He developed chronic conditions and did not take medicine regularly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One day, Uncle Ong injured his toes and it turned gangrene soon after.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The gangrene spread upwards towards the shank and he had an amputation just below his knees.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our volunteers prepared special meals for him which we brought to him daily.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Initially, Uncle Ong was uncomfortable to be "served" and "cared" for by several volunteers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But, over time, he accepted the services supported.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And now, he complies with his medication and goes for reviews.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There are many more such seniors beyond our rental blocks – in our HDB estates, in our private estates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
