text: And more importantly, I have seen first-hand how the various aspects of Healthier SG can come together – personal healthcare plans, social prescription, healthcare workers working hand-in-glove with our community partners and local volunteers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I have also seen our frail seniors, having received support and concern, take personal responsibility of their health.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Healthier SG is, indeed, the decisive shift that our healthcare system needs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But preventive health is better than curative health or rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I believe the future of preventive health can be found in the science of longevity medicine which Minister Ong Ye Kung mentioned at the end of his opening speech.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Over the last few decades, researchers have made tremendous progress in understanding the science of ageing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There is now ample evidence on how affordable preventive interventions can slow down ageing and increase our health span, which is the proportion of our lives that we spend in good health.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is now clear that a person can be much healthier than what his age suggests, with the right lifestyle and clinical intervention.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Lifestyle intervention can include things we already know very well, such as intermittent fasting or exercises.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But what is more interesting are clinical interventions – potential new supplements, existing drugs repositioned for healthy longevity and new drugs over time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And it is more and more possible to measure one's biological age through a series of biomarker tests, so that we can see the progress or the regression of our health span more clearly so that we can take better responsibility for our own health.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I would now like to make a few brief points about the implementation of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also concur with member Dr Tan Wu Meng that we must build a world- class healthcare IT system.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our family doctors must have access to quality medical history pulled from all different healthcare institutes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They need prompt and relevant information to create meaningful health plans that Singaporeans trust.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: While we have done much, much more can be done.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It would be helpful to hear concrete plans from MOH.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I certainly hope it is true for the National Healthcare Group, which serves Kebun Baru and which sees many seniors, perhaps even more than other regions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, I can understand why MOH wants to use population size as the basis for funding our healthcare clusters.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The more time we spend debating on what is the precise level of funding, the more time we lose in pivoting towards preventive care.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because being roughly correct today, is better than being precisely correct after the ship has sailed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And that MOH can also help clusters scale up particularly innovative efforts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It deserves our full support, even though there are many challenges ahead, even though it will take a decade for us to see real dividends.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My volunteers and I are also deeply committed to making Healthier SG work for Kebun Baru.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We feel this way because we understand the possibilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We will grow as many exercise and wellness groups as we can and build bridges between them and NHG.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We will create a single service directory on how to care for our seniors and we will share it with all our local partners including family doctors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We will join Ang Mo Kio GRC’s efforts to set up a dedicated helpline to serve the seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We will improve our existing local efforts on dementia, palliative care, assisted living and we will build up support groups for stroke and cancer.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker I stand in full support of the White Paper.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Family doctors, General Practitioners (GPs) will play an important role.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOH is supporting GPs to help them on board to Healthier SG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have consulted GPs extensively about this and I thank them for their time and valuable feedback.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: GPs are supportive of Healthier SG and agree with the focus on health, not illness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They have raised some concerns and suggestions on how this will be implemented.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan suggested we strengthen the integration between GPs and the healthcare clusters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our clusters will work closely with the Primary Care Networks (PCNs) to do this, developing clinical programmes for shared care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Janet Ang and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the enrolment process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Enrolment is tagged to the clinic, to enable service delivery even when a specific doctor is away or unavailable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: After enrolment, residents can still visit other clinics if needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Residents can also choose to change their enrolled clinic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For example, if your doctor leaves the clinic to join another group, you have the option to switch and enrol with your doctor's new clinic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Others may prefer the convenience of staying with the same clinic in the same location.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Ang also asked if three generations could enroll to the same doctor as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But for now, we have to consider the capacity of GPs for the enrolment process, especially early in the roll out of Healthier SG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And we will consider this approach that Ms Ang described as we open up to other age groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Mr Gerald Giam also asked about enrolment to polyclinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They will assign enrolled patients to a regular care team, so that there is one team looking after the resident for continuity of care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked if enrolled patients can use branded drugs at their own cost.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: However, the enhanced CHAS chronic drug subsidies will not apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The enhanced subsidy tier applies to a targeted list of clinically effective and cost-effective chronic drugs, which will be reviewed regularly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For drugs outside of this list, the current CHAS subsidies will still apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOH will announce more details next year, including standard safeguards and reviews to guard against excessive purchases as raised by Mr Gan Thiam Poh.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: GPs have questions about their remuneration, the design of the annual service fee, will they be penalised if patients refuse to adhere to their health plan and would some GPs be incentivised to cherry-pick patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They are also concerned about the impact on their business when drug prices are made more comparable with those at the polyclinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These points were also raised by Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Mr Gan Thiam Poh.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There will be a base rate that will differ for enrolled patients with and without chronic conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is regardless of whether the enrollees, the residents, are compliant with the health plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: On top of this base rate, additional payouts will be provided upon the completion of critical care components recommended in the GPs' care protocols and the residents' Health Plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For example, have patients with diabetes gone for their annual eye and foot screening?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, at the start, doctors will be paid not on the basis of whether the blood pressure or the blood sugar levels have come down, but whether the patient has engaged with the interventions that will help bring down the blood pressure and the blood sugar levels – at the start.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: GPs have shared that educating and encouraging Singaporeans to turn up for screening requires dedicated time and effort, and the design of the service fee addresses this and minimises the impact of cherry-picking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This new annual service fee is on top of the existing Government subsidies and the patient revenue that GPs already receive for services rendered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: GPs can also expect more revenue from these patients with the increased uptake of recommended preventive care services which will be fully subsidised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And more comparable drug prices will help patients, who may have otherwise visited polyclinics, to see their GPs instead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Taken together, all of these means that GPs will be fairly remunerated for the care that they deliver under Healthier SG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Denise Phua highlighted the plight of busy GPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We hope this set of changes will also help them gradually evolve from a volume-driven model to one with more opportunities to connect with and empower their residents for health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Gerald Giam's comments on MediSave, we have limits on the use of MediSave to ensure Singaporeans have sufficient savings to meet their various healthcare needs throughout their lifetime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to review the adequacy of each Medisave limit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOH also reviews the list of conditions on the Chronic Disease Management Programme (CDMP) regularly and has recently expanded the list to include three new conditions such as gout, allergic rhinitis and chronic hepatitis B, bringing the total to 23 conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The annual intake for family medicine has been increasing and we will continue to review the training numbers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOH has been working with the Family Medicine Training Advisory Committee and the College of Family Physicians Singapore on expanding the number of training places.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are also increasing exposure to family medicine in the undergraduate curriculum and have incorporated preventive care in all clinical modules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We conduct regular recruitment and retention efforts to reach out to overseas Singaporean medical students studying in medical schools recognised by us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We provide them with details on applying for jobs in Singapore and offer them Pre-Employment Grants to help with their school fees, in return for being bonded to work in our public sector healthcare institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We also offer, as appropriate, housemanship training positions or more senior jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our aim is to facilitate as many of them as possible to return home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In line with this, we will also consider how remote providers, without standard in-person clinic facilities, can be included.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will share more on how GPs can leverage telemedicine to offer regular check-ins for their residents under Healthier SG in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to ensure that as many GPs as possible who are on employer panels join Healthier SG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) and NTUC, employers and union leaders agree that they will need to get more of their panel GPs to join the Healthier SG programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If most panel clinics are on Healthier SG, the employee can benefit from Healthier SG benefits and employer medical benefits when they enrol with a Healthier SG provider that is on their employer's panel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If and when they change employers or retire, they can stay with the same clinic and continue to enjoy the Healthier SG benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These Healthier SG benefits will build on top of the employer medical benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Regardless of the coverage of the employer medical benefits, employees on Healthier SG will receive a free consultation on their health plan and will be encouraged to complete the free nationally recommended screening and vaccinations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: With effective preventive health, some employers may see savings in employer medical benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: SNEF has been urged to plough back these savings into other health and wellness programmes to enhance the health of employees and SNEF is supportive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the family physician requirements and how it will impact solo clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is a seven-year runway to achieve this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: PCNs support clinics in their network to achieve the requirements for Healthier SG and AIC can also provide support to clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will find ways to facilitate the participation of solo GPs in Healthier SG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Ms Joan Pereira raised concerns about the administrative burden of data submission and whether the IT systems would adequately support the work of GPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Many GPs we engaged also highlighted the importance of IT and that the systems need to be improved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will work closely with GPs and their IT vendors, this work has already started with GPs and their IT vendors, to support the enhancement of IT systems, to simplify administrative processes, improve data flows and sharing – all while ensuring data security.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The indicators that will need to be submitted for outcome tracking and remuneration have been streamlined, taking reference from existing clinical indicators that doctors would routinely document and track, in their own records, to deliver good care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We want GPs to use a Clinic Management System (CMS) that supports their daily operations well and connects to all the key public health IT systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And this then, will save them time on administration so that they can focus on the patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are working closely with the commercial CMS vendors to improve their products and strengthen their backend services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Some GPs today continue to use pen and paper services, we will provide them an interim web portal, for them or their staff to enter the essential information while they adopt a CMS and we have given them some time to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOH and AIC will continue to support GPs in this process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We want them to come on board Healthier SG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our plans will require a close collaboration among family doctors, the healthcare clusters and a wide range of service providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: However, the use of IT and record-sharing differs widely, hindering coordination and communication across partners today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Going forward, to deliver Healthier SG, we must transform how we communicate and share data for more holistic, integrated and coordinated care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar and Dr Tan Yia Swam spoke about this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One key tool will be the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: NEHR will capture summaries of patient medical records in one platform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Those healthcare workers who need it to support the clinical care that they are delivering, such as family doctors, will be able to draw from, and contribute to, a common platform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have put in place controls to restrict the access to sensitive health information to selected user groups only.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are also additional authentication processes for the sensitive health information and we audit the access to this set of information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This includes our healthcare clusters who will serve our residents as regional health managers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOH will be seeking feedback on the Bill later this year and we look forward to hearing your views.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Mariam also highlighted the importance of data analytics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to work with clusters and partners to share data and deploy such capabilities to help our residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is important therefore that we set up the NEHR, with the safeguards and obligations spelled out in the proposed Health Information Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are strengthening the IT platforms, the services and the connections across all the partners: family doctors and healthcare clusters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is with their help that we will improve the flow of data, impact health outcomes and optimise the user experience for residents and our healthcare providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I am glad that Mr Xie Yao Quan has also highlighted the importance of having sufficient IT and cybersecurity talent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: While we have built up expertise, a key challenge remains to attract and retain skilled IT professionals in a competitive market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We also hope that healthcare IT colleagues see the contribution they make and the fulfilling career they can have in transforming our system, caring for our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling suggested that more comprehensive health screening is needed as we move towards preventive health and Mr Abdul Samad further suggested more MediSave utilisation for this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We take guidance from the recommendations of the Screening Test Review Committee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This guidance is based on scientific evidence to ensure that screening tests are safe, effective and suitable for population level screening, means it applies to everyone across the population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to strike a balance, to balance the practice good preventive care, but consider what the test involves, without going overboard.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In some cases, some of the tests, some of the screening tools, are better applied to targeted population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It may be better for some cases to take a calculated, risk-based approach, to offer tests that are effective and easy to administer to high-risk groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, there are some tests which the science suggests we should apply it to the entire population and there are some tests which the science suggests we should apply to targeted population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to review emerging scientific evidence on these screening tests as well as the effectiveness of our financing models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Fundamentally, access will not be denied to those who need it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Janet Ang asked about regular eye and dental screening.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These are important, we must look after our teeth and have our eyes checked, and most of us do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The screening processes and tools are less appropriate as a mass exercise for all under the population approach for Healthier SG and again, are more suitable as targeted effort for certain groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Healthier SG is a multi-year effort, we will continue to review and include other necessary care protocols in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Meanwhile, to reassure Members of the House, regular oral health and eye screening programmes are already easily and readily available as a routine service in many settings, and we will continue to offer these.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For example, Project Silver Screen conducts check-ups for seniors at community locations for age-related decline in vision, oral health and hearing, so that they do not have to visit a clinic or hospital, and so that timely interventions can be provided.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Likewise, we would like to assure Mr Dennis Tan that there are already similar preventive dental health programmes in place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To Mr Abdul Samad's comment, there are nationally recommended health screening tests widely available at CHAS GP clinics, polyclinics and participating community providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In future, Singaporeans should go to their enrolled clinic to enjoy free screening.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Several members such as Ms Tin Pei Ling, Ms He Ting Ru, Dr Wan Rizal, Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Dennis Tan have also raised this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Good health is also about good mental health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The current planned interventions under the first phase of Healthier SG will support mental well-being.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: People have asked when will we start to look at mental well-being?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The interventions we already planned under Healthier SG, starting with our initial emphasis on eating well and regular exercise, will have a positive effect on mental health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But allow me to also highlight what we have put in place over the last few years to promote mental health and well-being, even before Healthier SG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To raise mental health awareness, we have developed MindSG, a trusted online resource portal that provides comprehensive and current information on mental health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have the redeveloped Alexandra Hospital coming up, which will provide psychiatric services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have been working closely with AIC and GP partners to have more GPs provide mental health support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The task force has reviewed our mental health needs and identified four focus areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: First, to strengthen services and family support for parents and youths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Second, to provide and improve access to quality and affordable mental health care by integrating health and social services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Third, to provide employment support for persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And four, to improve mental health literacy among the citizens and create an inclusive society for persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have completed our public consultation on the issue of Mental Health Strategy in August.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Members of the public and key stakeholders have shared their feedback, and we are now refining the recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The task force will share its findings soon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need the support of all healthcare professionals, the healthcare clusters, community partners and many more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to, and will, put in place systemic enablers for this challenging set of reform to succeed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ultimately all of us need to also play our part in taking some responsibility for own health and change our behaviours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: By working together, we can improve health for all of us.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Gerald Giam, I will take clarifications at the end of the Debate, please.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In closing, I will address the few remaining issues and then, I will then take a step back and share the broader perspective of the challenge that we are facing concerning healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Maybe I will start with – we seem to have this mood here where we talk about who made what speeches in the past.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I came into MOH about a year and a half ago, what struck me was the tremendous amount of groundwork that was done by my predecessor in laying a preventive health infrastructure, the IT system, the three clusters and all the medical protocols.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the new Health Minister, I had to speak to the senior doctors and management.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the workplan seminar, it was very daunting.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I discussed with three very learned persons, our three Director of Medical Services (DMS), Prof Kenneth Mak, Prof Benjamin Ong and Prof Tan Chorh Chuan.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I had in-depth discussion with them, discussed what was the next phase of healthcare and I think we zoomed in on preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The good thing is, so much groundwork has been laid.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On 23 May 2021, I think, I made my first speech in MOH.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One was COVID-19 – Living with COVID-19 and second was preventive care, that was when Healthier SG, was first talked about.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But really, thank you to the several Ministers before me and the whole team who laid so much groundwork.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then then we had COVID-19 closures and all that.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We did not have many events until December.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I got invited in December to an event by the TCM community and that is why I spoke to them, with the indication that if we focus on preventive care, I think it is an impetus that we can make a breakthrough and feature TCM in preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And that was how the thinking first started.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And my last two speeches about TCM, I made quite a few TCM speeches, they are all in Chinese.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The coverage has been uneven, so it is good that I have this opportunity now to explain it in English.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The two speeches I last made was quite recent, Mr Patrick Tay was there, in one of the events in September last month.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In summary, this was what I have been telling the TCM community and what we have been doing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One, MOH has always recognised the tremendous value of TCM and the benefits they have brought to the community.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I specifically always mention, during COVID-19 – and the Leader of the Opposition mentioned this as well – I personally wrote to our TCM clinicians to say: "Please advise your patients to take the vaccines." They were a great help and really helped us moved the needle in getting heartlanders to take the vaccine.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But, I also explained, we must recognise that Western medicines and TCM, they evolve very differently throughout history.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are two separate systems, complete systems with their own disciplines and their own know-how.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They may intersect at some point, they may overlap, but you cannot make one to be like the other.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Take for example, you ask a western doctor, "how do you balance the five elements of a human body to keep him healthy?" Most western doctors would profess they would not know.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have doctors in the House, I do not think you would profess that you know.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you ask a TCM doctor, "This patient need a life-saving, urgent operation, can you replace it with herbal medication?" They would say "No, go for the operation." Most TCM practitioners I know, would say that too.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think they respect each other's space, their strengths and their disciplines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When it comes to regulation, there is a fundamental difference as well.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Western medicine is a lot about research, clinical evidence, efficacy, safety.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You get the data, then, the drug, the treatment can be approved.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: TCM is passed down from generations, great-great-great-great grandfather took that and passed down to great-great-great grandfather.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today's rules mean it must be a medicine, it must be certified by HSA with clinical data.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For TCM, that is hard to come by.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What TCM is very strong in is preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: More than 2,000 years ago there was already the saying: 养生三法：“饮食有节、起居有常、不妄作劳.” Very hard to translate, but let me try.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even the literal translation does not capture the full meaning.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It means there are three key aspects to health: you eat not just in moderation, but 饮食有节 means you eat what your body requires, you go according to the seasons. 起居有常 means you have a healthy daily routine that follows the rhythm of the day, the month and the year probably, and not to over-exert your body, heart and mind.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in the area of preventive health, that is where I think Western medicine and TCM share a common understanding.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You would notice in my opening speech, I have a symmetry, where I talk about preventive care and how the other side also has been emphasising on it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Both disciplines believe that early management of risk factors and disease can stave off problems and complications later on in life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Therefore, I believe, when we focus on preventive care under Healthier SG, we hope TCM can play a role.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I do not think, as one Member suggested, I do not think we should impose the regulation of Western medicine on TCM.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is MOH's partner in the TCM community.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mrs Yu-Foo Yee Shoon has been Chairman for I think at least three terms or more, a lot of contributions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He has taken up the Chairmanship with gusto.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He understands the big shoes he has to fill, MOH's position and thinking, especially in the context of Healthier SG, and I think he understands his task as the TCM Board Chairman.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once we can feature TCM in Healthier SG, then the suggestions that the Leader of the Opposition has put forth, I think will be considered.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And there will be a certain natural forward movement in our policy thinking.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I just have one last thing before I move to another topic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is not that one is Western medicine and one is TCM, one is funded and one is not – I am not wrong.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are doctors in the House, please correct me.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Psyllium is the seed for fibre supplements, fybogel is essentially psyllium with a brand, called Fybogel.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Both are not medicine, both are dietary supplements, fibre supplements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But like all things sold in the polyclinic, including the gauze used to dress your wounds, they will all be subsidised, including supplements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But there are doctors in the House; so, please correct if I am wrong.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Ang Wei Neng, all expressed concerns that if GPs become very popular, residents can get squeezed out by the huge demand.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How many will depend on the clinic and the doctor's own judgement, how many more can he take.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it will differ from clinic to clinic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are also implementing enrolment in phases; we will prompt residents to enrol with their usual GPs, the dropdown list, your most frequented GP will be first; and we will encourage residents to enrol early and not wait.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I take comfort that we are discussing this because we are worried the demand will be overwhelming.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is in a way, a good problem.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is better than if the feedback comes back as, "We think nobody will enrol".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But if GPs are to over time accept enrolment from the entire population and help keep them healthy, they have got to shift out of some current load.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I am glad that a couple of Members have given a good suggestion.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Melvin Yong suggested for employers not to insist on workers producing medical certificates (MCs) whenever they are sick.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many common ailments like cough and cold can be managed with more rest, drinking more water and perhaps some off-the-shelf, over the counter medication, including TCM medication.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ironically, the disease where this is most practised now is COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But if we insist we want to see a GP, we queue up and see the family doctor in order to get an MC – today, a lot of people practice that – but actually it is not the best use of the doctor’s precious time and resources.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many employers already do not insist on MCs for COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Melvin Yong mentioned that our healthcare clusters today accept up to three days of sick leave without the need to produce an MC; the Civil Service grants officers up to two days for mild conditions like cough and cold.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I hope this can become a prevalent practice.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked a series of questions about our effort to substantively remove difference in drug prices, between GP clinics and polyclinics for residents enroled in Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As I said in my opening speech, the basis of subsidy for polyclinics and for CHAS in GP clinics are different.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The former, which is polyclinic, takes into account age.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But for CHAS in GP clinics, a major factor for consideration is income.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we cannot remove the differences up to the last cent and for the higher-income households, the difference may well remain in dollars.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A number of Members talked about KPIs and outcomes and there was an exchange between Mr Gerald Giam and Ms Mariam Jaafar yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Of course, we have to measure outcomes and set targets.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why we listed short-, medium-, long-term KPIs in the White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthier SG is a dynamic multi-year transformation exercise.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There will be twists, turns and uncertainties along the way.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH is having extensive discussions with clinicians and other stakeholders to set out the technical definitions and our approach to data sharing and measuring these outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And from there, we will establish the baselines of various indicators and then, determine what targets we want to achieve and by when.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While it is important to measure outcomes and targets, those who have run organisations before will know that this is not straightforward.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I used to be involved in workers' training, so I interacted a lot with HR practitioners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And HR practitioners always lament – and this is not just for Singapore, it is the whole world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They always lament employees are over-managed but under led.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because if you are manager and you are in the middle of a big change management exercise, you will likely instinctively say, what are the targets, let us measure the targets, whatever gets measured, gets done.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Hazel Poa went further to say, let us measure the targets achieved by the GPs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And if they do not achieve, clawback the service fee.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as Dr Tan Yia Swam cautioned, it is important for GPs and MOH to work together, for GPs to feel that they are integral part of this change.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar, my colleague from Sembawang, and an experienced management consultant, immediately raised a red flag.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think she has seen enough organisational changes to notice the danger of blindly chasing KPIs and targets.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because I talked about what the manager would do.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A leader that is driving the change will have a different starting point.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He or she, the starting point is, bring everyone on board, make sure everyone understands and buys into the mission in objective.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, we jointly set KPIs and targets and then do our best to achieve them in the right spirit.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we do not do that, then we are not leading.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And if in our zeal to over-manage, we penalise people for not meeting targets in the middle of a big change, that is when people become cynical and they lose heart, and then you get perverse outcomes like what Dr Lim Wee Kiak said.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Imagine if we really say to the doctors, "If you do not meet your KPI, we will claw back your service fee".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, it is very simple for the doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Number one, either I do not join Healthier SG; or two, I join, but I cherry-pick the healthy residents.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the way we look at KPIs, always, you are able to differentiate the leaders from the managers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Since we are on the topic of outcomes, I want to respond to Ms Mariam Jaafar.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She is not here today, she has to fly off for work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But she had a very thoughtful and insightful explanation of value-based care and I think it is worth responding to her.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I want to assure the House that our hospitals have already been implementing value-based healthcare through many such initiatives too.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We just did not feature them in the White Paper under Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Changi General Hospital has set up a post-acute myocardial infarction clinic to support patients in their post-heart surgery recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are many such examples and I hope Ms Mariam Jaafar and the House will be comforted that our clinicians are always thinking of better ways to deliver better clinical outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A few Members have raised the issue of capitation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I agree with Members on the benefits of capitation funding, but we are doing it step-by-step and carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I explained how we are doing it at the GP level during my opening speech by extending them a standard base fee per enrolled resident.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They still get the same budget, except that the basis of calculation has moved away from based on workload to capitation – the population that they are taking care of.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, they receive fixed capitated budgets for residents of different age bands.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For the very young, they have to do a lot more work, at a higher capitation rate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Young adults will have the lowest capitation rates and as you get older, as you need to pay more attention to their healthcare, capitation rate goes up again.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, age bands are a reasonable proxy for both workload as well as health risks.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether we can publish the rate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In any case, the annual reports and financial statements of the clusters are available, if you get them from ACRA.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clusters, in turn, will cascade down Healthier SG key performance indicators (KPIs) to all their institutions and partners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But they will not yet capitate the budgets of hospitals, polyclinics or community hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, below the clusters, healthcare institutions will still be funded the same way for now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But capitation funding is a direction we want to move towards.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a big change and we will have to study and plan each move carefully, making sure every institution, every partner is ready before we do so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When it happens, it must be accompanied by a significant granting of autonomy so that healthcare institutions can make the right-siting decisions properly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Let us take a palliative care hospice, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, we fund them through workload – same formula – but we can capitate their budget.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, a palliative care provider can receive a standard based fee for each palliative patient they take care of and then they decide which services are in the best interest of each patient, whether they should go to inpatient hospice care, home care or day care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They do not have to worry about separate funding for separate services under separate settings.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is where we have a lot of potential.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Several Members – Dr Tan Wu Meng, Dr Tan Yia Swam, Ms Mariam Jaafar, Mr Dennis Tan and Ms He Ting Ru – raised concerns about manpower and I appreciate that.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will broaden training for our healthcare workers – nurses, allied health professionals and pharmacists – so that they can take on the crucial roles alongside doctors in preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, nurses in the community will be trained in lifestyle coaching to empower residents to make good choices according to their care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Undergraduate allied health courses comprise specific modules on population health, health promotion and chronic disease management.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Mark Chay suggested some useful training for doctors on physical fitness.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think we will follow up with discussions with him on how we can improve or broaden the range of courses that doctors can go to for their continuous training.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our community pharmacists are now able to provide smoking cessation and weight management services and there are plans to train them in influenza vaccination.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But first, there must be enough people to train.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is, again, a certain narrative going around – some Members alluded to this narrative	– that hospital staff are leaving because they are overworked, attrition rate is at a record high, people are avoiding the healthcare sector and that we must do campaigns, reduce workload and raise salaries to attract more people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is the common narrative now going around.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are some elements of truth in this narrative, such as there is, indeed, a manpower crunch and hospital staff have been working very hard, especially during the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the rest is less than fully factual.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They propagate some negative energy and may not help us tackle the actual problems.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our education institutions receive many more applications than there are places.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At this number, we are attracting 4% of the student cohort into nursing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we maintain that number while cohort sizes shrink, the percentage will drift up to maybe 5% of each cohort.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That means that for every 20 local students you see in a class, one will be trained to become a nurse and they are applying.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, healthcare has a very fair share of the local talent pool, considering there are so many sectors vying for local talent.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On attrition rate – is it really at a record high?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we look at local nurses, the normal annual attrition rate every year is about 6.4%, which is not high by any industry standard.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2020, when the pandemic struck, it went down to 5.4% because many of our nurses who were planning to retire or resign, in the face of the pandemic, decided to stay and fight.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2021, there was a slight rebound to 7.4%.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2022, this year, so far, the numbers have reverted to that of normal years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There was no mass exodus of local nurses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Nurses have remained dedicated and steadfast and bravely stood their ground in the face of the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is where there is record high attrition, at least, over past few years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We know the main reason, and Dr Tan Yia Swam talked about it, which is that the pandemic has increased the demand for nurses all over the world and our foreign nurses are being poached by other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They go to New Zealand, Australia, the UK, UAE.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, if we want to tackle the manpower crunch in healthcare, the starting point is to hold on to our foreign nurses in the face of heightened international competition.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only then can we reduce the workload for all nurses, which many Members have called for.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we must be clear where our starting point is.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Remember, healthcare is one sector that is directly affected by our demographic changes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: An expanding aged population needs more healthcare and more healthcare manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A shrinking young population limits the number of new local talents that we can bring into healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Therefore, if we are honest with ourselves, we know the numbers simply will not add up if we just rely on local nurses or local manpower, no matter how hard we try to expand the local pipeline.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Therefore, if we want to take care of our seniors and the sick, if we want to reduce the workload of healthcare workers or at least make it more manageable, we must expect foreign healthcare workers to play a bigger role in the coming years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is especially so in areas where there is a more severe manpower crunch, such as aged care or palliative care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The great majority of our nursing workforce will still be locals but the number and role of foreign nurses will need to grow.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH is, therefore, securing various pipelines of good foreign healthcare workers from different source countries to bring them here and further train and develop them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some may leave us after a few years but we will try to keep the majority, especially those who have become an integral part of our care teams.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Tan Yia Swam suggested granting the good performers PR and MOH is supportive of this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: ICA always assesses PR applications holistically, including taking into account the economic and social contribution of the applicants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, when it comes to evaluating applications from foreign healthcare workers, ICA will certainly consider the important contributions of healthcare workers and MOH's support for the applicants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At this juncture, Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to say a few words to our healthcare workers through you.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I believe the great majority of Singaporeans respect and appreciate our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have seen the outpouring of public support in the recent past for the sacrifices made by frontliners as they steadfastly battled the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, many of our healthcare workers have also experienced abuse by patients and family members who lashed out at them because hospitals and clinics are high-stress environments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I hope that our healthcare workers will look past a small minority that show disrespect and have faith that the great majority salute you, which includes everyone in MOH.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I believe I speak for every one, every Member of this House, that we, too, respect them and their work, whether they are men or women, young or old, locals or foreigners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Abuse against healthcare workers cannot and should not go unaddressed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We hope to raise public awareness on abusive behaviour that should be stopped and equip healthcare workers to better handle such situations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By 2030, the old will outnumber the young in the world – the first time in recorded human history.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: East Asia, in particular, is ageing faster than any other region in the world due to declining fertility and people living longer lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Within East Asia, the countries ageing the fastest are Japan, South Korea and Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For schools, shrinking student intakes, which is why MOE has to merge schools and some of us find our alma maters gone.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Within communities, we have to make sure estates are now barrier-free.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At traffic light junctions, the green man will have to appear longer because people take longer to cross the road.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you are a driver, you will have to slow down in the HDB estates and we already have silver zones.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For families, more and more couples will find that they have to take care of two sets of aged parents, in addition to their own children.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the healthcare sector, we see rising disease burden and escalating demand for hospitals, clinics, doctors, nurses, budget and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most importantly, the seniors themselves, as they see more of them, they will be asking, "How do I live purposefully and healthily, with dignity, in my old age?" Mr Henry Kwek, Ms Tin Pei Ling, Miss Cheng Li Hui and Ms Carrie Tan raised these concerns and, importantly, they warned us of the danger of isolation of seniors and the importance of social contacts for seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, let me just address the implications on healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can manage this, provided we stay healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of us, myself included, are guilty of being caught in the old mould where life stages are determined by age – five years old, go preschool; 12 years old, take PSLE; 20-plus, graduate; by then, roughly, you should find a boyfriend or girlfriend and apply for BTO; late 20s, get married; 50s, beware of onset of chronic illness; 60-plus, retire; beyond 80, you may start to become frail.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The age markers remain relevant and can continue to guide us in understanding life stages, key events and risks throughout our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we need not be strait-jacketed by them, especially when it comes to health and ageing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, there is no reason why 50s has to be the onset of chronic illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can stay healthy and not have chronic illnesses in our 50s.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is no reason why once you cross 65, you go into the wrong side of the dependency ratio.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is also no reason that why being in our 80s must be associated with frailty.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can delay it as long as you can, well into your 80s or 90s.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Policy planners will continue to monitor the statistics based on age, but as individuals, we can choose to differ from these widely accepted assumptions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And the Government can make policy changes and reform our systems to help individuals achieve that.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To do so, we need to recognise now that the healthcare system is not one system, but three interconnected systems, working together to deliver good outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first system is the acute care system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is what typically comes to mind when we think of the healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It comprises hospitals, specialist clinics, emergency departments – the places that treat us and cure us when we are very sick.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are expanding this system, building more acute and community hospitals in the coming years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second system, less known, is the public health system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One important part of the public health system is the control of infectious diseases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we can see these systems springing to rigorous action during the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The other important part of the public health system is the one that improves the health of our population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This comprises the policies and processes for preventive care, including the network of family doctors, their long-lasting relationships with residents, the practice of regular health screening, the culture of good lifestyle habits, all of which keep a people healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the system that we are now building and strengthening through Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have seen how the two systems complement each other during COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The public health system strengthened the surveillance of the virus, got people to adopt good hygiene habits, received vaccinations, stayed home if unwell.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The acute care system took care of those who got infected and experienced more severe symptoms.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But still, the two systems are not enough.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In an ageing society like ours, the third system is equally critical and that is the aged care system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the support system for the large segment of people who are advancing in age.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this system is not only about nursing homes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The nursing homes, they serve an important purpose, which is to care for seniors who are very frail and unable to live independently, whose families cannot support them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am sure we need them as our population ages, but the projected pace of expansion is worrying.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In our Asian culture, we value caring for our seniors at home.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our seniors also prefer to age in a familiar environment and we should not lose this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a society, we must guard against the assumption that seniors will always become sick and frail, and unable to take care of themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is quite a risky mindset because it will exacerbate our challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because over time, society will, perhaps unintentionally, push more older people to become isolated – which many Members have warned us of.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Let us say, a senior went marketing in a wet market and then he fell.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The family may, to protect him, tell him, "Do not go out anymore, we will hire a domestic helper to watch after you." Or a senior cooks forgot to switch off the stove, and fortunately, it was discovered early.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The family may tell her, "Do not cook anymore, we order in for you, every meal." We might do all these out of concern for our loved ones, but in so doing, we deprive them of physical activity, a sense of agency, a sense of dignity.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We want to protect them, but we unintentionally expose them to an even greater risk of isolation and loneliness.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is when the spirit wears out, the body gives way.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If that mindset becomes entrenched, then over time, seniors become a problem to be contained, put aside in nursing homes – out-of-sight, out-of-mind.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is like a room in your house, where you put all your problems and you do not want to see.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must support as many seniors as possible to continue to live in the community, independently or with some help, contributing to the best of their ability, able to choose their own activities, having a full social life with friends and family.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I visited Block 115 that Mr Henry Kwek talked about.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must maintain or improve that share and not inadvertently give them the equivalent of 15 cigarettes a day, and weaken their health and ability to live independently.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For the large majority of seniors, what they need most is social care, more than healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The way to deliver that is to enable ageing in communities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will need a range of solutions to anchor ageing in communities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These include building more Community Care Apartments that Second Minister Masagos Zulkifli talked about, on releasing land for private assisted-living facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the greatest asset for managing ageing is actually right before us – and that is our HDB estates.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most estates already have ample shared spaces for interaction and activities, you got your void deck, your coffeeshop, your supermarket, your RC centre, our Eldercare Centre, your community clubs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are working closely with AIC to provide training opportunities for our centres to take on an expanded role under Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a social worker told me, a very effective initiative is to simply bring the seniors to that shared space to cook and enjoy a meal together and once they eat together, they socialise, they start doing different kinds of activities together.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is no risk of forgetting to switch off your stove and we will definitely improve the way the Eldercare Centres work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As suggested by Ms Janet Ang, for those who are in their last lap of their health journey, we are expanding palliative care, especially at home, to allow our loved ones to pass on as comfortably and with as much dignity as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the wish of most seniors and we should try our best to fulfil it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When all three systems – acute care system, public health system, aged care system – work together synergistically, healthcare happens everywhere and not just in medical facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I thank Dr Tan Wu Meng for sharing the story of Ah Ma, and pointing out that the healthcare subsidy should not be tied to services being delivered in brick-and-mortar facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will naturally have to be reviewed as we shift our paradigm.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some countries may place a stronger emphasis on just one of the three systems or organise them in a way that they end up working in silo.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, Japan, as a super-ageing society, has a great focus on aged and institutional care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The US acute care system is state-driven, but public health is driven at the federal level.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Acute care, public health, aged care, all come under MOH.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Minister for Health, is also the Minister in-charge of ageing issues and chairs a multi-Ministry task force going beyond healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this is an important advantage for us.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH is in a position to develop a cogent and comprehensive plan, muster resources to transform and fire up all three systems, to deliver health outcomes for our people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need all stakeholders – doctors, community partners, healthcare clusters, employers, residents – to join us in this effort, to shape a healthier Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We do this for ourselves, we do this for each other.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We have had a healthy debate over two days.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: This will also allow MOH's officeholders to further explain MOH's priorities.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: In the interest of time, Members are invited to ask short clarifications, please.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also want to thank Minister for recognising the challenge that my Clementi resident, Ah Ma, went through, the family had asked me to tell her story and I am glad that the difficulties she and her family went through, have been recognised and will be looked at by MOH.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have a clarification to ask about how we support residents and patients who are in the frail stage of their health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These are residents who may have a number of medical conditions, who are not quite so ill that they may need to be admitted or have to go to a care home, but not quite in the pink of health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And they often have many medical conditions, with many, many follow-ups.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will try our best to streamline the procedures, but without belaboring what I have just said in my closing speech, frailty, we may see it as a permanent condition but they can improve.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if you ask Mr Henry Kwek, in his Block 115, people have improved.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They saw seniors who could not walk, you create that common space in that block.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First step, make sure they stick to their medication; take their medication; gradually, they improve; then, give them better food, social connections with nutrition and confidence interacting with people; they actually become better, even though they are in their 80s.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think Mr Henry Kwek can tell more of that story.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We see in Kampung Wellness that Ms Carrie Tan spoke about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, without belabouring the point, I think there is a lot of potential we can do for the current generation of aged, ageing in community's social care, including healthcare, can improve their health and push back frailty as long as possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the younger group, Healthier SG – postpone frailty as long as we can, make sure our healthy life is as long as our biological life.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a minor point to clarify the query the Minister raised about the particular product I was referring to, psyllium husk.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think Minister will understand why I had some trouble when I identify the name it is marketed under because the box says, Telephone Brand (Sat-Isabgol) Psyllium Husk.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And so this product is produced in Gujarat, that means, as the Minister said, substantively the same product as Fybogel.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And Fybogel, as we know, is commonly prescribed especially after invasive surgical procedures where individuals may suffer from constipation.
